example_sentence: The children picked blackberries along the hedgerow all afternoon. Blackberry jam is a favourite spread in our house. Wild blackberries ripen in late summer here. She stained her fingers while eating fresh blackberries.

english_meaning: The act of demanding money or favors by threatening to reveal damaging information. To extort someone by using threats of exposure. Pressure applied to force someone into doing something against their will. Money or advantage obtained through such threats. To coerce someone through fear of disclosure.
example_sentence: He was arrested for trying to blackmail a politician. She refused to give in to blackmail. The letters were used as a form of blackmail. Blackmail is a serious criminal offense.

english_meaning: A period when electrical power goes out. Temporary loss of consciousness or memory. Suppression of information, especially by authorities or media. Loss of visibility, especially at night due to lights being turned off
example_sentence: The city experienced a blackout during the storm. She suffered a blackout after the accident. The government imposed a media blackout before the announcement. During wartime, coastal towns had to enforce blackouts at night.

english_meaning: A person whose work is making and repairing things from iron by heating and hammering the metal. A craftsman who forges tools, horseshoes, gates, and other iron objects. A skilled worker who shapes hot metal on an anvil. An artisan working with iron in a forge.
example_sentence: The village blacksmith made horseshoes for the farmers. My grandfather worked as a blacksmith all his life. The blacksmith heated the iron rod until it turned red. A skilled blacksmith can shape almost anything from iron.

english_meaning: It refers to trivial, meaningless, or boring talk or chatter. It is used as an interjection to substitute for predictable, tedious, or unimportant details in a conversation. It describes filler or placeholder content when the actual words are considered irrelevant or self-evident.
example_sentence: She kept going on about her daily routine and blah blah until I stopped listening. Instead of giving us concrete facts, the presenter just gave us a lot of corporate blah blah. The contract was full of legal terms, safety clauses, and blah blah that nobody really read. He told me he was busy with work, meetings, and blah blah, but I knew he just wanted to stay home.

english_meaning: To hold someone responsible for something bad that has happened. To say that a fault or wrong is caused by a particular person or thing. Responsibility for a mistake or offence. Criticism directed at someone for a fault.
example_sentence: Don't blame me for the delay. She was quick to blame the weather for the poor harvest. He accepted full blame for the accident. The blame lies with the management, not the workers.

english_meaning: Free from any fault or guilt. Not deserving criticism or accusation. Leading an innocent and upright life.
example_sentence: The inquiry found the driver entirely blameless. He led a blameless life in the village. Nobody in this dispute is completely blameless. Her conduct throughout was blameless.

english_meaning: To make white or pale by extracting color. To grow suddenly pale from shock, fear, or a strong negative emotion. To briefly boil food, especially vegetables, in water or steam to shrink them or carefully remove their skins.
example_sentence: He blanched visibly and stumbled back when he heard the terrible news. You always need to blanch the fresh tomatoes briefly before peeling them for the sauce. Her expression blanched with pure terror as the shadow moved deliberately across the dark room. The bitter cold winter air rapidly blanched the sensitive tips of his weary fingers.

english_meaning: A sweet, creamy dessert typically thickened with cornstarch or gelatin and flavored with vanilla or almonds. It is usually molded into a specific shape before being chilled. A dish that traditionally used milk or cream as its primary liquid base. Sometimes used metaphorically to describe something that is soft, white, and lacks a firm structure or substance.
example_sentence: She prepared a delicate vanilla blancmange for the dinner party guests. The chef carefully unmolded the almond-flavored blancmange onto a silver platter. After the heavy main course, a light blancmange served with raspberry sauce was a perfect choice. The writer criticized the politician's speech, calling it a sugary blancmange of empty promises.

english_meaning: Lacking strong features or characteristics and therefore uninteresting. Unpleasantly tasteless or dull when referring to food. Showing no strong emotion or reaction. Mild and soothing in effect or nature. Lacking in stimulation or excitement. Lacking a distinctive or noticeable flavor.
example_sentence: The hospital food was incredibly bland and needed more salt. He gave a bland smile that didn't reach his eyes. The interior of the office was decorated in bland shades of beige and grey. The diplomat gave a bland statement to avoid any controversy.

english_meaning: Flattering or coaxing words or actions intended to persuade someone to do something. The use of gentle language to influence or entice a person. A series of complimentary remarks designed to win favor or gain an advantage. Artful expressions of praise that often lack genuine sincerity. Enticements or allurements used to overcome resistance or gain cooperation.
example_sentence: Despite his persuasive blandishments, the committee refused to change its mind on the budget. She was immune to the salesman's blandishments and insisted on seeing the product's flaws. The politician used various blandishments to win over the skeptical voters during the rally. The manager relied on blandishments rather than threats to improve the morale of his team.

english_meaning: A lack of strong flavor or zest in food or drink. The quality of being uninteresting, dull, or lacking distinctive character. A gentle or soothing manner that lacks intensity or emotion. The state of being mild and non-irritating to the senses. An absence of excitement or stimulation in an environment or experience. A characteristically flat or monotonous presentation.
example_sentence: The blandness of the hospital food made the patient lose his appetite entirely. Critics often complained about the blandness of the protagonist's personality in the novel. The room was decorated with a deliberate blandness to avoid distracting the office workers. There was a certain blandness in his voice that suggested he was hiding his true frustration.

english_meaning: Displaying a lack of strong characteristics or flavors. Characterized by being uninteresting or dull in nature. Having a mild or soothing effect on the senses or temperament. Lacking in distinctive flavor or zest. Being overly gentle or non-provocative in a way that suggests a lack of personality.
example_sentence: The soup was rather blandy and required much more salt. He gave a blandy smile that hid his true frustrations. The documentary offered a blandy perspective on a very complex political issue. Her choice of decor was somewhat blandy and lacked any personal touch.

english_meaning: A complete ban that applies to everyone or everything without any exceptions. A total and unconditional prohibition applied broadly to all people, places, or situations.
synonyms: ["Total ban","Complete prohibition","Absolute ban","Across the board ban"]
example_sentence: The government imposed a blanket ban on plastic bags across the country. The university announced a blanket ban on mobile phone use during exams. A blanket ban on protests was enforced due to security concerns. The company placed a blanket ban on overtime work to reduce costs.

english_meaning: In a way that shows no understanding, expression, emotion, or awareness. Staring without focus, comprehension, or any visible reaction. Done or said in a dull, empty, or expressionless manner. Responding without any clear thought, recognition, or feeling.
example_sentence: She stared blankly at the screen, unable to process what she had just read.  He looked at her blankly when she mentioned the meeting they had clearly discussed before.  The child gazed blankly out of the window, lost in thought.  When asked for his opinion, he simply smiled blankly.  She responded blankly to the question, clearly exhausted after the long shift.

english_meaning: Clever, flattering, or persuasive talk that may be used to mislead or charm someone. Smooth-talking or skillful use of exaggerated compliments and flattery to get what one wants. A type of charming but often insincere speech, typically associated with Irish folk tradition and the legend of the Blarney Stone. To talk in a flattering, coaxing, or mildly deceptive way.
example_sentence: He was full of blarney, always managing to talk his way out of trouble.  She laughed and said his speech was pure blarney from start to finish.  The salesman's blarney eventually convinced her to buy a product she did not need.  People say that kissing the Blarney Stone grants you the gift of blarney.  Despite knowing it was blarney, she found herself charmed by his words.

english_meaning: To launch into the air or space, often used for rockets or spaceships.
example_sentence: The rocket blasted off successfully. They watched the shuttle blast off. The fireworks blasted off at midnight. The plane blasted off into the sky.

english_meaning: Completely obvious, conspicuous, and undisguised, especially in a negative or shameless way. Done openly and without any attempt at concealment, often in violation of rules or expectations. Glaringly noticeable, leaving no doubt about its nature. Often used to describe lies, disregard for rules, or wrongdoing that is shockingly obvious.
example_sentence: His blatant disregard for the rules angered the entire team.  The advertisement was a blatant attempt to mislead consumers.  She told a blatant lie right in front of everyone.  The blatant unfairness of the decision sparked widespread protests.  It was a blatant case of plagiarism that could not be denied.

english_meaning: In a completely open and shameless way. Very obviously, without any attempt to hide. In a loud or brash manner. Clearly and undeniably. In a way that is impossible to ignore.
example_sentence: He blatantly ignored the traffic signal. She blatantly lied in front of everyone. The rules were blatantly violated during the match. The advertisement blatantly copied another brand's design.

english_meaning: A person who talks at great length without making much sense. Someone who speaks foolish or nonsensical talk. Foolish, empty or long-winded talk itself. A babbling, boastful and tiresome talker.
example_sentence: The old blatherskite talked for an hour without saying anything useful. Ignore that blatherskite; he never knows what he is talking about. The meeting was ruined by the blatherskite in the front row. His speech was pure blatherskite from beginning to end.

english_meaning: To burn brightly or intensely. To shine with intense light. To display something vividly or show passion/energy. A large, strong flame or fire. A brilliant display of light or color. An intense outburst of emotion.
example_sentence: He rushed back into the blazing house. The sun blazed down from a clear blue sky. The campfire blazed through the night. Her eyes blazed with anger. The team blazed a new trail in science. Flames blazed across the forest.

english_meaning: To cut or mark a path through a forest or wilderness for others to follow. To be a pioneer in a particular field or activity by performing a new and significant action. To initiate a completely new development that creates a precedent for future progress. To lead the way in establishing a new method or technique where none existed before. To mark trees with notches or paint to indicate a specific route through uncharted territory. To act as a vanguard for a social or political movement through bold innovation. To demonstrate a successful way of doing something that serves as a guide for successors. To break ground in a scientific or intellectual pursuit through original research. To open up new opportunities or regions for others through one's primary efforts. To establish a new standard or tradition in a creative or professional endeavor.
example_sentence: She decided to blaze a trail for women in the male-dominated field of aerospace engineering. The explorers had to blaze a trail through the dense jungle using only their machetes. His groundbreaking research on renewable energy will blaze a trail for future scientists to follow. The company continues to blaze a trail in the tech industry with its innovative software solutions.

english_meaning: To do something in a new and independent way without following others. To act independently and create a unique path in life, career, or ideas. It often refers to someone who is innovative, courageous, and willing to take risks instead of copying what others do.
example_sentence: She decided to blaze her own trail and start a business instead of taking a regular job. Rather than following trends, he always blazes his own trail in fashion. The scientist blazed her own trail in research and made groundbreaking discoveries. Young entrepreneurs today are eager to blaze their own trail in the digital world.

english_meaning: Cold, empty, or not promising, depressing or discouraging. Something that is bare, exposed, or lacking in warmth or hope. It can describe weather, landscapes, situations, or moods that seem harsh, hopeless, or discouraging.
example_sentence: The town looked bleak after the storm. He felt bleak about his chances of getting the job. The landscape was bleak and empty, with no trees in sight. She gave a bleak smile, hiding her disappointment.

english_meaning: To make the typical crying sound of a sheep or goat. To complain in a weak, repetitive, or annoying way. The sound made by a sheep or goat.
example_sentence: The lambs bleated loudly in the field. He kept bleating about how unfair the rules were. Cows low and calves bleat when separated. A frightened sheep bleated loudly as the dog ran toward it. Instead of taking action, he just bleated about his problems.

english_meaning: To lose blood from the body as a result of injury, illness, or a medical procedure. To draw blood from a person or animal, either medically or as a result of harm. To gradually lose money, resources, or vitality over time, especially in a slow and damaging way. Used in printing to describe an image or color that extends to the very edge of a page with no margin.
example_sentence: The wound on his hand continued to bleed despite the pressure applied.  The prolonged legal battle caused the company to bleed money for years.  First aid training teaches you how to stop a wound from bleeding.  The design required the image to bleed off the edge of the page.  Her heart bled for the families who had lost everything in the disaster.

english_meaning: To spoil, damage, or make something imperfect in appearance, quality, or reputation. A mark, spot, stain, scar, or defect that reduces beauty, perfection, or reputation. It can refer to a physical mark on skin or an object, or a moral fault that damages someone's image.
example_sentence: The small scar on his cheek was the only blemish on his face. A stain on the carpet became a noticeable blemish in the room. The scandal left a serious blemish on the company’s reputation. Scratches can blemish the surface of a new car.

english_meaning: To mix two or more substances together. To form a mixture with something. To combine with something in an attractive or effective way, to combine something in this way. To produce something by mixing different types together. A mixture of different types of the same thing. A pleasant or useful combination of different things.
example_sentence: Blend the flour with the milk to make a smooth paste. Blend together the eggs, sugar and flour. Oil does not blend with water. The old and new buildings blend together perfectly. Their music blends traditional and modern styles. The barman prepared a cool blend of tropical fruit juices. We offer several different blends of freshly ground coffee. This charming hotel is a delightful blend of the old and the new.

english_meaning: To mix or fit smoothly with surroundings or a group so as not to be noticed.
example_sentence: She tried to blend in at the party by wearing casual clothes. The new student struggled to blend in with the classmates. The building’s design blends in with the surrounding architecture. Camouflage paint helps soldiers blend in with the forest.

english_meaning: To gradually merge or become part of something else. To become similar to or indistinguishable from the surroundings or group; to merge naturally without drawing attention
example_sentence: The new employee tried to blend into the team quietly. The chameleon can blend into its surroundings easily. The colors of the painting blend into each other smoothly. She blended into the crowd to avoid being noticed.

english_meaning: To gradually fade or remove something, usually in audio, visual, or general context.
example_sentence: The sound of the drums was blended out at the end of the track. In the video, the bright colors blended out to black. He tried to blend out his nervousness during the presentation. The chef blended out the strong spices with cream.

english_meaning: To combine different substances, ingredients, or elements until they form a uniform mixture. It is often used in cooking (making smoothies, sauces, soups) but can also be metaphorical for combining ideas or styles seamlessly.
example_sentence: She blended up the fruits to make a fresh smoothie. The chef blended up the spices before adding them to the curry. You need to blend up the ingredients until smooth. The designer blended up traditional and modern styles in the collection.

english_meaning: A plant disease, especially one caused by fungi or bacteria, that causes plants to wither, decay, or die. Something that has a severely damaging or destructive effect on a person, place, or situation. To cause harm, damage, or ruin to something, preventing it from developing or thriving. Urban blight refers to the deterioration of buildings and neighborhoods in a city.
example_sentence: The potato blight of the 1840s caused widespread famine across Ireland.  Urban blight had left many buildings in the neighborhood abandoned and decaying.  Unemployment can blight an entire community for generations.  The disease blighted his career at the very moment it was reaching its peak.  Scientists developed new crop varieties resistant to the devastating wheat blight.

english_meaning: To shut and open the eyes quickly. To flash on and off, as a light does. To hesitate or pause (figuratively). The natural, quick closing and opening of the eyes.
example_sentence: She blinked when the bright light flashed in her eyes. The red light on the tower blinked every second. Don’t blink, or you’ll miss the shooting star. He didn’t blink even when he heard the shocking news.

english_meaning: To remove tears or moisture from the eyes by blinking. To try to clear one's vision or drive away sleepiness by blinking repeatedly. To push aside an emotion or thought by blinking, as if refusing to show it.
example_sentence: She blinked away her tears and smiled at the guests. He blinked away the dust that had blown into his eyes. The driver blinked away his sleepiness and kept going. She quickly blinked away the memory and carried on.

english_meaning: To hold back tears by blinking the eyes. To stop oneself from crying by blinking rapidly. To restrain an emotion from showing in the eyes.
example_sentence: He blinked back tears as he read the letter. She blinked back her tears and thanked the audience. The boy blinked back tears after losing the race. He blinked back the emotion and continued speaking.

english_meaning: To be the one who gives in, surrenders, or backs down first during a confrontation or stand-off. To show weakness or hesitation before the opponent does. Used especially in tense negotiations or political and military stand-offs.
example_sentence: Neither leader wanted to blink first during the long negotiations. In a price war, the smaller company usually blinks first. The general warned his soldiers not to blink first on the battlefield. In the diplomatic stand-off, no country was willing to blink first. He stared at his rival and refused to blink first.

english_meaning: To stop shining or go dark, especially of a light or indicator. To switch off suddenly or after a flicker.
example_sentence: The indicator blinked off as soon as charging finished. The lights blinked off and the hall went dark. His computer screen blinked off without warning. The sign blinked off at exactly midnight.

english_meaning: To begin to shine or light up, often suddenly or with a flicker. To become active or start working, especially of a light or display.
example_sentence: The warning light blinked on as the engine started. A small green lamp blinked on inside the machine. The screen blinked on after he pressed the button. Street lights blinked on all along the road.

english_meaning: To stop shining or working suddenly, especially of a light. To fade out or disappear after flickering. Of a signal or screen, to go dark or cease abruptly.
example_sentence: The street lamp blinked out in the middle of the night. One by one the stars blinked out as dawn broke. The screen blinked out during the presentation. His torch blinked out and left them in darkness.

english_meaning: A device that blocks side vision. A flashing light on a vehicle that shows turning direction. A person or idea that limits open thinking. Pieces of leather or plastic placed beside a horse’s eyes to prevent it from seeing sideways, helping it stay focused. A narrow or limited viewpoint that prevents someone from seeing the full situation.
example_sentence: His blinkers stopped him from understanding the issue. Remove your blinkers and look at the facts. The teacher told him not to have blinkers on. Blinkers can make you narrow-minded. He turned on the blinker before changing lanes.

english_meaning: Having a narrow or limited outlook; unwilling to consider other views. Restricted in understanding because of prejudice or fixed ideas. Of a horse, wearing blinkers that limit side vision.
example_sentence: His blinkered approach to the problem annoyed his colleagues. Such blinkered thinking will only harm the company. She criticised the blinkered attitude of the committee. The blinkered horse trotted calmly through the traffic.

english_meaning: Opening and closing the eyes quickly. Flashing on and off, as a light does. Used in informal British English as a mild word to express annoyance. Extremely, used for emphasis in informal speech.
example_sentence: He sat blinking in the bright sunlight. A blinking red light warned us of the fault. Where is that blinking key I left here? The blinking cursor waited on the empty screen.

english_meaning: A thin pancake, usually filled with cheese or fruit, then folded and fried. A traditional dish of Jewish and Eastern European cuisine.
example_sentence: She served warm cheese blintzes with sour cream. My grandmother made blintzes every holiday morning. The café is famous for its blueberry blintz. He learned to fold a blintz without tearing it.

english_meaning: A small spot of light on a radar or electronic screen. A short high-pitched electronic sound. A brief and usually unimportant change or interruption in a trend. A minor problem that does not last long.
example_sentence: A faint blip appeared on the radar screen. The machine gave a soft blip every few seconds. Last month's fall in sales was only a blip. Officials described the delay as a temporary blip in the schedule.

english_meaning: Perfect happiness and great joy. A state of deep peace and contentment. Spiritual joy or heavenly happiness. To experience or cause a feeling of pure delight.
example_sentence: Their first year together was pure bliss. He closed his eyes in bliss as the music began. A quiet Sunday morning at home is my idea of bliss. The poem describes the bliss of the faithful in paradise.

english_meaning: To enter a state of complete happiness and relaxation. To become blissfully unaware of one's surroundings. To make someone feel deeply calm and contented.
example_sentence: She likes to bliss out with music after a long shift. The warm bath completely blissed him out. They blissed out on the beach for the whole afternoon. A good massage will bliss you out in minutes.

english_meaning: A small swelling on the skin filled with fluid, usually caused by burning, rubbing, or infection. A raised bubble-like spot on a surface such as paint or metal. To develop blisters or to cause blisters to form due to heat, friction, or pressure.
example_sentence: Tight shoes can cause painful blisters on the feet. A blister formed on his hand after working in the garden. The hot iron left a blister on her finger. Sunburn often leads to blisters on exposed skin. Old paint on the wall began to blister in the sun.

english_meaning: To attack suddenly and with great force, or to carry out a fast and intensive effort to complete something. A sudden, fast, and intense attack or concentrated effort to achieve something quickly.
example_sentence: The city faced a heavy air blitz during the war. The team organized a marketing blitz before the product launch. The workers did a weekend blitz to finish the project. The defense called a blitz to pressure the quarterback.

english_meaning: Overwhelmed or defeated by a sudden and powerful attack. Very drunk or heavily intoxicated. Subjected to a blitz, especially the German aerial bombing campaigns of the Second World War. Completely overwhelmed with work, activity, or a sudden rush of something.
example_sentence: The city was blitzed during the Second World War and had to be rebuilt.  He came home completely blitzed after the office party.  The team was blitzed in the first half of the match.  She was blitzed with emails the moment she returned from her holiday.  The enemy positions were blitzed before the ground troops advanced.

english_meaning: An intense, swift, and overwhelming military attack designed to defeat the enemy quickly using fast-moving forces. Any sudden, forceful, and concentrated effort or campaign aimed at achieving rapid results. The word originated in the German military strategy of World War II but is now used broadly for any rapid and powerful offensive.
example_sentence: The German army used blitzkrieg tactics during World War II. The company launched a marketing blitzkrieg to capture the market. The opposition faced a political blitzkrieg from the ruling party. The team's blitzkrieg in the first half secured them the victory. Their blitzkrieg of questions left the witness confused.

english_meaning: A storm with widespread snowfall accompanied by strong winds. A snowstorm with very strong winds. A large quantity of things that may seem to be attacking you. A large amount of something that arrives or is produced together in a confusing or badly organized way. A series of unexpected and unpleasant occurrences.
example_sentence: The blizzard struck the north-east yesterday, causing serious damage. A blizzard of documents. We once got stuck in a blizzard for six hours. Blizzard conditions made the main roads almost impassable. Their trip was delayed by a week because of a blizzard.

english_meaning: To cause something to swell or expand, especially with gas or liquid, in an unpleasant or uncomfortable way. To become swollen or puffed up in size, often due to gas, water retention, or excess food. Used figuratively to describe something becoming unnecessarily large, excessive, or inefficient. A condition in which the body or stomach becomes swollen and distended.
example_sentence: Eating too quickly can cause your stomach to bloat uncomfortably.  The bureaucracy had bloated over the years with unnecessary administrative layers.  The software update caused the file size to bloat significantly.  He suffered from bloat after eating a large meal late at night.  The company's costs began to bloat as management kept hiring without oversight.

english_meaning: Swollen with fluid, gas, or food. Uncomfortably full or distended. Made excessively large, complicated, or costly. Containing unnecessary features, words, staff, or expenses. Filled beyond a healthy or reasonable level.
example_sentence: I felt bloated after the heavy meal. The river carried the bloated carcass downstream. The report was bloated with unnecessary detail. Users complained that the update made the software slow and bloated.

english_meaning: A thing that is swollen or enlarged. A herring that has been lightly salted and smoked whole. A person or thing considered excessively large or inflated. In computing, software or a file that has become unnecessarily large.
example_sentence: The fishmonger sold bloaters for breakfast. A traditional bloater has a strong smoky flavor. Developers called the oversized program a bloater. The dead fish became a bloater in the summer heat.

english_meaning: Software that uses excessive storage, memory, or processing power. Unwanted software preinstalled on a device. A program overloaded with unnecessary features. Software that has grown inefficiently large and complicated.
example_sentence: I removed the manufacturer’s bloatware from my new laptop. Too much bloatware can slow a phone down. The update turned a simple tool into frustrating bloatware. Users wanted a clean installation without bundled bloatware.

english_meaning: A group of countries, parties, or people that have formed an alliance to act together for a common purpose. A united group working toward shared political, economic, or social goals. A combination of members joined by common interests or ideology.
example_sentence: The European bloc issued a joint statement on the crisis. The two countries formed a trade bloc to boost exports. The voting bloc played a decisive role in the election. A new political bloc emerged after the summit.

english_meaning: A large solid piece of hard material such as rock, stone, or wood. An obstacle that makes movement or progress difficult. A group of buildings bounded by four streets in a city. The action of stopping or obstructing something from happening or moving. A mental inability to remember something or to think clearly.
example_sentence: The sculptor carved a beautiful figure out of a solid block of marble. The protesters used heavy trucks to block the main highway. I walked around the block three times to get some fresh air. She suffered a sudden mental block during the final exam.

english_meaning: A system of two or more pulleys with a rope or cable threaded between them. A mechanical device used for lifting or pulling very heavy loads with minimal effort. An arrangement of blocks with a line passed through them to provide mechanical advantage. A configuration of tackle used extensively in sailing and construction for hoisting weights.
example_sentence: The sailors used a block and tackle to hoist the heavy mainsail into position. We needed a sturdy block and tackle to lift the engine out of the old car. The construction workers rigged a block and tackle to move the marble slab to the upper floor. Understanding the physics of a block and tackle helps explain the concept of mechanical advantage.

english_meaning: To stop someone or something from moving by parking too close or blocking the way. To park so close to another vehicle that it cannot move, to enclose or trap.
example_sentence: Someone blocked me in at the parking lot. Don’t block in the driveway. The car was blocked in by others. He blocked in the area with fences.

english_meaning: To close or seal a road, path, or area so that people cannot enter.
example_sentence: Police blocked off the main street. The road was blocked off due to flooding. They blocked off the entrance for repairs. Workers blocked off the tunnel.

english_meaning: To obstruct the path of light or a view, making it invisible or dark. To stop yourself from thinking about or remembering something unpleasant. To reserve a specific period of time in a schedule for a particular activity. To stop something from being heard or noticed by creating a barrier. To mark or sketch the basic shape or outline of something without details.
example_sentence: She wore dark sunglasses to block out the bright morning sun. You must block out at least two hours for your focused study session. He tried to block out the painful memories of the accident. The artist began to block out the main shapes of the landscape on the canvas.

english_meaning: To obstruct or clog an opening, path, or pipe so that nothing can pass through. To build a wall or barrier across an entrance to prevent access. To fill a space completely with objects so that it is no longer usable. To hinder or prevent movement or progress by placing obstacles. To cover an area or vista by standing in the way.
example_sentence: The fallen tree branches will block up the narrow stream if they aren't removed. They decided to block up the old doorway with bricks to create a solid wall. Heavy snow began to block up the mountain passes, making travel impossible. Don't block up the hallway with those large boxes because people need to get through.

english_meaning: A military or economic measure that prevents goods, people, or communication from entering or leaving a place. The act of sealing off an area, port, or city to prevent movement in or out. To obstruct or seal off a place in order to prevent the passage of supplies, reinforcements, or people. A situation in which access to a place is deliberately cut off as a form of pressure or siege.
example_sentence: The naval blockade prevented food and medicine from reaching the besieged city.  Economic sanctions were paired with a trade blockade to increase pressure on the regime.  Protesters formed a human blockade outside the government building.  The country attempted to break the blockade by sending supply ships.  The blockade of the port lasted for several months and caused severe shortages.

english_meaning: A physical obstruction that prevents flow or passage through a space. The state of being clogged or shut off from movement. A physiological condition where a vessel or organ is closed up. An act of hindering progress or preventing an action from proceeding. A systematic barrier or interference in a process.
example_sentence: The surgeon identified a severe blockage in the patient's coronary artery. Heavy snowfall caused a major blockage on the mountain pass for several hours. You need to clear the blockage in the kitchen sink before using the water. The new regulations have created a bureaucratic blockage that delays all trade permits.

english_meaning: Something extremely successful, especially a movie, book, or product that earns huge popularity and profit. A very large bomb capable of destroying an entire city block. Today, it is commonly used to describe highly successful movies, books, or products that achieve massive sales, attention, or impact. It can also describe anything big, powerful, or highly impressive.
example_sentence: The new action movie became a blockbuster within a week of its release. Her novel turned into a blockbuster and sold millions of copies worldwide. The company launched a blockbuster product that changed the market. The summer season is full of blockbuster films in cinemas.

english_meaning: An informal or insulting term for a very stupid or dull-witted person. Someone who is slow to understand or incapable of intelligent thought. A foolish person who acts without thinking or lacks common sense. Used to express frustration at someone's stupidity or obtuseness.
example_sentence: Don't be such a blockhead and think before you act.  He called himself a blockhead for forgetting the anniversary.  Only a complete blockhead would ignore such clear warning signs.  She muttered under her breath that her colleague was a total blockhead.  The cartoon featured a lovable blockhead as its main character.

english_meaning: A regularly updated website or web page typically run by an individual or small group. A digital journal or informational website displaying information in reverse chronological order. A medium for sharing personal opinions, experiences, or expertise with an online audience. The act of writing and publishing content on a weblog. A platform used for content marketing, news reporting, or social commentary.
example_sentence: She decided to start a travel blog to document her journey across Asia. I spent the whole afternoon reading his blog about artificial intelligence. You can blog about almost any topic that interests you. Many companies use a corporate blog to communicate with their customers directly.

english_meaning: Pertaining to content that is suitable or interesting enough to be published on a blog. Having characteristics that are likely to attract readers or generate online discussion. Describing experiences or events that are noteworthy and visually or textually engaging for a digital audience. Categorized as being worthy of a weblog post due to its unique, trending, or informative nature.
example_sentence: The new cafe had such a unique aesthetic that every corner felt instantly bloggable. She decided that the political scandal was not bloggable until more facts were confirmed. Our vacation photos were so stunning that they were definitely bloggable material. Not every mundane detail of your life is bloggable or interesting to a general audience.

english_meaning: Having light-colored or golden-yellow hair, used especially to describe a person or their hair. A person with fair or light-colored hair. Light or pale in color, used to describe wood, beer, or other materials with a similar golden hue. Often spelled blonde when referring specifically to a female person.
example_sentence: She had naturally blond hair that darkened slightly as she grew older.  The child in the photograph had bright blond curls and blue eyes.  The furniture was made from pale blond wood imported from Scandinavia.  He dyed his hair blond before the summer holiday.  The blond actor was immediately recognizable from across the room.

english_meaning: The red fluid that circulates through the heart, arteries, and veins of the body. A body tissue that carries oxygen, nutrients, hormones, and waste products. The fluid connective tissue made of plasma, red cells, white cells, and platelets. Family relationship or descent, used figuratively. To give a person or animal first experience of an activity, used as a verb.
example_sentence: Blood carries oxygen from the lungs to every part of the body. The nurse took a sample of his blood for testing. They are related by blood, not by marriage. The young officer was blooded during his first mission.

english_meaning: Family bonds are stronger and more important than other relationships. It means that loyalty to family members comes before loyalty to friends or others.
example_sentence: He helped his brother instead of his friend because blood is thicker than water. Even after many fights, she supported her parents; blood is thicker than water. Though they disagreed, he stood by his cousin in trouble because blood is thicker than water. You can always depend on your family, as blood is thicker than water.

english_meaning: The flower or mass of flowers on a fruit tree or other plant, especially before the fruit has formed. To produce flowers or bloom, especially said of fruit trees in spring. To develop, grow, or flourish in a positive and pleasing way, especially used of a person, relationship, or talent. A state of flowering or fresh, promising development.
example_sentence: The cherry trees came into blossom in early April, drawing large crowds to the park.  Their friendship gradually blossomed into a lasting and deep romance.  The young singer has blossomed into one of the most talented performers of her generation.  Spring blossom filled the orchard with color and fragrance.  With encouragement and practice, his confidence began to blossom.

english_meaning: A hard hit or strike delivered by a fist, weapon, or object. An act of breathing out through the mouth with force. A sudden event or piece of news that causes shock, distress, or a significant setback. The movement of air, especially wind.
example_sentence: He struck the nail with a single blow of the hammer.  The unexpected resignation was a serious blow to the company's leadership.  She blew out all the candles on her birthday cake in one blow.  A strong wind blew through the valley overnight.  Losing the contract was a devastating blow to their plans.

english_meaning: To impress someone greatly, or to move something by the force of wind.
example_sentence: The performance blew me away. The wind blew the papers away. That movie really blew everyone away. The storm blew away the roof.

english_meaning: To be knocked over or destroyed by the wind. To make something fall by the force of the wind or air.
example_sentence: The old tree was blown down in the storm. Several signs blew down last night. The wind blew down the fence. The hurricane blew down many houses.

english_meaning: To arrive suddenly or unexpectedly. To arrive without prior notice, often from another place or after a long absence. It gives a sense of surprise or unplanned arrival, as if carried by the wind.
example_sentence: He just blew in from New York. My cousin blew in without calling. They blew in late last night. The guests blew in during the rain.

english_meaning: To fail badly at something, especially through carelessness. To lose a good opportunity by making a mistake. To ruin one's chance of success. To perform very poorly when it matters most. To waste something valuable through poor judgment.
example_sentence: Don't blow it, this is your best chance to get the job. He worked hard for months but blew it in the final interview. She was ahead in the race but blew it in the last lap. If you blow it now, you may not get another chance.

english_meaning: To ignore, avoid, or dismiss someone or something, or to release air, gas, or pressure suddenly.
example_sentence: He blew off the meeting. Don’t blow off your homework. She blew off some steam at the gym. The valve blew off due to pressure.

english_meaning: To release anger, stress, or frustration by doing something active or relaxing so that you can feel calmer afterward. To relax or get rid of built-up emotions.
example_sentence: He played football to blow off some steam. After a long day at work, I went jogging to blow off some steam. He shouted just to blow off some steam, he didn’t mean to be rude. Let’s play a game to blow off some steam after the exam. She went out with her friends to blow off some steam after the argument.

english_meaning: To lose one's temper suddenly and completely. To become extremely angry and shout at someone. To explode with rage after holding back frustration for a long time. To react in an uncontrolled, furious manner to something annoying or unacceptable.
synonyms: ["Explode","Lose one's temper","Fly off the handle","Hit the roof","See red","Go ballistic","Erupt","Blow a fuse","Rage","Flare up"]
antonyms: ["Stay calm","Keep cool","Remain composed","Control oneself","Simmer down","Relax","Tolerate","Overlook","Restrain","Keep one's temper"]
example_sentence: He blew his top when he saw the damage to his new car. My father will blow his top if he finds out about the broken window. She blew her top after waiting for two hours in the rain. Try to explain calmly instead of blowing your top.

english_meaning: To make a problem, event, or situation seem much bigger, worse, or more serious than it really is. Make a mountain out of a molehill. Overdramatize a situation. Stretch the truth. Overemphasize a problem. Turn a small issue into a big one.
synonyms: ["Exaggerate","Overreact","Magnify","Overstate","Make a mountain out of a molehill","Dramatize","Inflate the issue"]
example_sentence: Don’t blow things out of proportion; it was only a small mistake. The media sometimes blows things out of proportion to attract attention. She blew the argument out of proportion and stopped talking to everyone. Parents should stay calm and not blow minor problems out of proportion.

english_meaning: To completely destroy something or someone by an explosion or with great force, so that nothing remains. It expresses total destruction or annihilation.
example_sentence: The bomb blew the building to kingdom come. The old building was blown to kingdom come during the storm. The bomb could blow the whole area to kingdom come. If you mix those chemicals wrongly, you might blow yourself to kingdom come. The ship hit a mine and was blown to kingdom come.

english_meaning: To explode. To destroy with explosives. To become very angry. To inflate
example_sentence: The bomb blew up in the field. He blew up at his friend. They blew up the balloons. The conflict blew up into a major issue.

english_meaning: To suddenly become very angry with someone and speak or shout harshly at them.
example_sentence: She blew up at her coworker after a minor misunderstanding. He rarely loses his temper, but yesterday he blew up at his brother. The coach blew up at the team for their careless mistakes. Try not to blow up at the children when they make small errors.

english_meaning: To praise yourself or talk proudly about your own achievements, skills, or success. To boast or speak proudly about yourself, your talents, achievements, or success. It is usually used when someone keeps praising themselves instead of letting others appreciate their accomplishments. Depending on the situation, it can be either slightly negative (showing arrogance) or acceptable when someone is simply promoting their work or abilities.
example_sentence: John is always blowing his own horn about how successful his business is. I do not like to blow my own horn, but I worked very hard on this project. She blew her own horn during the interview to impress the hiring manager. Instead of blowing your own horn, let your work speak for itself.

english_meaning: To boast about your own abilities or achievements. To praise yourself publicly. To draw attention to your own success. To speak proudly of what you have done. To promote one's own accomplishments loudly.
example_sentence: He loves to blow his own trumpet at every meeting. Modest people rarely blow their own trumpet. Stop blowing your own trumpet and let the results speak. It is time to blow your own trumpet a little.

english_meaning: To suddenly become very angry and lose control. To lose your temper quickly and express anger in a strong or uncontrolled way. It often involves shouting, arguing, or reacting emotionally without thinking.
synonyms: ["Lose your temper","Fly into a rage","Hit the roof","Go ballistic","Explode"]
antonyms: ["Stay calm","Keep your cool","Remain composed","Control yourself","Stay relaxed"]
example_sentence: He blew his top when he saw the broken laptop. She tends to blow her top over small mistakes. The manager blew his top during the meeting. Don’t blow your top, we can fix the problem calmly.

english_meaning: The plural form of blow, referring to multiple hits, strikes, or impacts. Third-person singular present tense form of the verb blow, meaning wind or air moves or someone exhales with force. Refers to multiple setbacks or shocks occurring in succession. The exchange of punches or hits between two or more parties.
example_sentence: The two boxers exchanged blows in the center of the ring.  The storm blows fiercely across the open countryside every winter.  The athlete suffered multiple blows to the head during the match.  The business received several blows in quick succession that year.  She blows out her birthday candles and makes a wish every year.

english_meaning: The thick layer of fat under the skin of whales and other marine mammals. To cry noisily and with a lot of sobbing. Excess body fat in humans, used informally. To speak while sobbing in a difficult-to-understand way. Soft, wobbly fat.
example_sentence: Whale blubber keeps the animal warm in cold seas. The child began to blubber when she lost her toy. He tried to lose the blubber around his waist. Between sobs, he blubbered out an apology.

english_meaning: A person of noble birth or high social status. Someone who comes from an aristocratic, royal, or highly respected family. It suggests inherited status, prestige, and social influence rather than personal achievement alone.
example_sentence: She comes from a blue blood family with a long history of influence. Despite his blue blood background, he lived a simple life. The event was attended by many blue blood members of society. He may not be blue blood, but he earned respect through hard work.

english_meaning: Someone who is favored. A person who receives special treatment, approval, or preference from someone in authority. The favor may be unfair or based on personal liking rather than merit.
example_sentence: He is the boss’s blue eyes, so his mistakes are often ignored. She became the manager’s blue eyes after completing the project successfully. The team complained that only the blue eyes get promotions. Being the teacher’s blue eyes can create jealousy among students.

english_meaning: A small round dark blue fruit that grows on shrubs. A sweet berry rich in antioxidants and vitamins. A fruit used in muffins, pies, jams, and smoothies. A superfood known for its health benefits. A cultivated or wild berry native to North America.
example_sentence: She added fresh blueberries to her morning cereal. Blueberry muffins are a favorite in our family. Studies show that blueberries improve memory and health. The children love blueberry ice cream in summer.

english_meaning: To mislead someone by false confidence, threats, or claims so they believe something that is not true. Often used in games, negotiations, or arguments. An act of deception in which someone pretends to have more strength, knowledge, or advantage than they truly have. A steep cliff or high bank, especially near a river or the sea. Speaking in a direct and honest way, sometimes in a slightly rough manner.
example_sentence: She tried to bluff her way through the interview. He was bluffing about having more money. The player called his opponent’s bluff. We stood on the bluff overlooking the river. She bluffed the doorman into thinking that she was a reporter. I don't think he'll shoot, I think he's just bluffing.

english_meaning: To keep pretending confidently in order to escape a difficult situation. To face trouble by refusing to admit the truth. To carry on a deception until the danger passes.
example_sentence: He decided to bluff it out rather than admit his mistake. She bluffed it out when the manager questioned the missing file. Instead of apologising, they tried to bluff it out. You cannot bluff it out once the records are checked.

english_meaning: To get through a situation by pretending to know or be able to do something. To manage a task by confident pretence rather than real knowledge. To deceive others just enough to succeed at something.
example_sentence: He bluffed his way through the interview without any real experience. She bluffed her way through the presentation after losing her notes. You cannot bluff your way through a practical exam. They bluffed their way through the checkpoint with a confident smile.

english_meaning: To escape or resolve a difficulty by confident pretence. To force an opponent to give up by bold deception. To maintain a false claim until the other side withdraws.
example_sentence: He tried to bluff out the accusation in front of the committee. She managed to bluff out a difficult negotiation. They bluffed out their rivals with an imaginary offer. Do not try to bluff out a charge that can be checked easily.

english_meaning: A person who bluffs, meaning someone who deliberately misleads others about their abilities, intentions, or situation. Someone who pretends to have knowledge, skill, or confidence they do not actually possess. A person who uses bold or deceptive talk to create a false impression. Someone who frequently uses bluffing as a tactic in negotiation, games, or social situations.
example_sentence: Everyone at the poker table knew he was a notorious bluffer.  As a negotiator, he was considered a skilled bluffer who rarely showed his true hand.  She was a convincing bluffer who had fooled almost everyone in the room.  The bluffer was eventually exposed when pressed for real evidence.  Being a good bluffer requires confidence and the ability to read other people.

english_meaning: The act of deliberately misleading others by pretending to have greater strength, knowledge, or resources than one actually possesses. Feigning confidence or capability in order to intimidate, deceive, or gain an advantage. A tactic used in card games, negotiations, or confrontations to create a false impression. Pretending something is true in order to manipulate another person's response.
example_sentence: He was clearly bluffing when he claimed to have already received a better offer.  Bluffing is a core skill in competitive poker.  The suspect was bluffing when he said he had an alibi for that evening.  She realized he was bluffing only after she called his bluff.  Bluffing in negotiations can sometimes backfire badly if the other side calls it out.

english_meaning: To make something less sharp or less strong. Not sharp or having a dull edge (used for objects like knives or pencils). (Of a person or speech) speaking in a direct, plain, and sometimes rude way, not trying to be polite.
example_sentence: The knife is too blunt to cut the fruit. He is a blunt person who always speaks his mind. Her blunt reply hurt his feelings. Years of use have blunted the edge of the scissors.

english_meaning: A shape or object that is not clearly visible because it has no distinct outline. The state of being unable to see things clearly or a loss of focus. A memory or period of time that is not clear in one's mind. To make something less distinct or to smear a surface so as to obscure visibility. A rapid or indistinct movement that makes observation difficult.
example_sentence: Everything was a blur without my glasses. The landscape passed by in a green blur as the train accelerated. The events of the last few days have become a blur in my mind. The rain started to blur the ink on the handwritten note.

english_meaning: To become red in the face due to embarrassment, shyness, shame, or modesty. A reddening of the face caused by strong emotion, usually embarrassment or pleasure. A pink or reddish color, often used in cosmetics to describe a makeup product used to add color to the cheeks. To feel embarrassed or ashamed about something.
example_sentence: She blushed deeply when he paid her an unexpected compliment.  The child blushed with embarrassment when the whole class laughed.  At first blush, the proposal seemed quite reasonable.  She applied a soft blush to her cheeks before the event.  He could not help but blush when he realized his mistake in front of everyone.

english_meaning: Loud, aggressive, or threatening talk with little real substance or follow-through. To talk in a boisterous, arrogant, or threatening manner without having the ability to back up the words. Of wind or weather, to blow loudly and with violent gusts. To behave or speak in a noisy, self-important, or blustering manner.
example_sentence: His bluster in the meeting convinced no one of his actual ability.  The manager blustered about consequences but never followed through.  Strong winds blustered through the coastal town all night.  Despite all his bluster, he backed down the moment he was challenged directly.  She was not intimidated by his bluster and calmly continued with her proposal.

english_meaning: A long, flat piece of wood or other hard material. A group of people who manage a company, school, or organization. A flat surface used for writing, displaying, or playing games. To get on a ship, aircraft, train, or bus. To provide someone with food and lodging in return for payment.
example_sentence: The teacher wrote the answer on the board. The board of directors will meet next Monday. Passengers should board the plane thirty minutes before departure. He agreed to board the students during the school year.

english_meaning: Past tense of board, meaning to get on or enter a vehicle such as a ship, train, or aircraft. Having wooden boards nailed or fixed across openings, doors, or windows, typically to secure an abandoned or damaged building. Referring to accommodation or meals provided in exchange for payment at a boarding house or school.
example_sentence: By the time they arrived, everyone had already boarded the flight.  The windows of the old house were boarded up after it was abandoned.  He boarded the ship just minutes before it departed from the harbor.  The students boarded at a small guesthouse near the university.  Several shops in the town had been boarded following the storm damage.

english_meaning: A boarder is a person who lives in someone else’s house or in a boarding school and pays for food and accommodation. Someone who stays in a place owned by another person or institution and pays regularly for living there. This is common in boarding houses, hostels, and boarding schools where students or tenants live away from their families and receive meals and lodging.
example_sentence: The boarder pays rent every month to stay in the house. She was a boarder at a school in Karachi during her teenage years. The family has three boarders living in their upstairs rooms. Many boarders return home during the summer holidays.

english_meaning: To speak proudly about oneself, achievements, possessions, or abilities. It can also mean something worthy of pride.
example_sentence: He always boasts about his expensive car. She boasted that she could finish the work alone. The city boasts beautiful historical buildings. They boasted of their team's victory for weeks.

english_meaning: A person who frequently praises himself or herself and speaks proudly about achievements, wealth, strength, or abilities. Such a person often exaggerates personal success to impress others.
example_sentence: He sounded boastful when he kept talking about his expensive car. The player gave a boastful speech after winning the match. Her boastful attitude annoyed her colleagues. The boy became boastful after scoring the highest marks in class.

english_meaning: The upper part of a woman's dress, covering the body from the shoulders to the waist. A close-fitting garment or vest worn over a blouse or dress. A woman's laced outer garment, often worn in traditional or period costumes. The fitted section of a dress above the waistline.
example_sentence: The bodice of her wedding dress was decorated with pearls and lace. She wore a red bodice over a white blouse for the folk dance. The tailor adjusted the bodice to fit her perfectly. Traditional bodices are often laced tightly at the front.

english_meaning: To become stuck or impeded, either physically (like in mud) or metaphorically (like in progress or action). Land that is wet, spongy, and often muddy, like a marsh or swamp.
example_sentence: He bogged in his explanation and lost the audience. The project bogged down because of lack of funds. The hikers avoided the bog to keep their boots clean. The car bogged down in the mud after the rain. Negotiations bogged down due to disagreements on funding.

english_meaning: To get stuck, delayed, or hindered. To physically get trapped in mud, water, or difficult terrain. To become overwhelmed or slowed by difficulties, obstacles, or excessive details. To impede progress in work, discussion, or process. To lose focus or energy because of complications.
example_sentence: The car bogged down in the swamp. The negotiations bogged down due to disagreements. She bogged down in paperwork and missed the deadline. The team bogged down in minor technical issues. The project bogged down because of lack of funds. He bogged down in unnecessary details.

english_meaning: Not genuine; fake, counterfeit, or fraudulent. Used to describe something that is presented as real or legitimate but is not.
example_sentence: The police discovered the bogus documents at the border. He made a bogus claim to receive the insurance money. The company was shut down for selling bogus medicines. She received a bogus job offer asking for personal information.

english_meaning: To become extremely angry at someone or something. It refers to a strong rise of emotions similar to boiling water when heat increases.
example_sentence: She boiled at his comments. He boiled at the unfair rules. They boiled at the insult. I boiled at the rude behavior.

english_meaning: To evaporate or disappear by boiling, when a liquid heats and turns into vapor gradually until little or nothing is left.
example_sentence: The water boiled away after hours on the stove. The sauce boiled away, leaving only a thick paste. Let the liquid boil away until it thickens. All the moisture boiled away in the sun.

english_meaning: To reduce something to its essential meaning; to simplify information or make it shorter by removing extra details
example_sentence: Boil down the sauce. The mixture boiled down nicely. The writer boiled down the report. Facts were boiled down for clarity.

english_meaning: To reduce a complex situation to a simple core idea. When something can be explained by one essential idea or cause.
example_sentence: It all boils down to trust. The issue boils down to money. Their argument boils down to a misunderstanding. Success boils down to hard work.

english_meaning: To turn or develop into something. Used when one situation, emotion, or condition gradually intensifies or transforms into something else, often after pressure, heat, or buildup.
example_sentence: The mixture boiled into syrup. Water boiled into steam. The sauce boiled into a thick paste. The sugar boiled into caramel.

english_meaning: To evaporate due to heat. To remove liquid by boiling until it turns into vapor. Also used for processes where heat reduces volume by evaporation.
example_sentence: Let the water boil off. Some liquid boiled off during cooking. The alcohol boiled off quickly. The mixture boiled off too much.

english_meaning: To cook a liquid until it reaches a vigorous boil so that impurities are removed or undesirable substances are eliminated. It can also mean to express or release strong emotions gradually.
example_sentence: Boil out the impurities. The dirt boiled out of the cloth. They boiled out the chemicals. The flavor boiled out too much.

english_meaning: To overflow or become uncontrollable. Used for liquids that rise and spill when boiling and for emotions or situations that become too intense to control.
example_sentence: The milk boiled over. The pot boiled over quickly. His anger boiled over during the meeting. The crowd's excitement boiled over.

english_meaning: To rise suddenly or start to develop with force, especially emotions or a liquid reaching boiling point.
example_sentence: The soup began to boil up. Anger boiled up inside her. Tension was boiling up between them. The water will boil up soon.

english_meaning: To be filled with a strong emotion such as anger, excitement, or frustration; to feel something intensely as if it is bubbling inside.
example_sentence: She boiled with anger. The crowd boiled with excitement. He boiled with jealousy. They boiled with frustration.

english_meaning: Noisy, energetic, and cheerfully rough or exuberant in behavior. Full of energy, excitement, and enthusiasm, often in a way that seems unruly or unrestrained. Used to describe a person, group, or event that is lively and loud in an uninhibited way. Of weather or the sea, wild, stormy, and tempestuous.
example_sentence: The boisterous children ran through the corridors despite repeated warnings to walk quietly.  A boisterous crowd of fans greeted the team at the airport.  Their boisterous laughter could be heard from the other end of the building.  The normally boisterous market was unusually quiet on that cold morning.  He had a boisterous personality that made him popular at social gatherings.

english_meaning: A Chinese cabbage with white stalks and dark green leaves. A mild vegetable used in stir-fries and soups. The plant grown for these crisp leaves and stems. A quick-cooking vegetable common in East Asian cuisine.
example_sentence: She stir-fried bok choy with ginger and soy sauce. Bok choy cooks in just a few minutes. The soup was topped with tender bok choy leaves. Fresh bok choy should look crisp and firm.

english_meaning: Courage and willingness to take risks or face danger. Confidence in speech or action without fear of consequences. Excessive forwardness or lack of proper respect. Strength and clarity of appearance, as in colours or design.
example_sentence: Her boldness in questioning the minister surprised everyone. The plan was carried out with great boldness. His boldness towards elders was considered rude. The poster is admired for the boldness of its colours.

english_meaning: To support, strengthen, or increase the strength, confidence, or effectiveness of something such as an argument, system, organization, or person. It can also mean providing physical support like a cushion or pad.
example_sentence: The government introduced new policies to bolster the economy. Good evidence can bolster your argument in a debate. The teacher tried to bolster the student's confidence. Community support helped bolster the relief program after the flood. She placed a bolster behind her back while sitting on the bed. The sofa had a decorative bolster on each side.

english_meaning: A sudden and completely unexpected event or piece of news. Something shocking that happens without any warning. It is used when an event or news surprises people because there were no signs or expectations beforehand. The phrase comes from the idea of lightning striking from a clear blue sky.
example_sentence: His sudden resignation was a bolt from the blue for the entire team. The announcement of early elections came like a bolt from the blue. Her illness was a bolt from the blue to her family. The company’s closure was a complete bolt from the blue.

english_meaning: A small rounded mass of chewed food ready to be swallowed. A soft mass of food or medicine prepared for swallowing in one portion. In medicine, a single large dose of a drug administered quickly, especially by injection. A rounded lump of any substance that is treated as a single unit.
example_sentence: The speech-language therapist assessed how the patient formed a bolus before swallowing.  The doctor administered a bolus of medication directly into the intravenous line.  Difficulty forming a bolus is a common symptom of certain neurological conditions.  A bolus dose of the antibiotic was given at the start of the treatment.  The nurse explained the difference between a bolus injection and a slow infusion.

english_meaning: High-sounding, inflated language that is full of exaggeration and self-importance but contains little real meaning or substance. Speech or writing that impresses through its grand-sounding words but is ultimately empty or insincere. Pompous or overly elaborate talk intended to impress but often coming across as ridiculous. Inflated language used to make something sound more important or impressive than it really is.
example_sentence: The speech was pure bombast with very little of any real policy substance.  Critics dismissed the minister's announcement as empty bombast.  His writing was often criticized for its bombast and lack of clarity.  Behind all the bombast, there was actually very little being offered.  She cut through the bombast and asked directly what the plan actually was.

english_meaning: A shocking or surprising event or person. Something that causes sudden shock, surprise, or excitement. Can also refer to a very attractive person, especially a woman.
example_sentence: The news of her resignation was a real bombshell. He dropped a bombshell during the meeting about the budget cuts. She appeared at the party looking like a bombshell. The celebrity’s sudden engagement was a bombshell for fans.

english_meaning: A person who enjoys good food, good drink, and a comfortable social life. Someone who loves to live well and enjoys luxury, especially fine dining, social gatherings, and entertainment. A person with refined tastes who actively seeks pleasure in social and cultural experiences.
example_sentence: He is known as a bon vivant who always attends the finest dinner parties in the city. The bon vivant spent his weekends exploring new restaurants and wine tastings. As a bon vivant, she enjoyed traveling to places famous for their cuisine and culture. The magazine described him as a charming bon vivant with expensive tastes.

english_meaning: Genuine, real, and without any intention to deceive. Made or carried out in good faith. Authentic and officially recognized as true. Sincere and honest in intention.
example_sentence: She is a bona fide expert in medieval history. The buyer acted as a bona fide purchaser for value. Only bona fide students may use the library. He produced bona fide documents to support his claim.

english_meaning: A Latin phrase meaning in good faith, used to express sincere and honest intention. The genuine and honest intentions or qualifications of a person. Evidence or proof of a person's good faith, honesty, trustworthiness, or legitimacy. Credentials or evidence used to establish that someone's motives or qualifications are genuine and can be trusted.
example_sentence: The charity was asked to provide its bona fides before receiving government funding.  He questioned the bona fides of the organization offering such unusually high returns.  Her bona fides as a human rights lawyer were beyond question.  The investigator was asked to verify the bona fides of the new business partner.  Establishing your bona fides early in a negotiation can help build trust quickly.

english_meaning: The soft, spongy tissue found inside the cavities of bones. The tissue in which red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets are produced. Red marrow, which actively forms blood cells, and yellow marrow, which stores fat. Marrow taken from bones and used as food in some cuisines.
example_sentence: Blood cells are produced in the bone marrow. The patient needed a bone marrow transplant. Doctors took a small sample of bone marrow for testing. Bone marrow soup is popular in many regions.

english_meaning: A cause of dispute. Something that causes disagreement or argument between people or groups
example_sentence: The property line became a bone of contention between neighbors. Funding for the project has been a bone of contention for months. The new law is likely to become a bone of contention among politicians. His refusal to attend the meeting was a bone of contention in the office.

english_meaning: To study or revise something intensively, especially before an exam or event, to refresh one’s knowledge quickly.
example_sentence: I need to bone up on my English grammar. She boned up on company policies before the interview. He’s boning up on history for his test. You should bone up on driving laws before your exam.

english_meaning: A large open fire built outdoors for celebration, warmth, or burning things. A ceremonial fire during traditional festivals. A large controlled fire for disposing of materials. A symbolic fire representing celebration or protest. A social gathering centered around a large outdoor fire.
example_sentence: The villagers gathered around the bonfire to celebrate the harvest festival. We sat near the bonfire to keep warm during the cold night. They built a bonfire on the beach and sang songs together. The old furniture was thrown into the bonfire.

english_meaning: Crazy. Mad. Insane. Wildly enthusiastic or excited. Behaving in a foolish or absurd way. An informal word used to describe someone or something that seems completely irrational, eccentric, or out of control. It can also describe a situation that is chaotic, ridiculous, or extremely unusual. Often used humorously in everyday conversation rather than as a serious medical or psychological term.
example_sentence: He went bonkers when he heard the good news. The kids drove their mother bonkers all afternoon. That idea sounds completely bonkers to me. The crowd went bonkers at the concert. She is bonkers about classic cars.

english_meaning: Having prominent or visible bones. Very thin, so that bones can be seen or felt. Containing many bones, as in fish. Resembling bone in shape or hardness.
example_sentence: The dog looked hungry and bony. She had long bony fingers. The fish was too bony to eat comfortably. His bony frame surprised the doctor.

english_meaning: A sound made to express disapproval, contempt, or to startle someone. To shout 'boo' at a performer, speaker, or team to show that you do not like them. A sudden exclamation used to frighten or surprise a person, often as a joke. Used as a noun for the sound itself and as a verb for the act of making it. In informal American English, it is also used as an affectionate term for a boyfriend, girlfriend, or close loved one.
example_sentence: The audience began to boo the politician during his speech. He jumped out from behind the door and shouted 'Boo!' to scare his sister. The crowd booed loudly when the referee made the wrong decision. Don't boo the players; they are trying their best. She called him her boo on social media.

english_meaning: To register or check in at a place such as a hotel, hospital, or event, to make a booking officially.
example_sentence: We booked in at the hotel before dinner. She booked in at the clinic for her appointment. They booked in early to get a good seat. Guests must book in before 9 pm.

english_meaning: A curved wooden missile that returns to the thrower, traditionally used by Aboriginal Australians. An action or plan that returns to harm the person who started it. To come back and have the opposite effect from the one intended. Something that rebounds unexpectedly on its originator.
example_sentence: He learned to throw a boomerang during his trip to Australia. The smear campaign became a boomerang for the party. Careless promises can boomerang on a politician. Their strict pricing policy boomeranged and drove customers away.

english_meaning: A blessing or something that is very helpful. A timely blessing or benefit. Something very helpful, useful, or advantageous.
example_sentence: The new hospital is a boon for the local community. For farmers, good rainfall is always a great boon. Mobile phones can be a boon if used wisely. The scholarship proved to be a real boon for poor students.

english_meaning: A rude, unrefined, or ill-mannered person. A person who lacks social refinement, manners, or consideration for others; someone uncultured or insensitive in behavior.
example_sentence: He behaved like a boor at the dinner party, interrupting everyone. Only a boor would laugh at someone else’s misfortune. Don’t be a boor; show some respect to your elders. The boor in the meeting spoke without considering others’ opinions.

english_meaning: Rude, crude, or insensitive in behavior or manner. Showing a lack of refinement, good manners, or consideration for others; behaving in a rough, insensitive, or socially awkward way
example_sentence: His boorish comments ruined the friendly atmosphere. She found his boorish behavior embarrassing at the dinner party. The manager criticized the boorish attitude of the staff member. Avoid being boorish when meeting new people; first impressions matter.

english_meaning: In a rude, ill manner. Behavior that is rough, impolite, insensitive, or lacking social manners. It is often used when someone speaks or acts without respect for others’ feelings or accepted social rules.
example_sentence: He spoke boorishly to the waiter and embarrassed everyone at the table. She laughed boorishly during the serious meeting. Acting boorishly at formal events can damage your reputation. He boorishly ignored her feelings and continued arguing.

english_meaning: Rude, rough, and bad-mannered behaviour. Lack of politeness or good manners. Coarseness in conduct. Unrefined or ill-mannered behaviour towards others. Used to describe the way a person acts when they are insensitive, impolite, or disrespectful in social situations.
example_sentence: His boorishness at the dinner table embarrassed the whole family. The guest's boorishness made everyone feel uncomfortable. People disliked him because of his constant boorishness in meetings. Such boorishness is unacceptable in a civilized society. The young man apologized for his boorishness towards the elderly woman.

english_meaning: To help or encourage something to increase or improve. To push or lift something upward. An increase in amount, strength, or level. A source of help or encouragement. To promote or advertise something strongly.
example_sentence: Exercise can boost your energy levels quickly. The new advertisement gave sales a big boost. He boosted the child up to see the parade. Winning the award was a huge boost to her confidence.

english_meaning: To help something progress or move forward more quickly. To encourage, support, or accelerate the progress of something, such as a project, process, or idea. It often implies providing help, resources, or motivation so that advancement happens more smoothly or faster.
example_sentence: The manager boosted the team along with additional resources to finish the project on time. A good mentor can boost a young professional along in their career. The new marketing strategy helped boost sales along faster than expected. Technological innovations can boost economic growth along significantly.

english_meaning: To help someone or something recover or return to a better state. To giving support, encouragement, or assistance to restore someone or something to a previous level of performance, confidence, or strength. It implies a return to a positive condition after a decline or setback.
example_sentence: The coach’s advice helped boost back the team’s morale after the loss. A good night’s sleep can boost back your energy levels. The government launched a program to boost back small businesses affected by floods. Positive feedback from her manager boosted back her confidence.

english_meaning: To help someone leave or exit, often by giving physical or metaphorical assistance. To push or lift someone or something out of a place, situation, or position. It can be literal, such as helping someone climb out of a window, or figurative, like helping someone leave a role or situation.
example_sentence: He boosted me out of the car after it got stuck in mud. The manager boosted out the lazy employee from the project. She boosted the child out of the tree carefully. They boosted out the old furniture to make space for new items.

english_meaning: To increase, improve, or raise something. To enhance or lift the level, amount, or quality of something. It can refer to physical, emotional, or abstract things like energy, morale, performance, or numbers.
