example_sentence: Police discovered a large cache of weapons in the basement. The hikers found a cache of food left by earlier travellers. Clearing the browser cache often improves website loading speed. Smugglers had cached the gold in a remote cave. A cache of ancient coins was unearthed by the farmer.

english_meaning: The state of being respected or admired. A distinguishing mark or seal. A flat capsule enclosing a dose of medicine.
example_sentence: The brand has a certain cachet that appeals to wealthy buyers. He felt that driving a luxury car would give him social cachet. The official document bore the royal cachet. The pharmacist prepared the bitter powder inside a cachet.

english_meaning: Relating to bad handwriting. Marked by poor or incorrect spelling. Written in an unclear or careless manner.
example_sentence: The teacher struggled with his cacographic notes. Her cacographic letters were difficult to read. The manuscript was dismissed as cacographic and careless. He apologised for his cacographic handwriting.

english_meaning: Bad or unreadable handwriting. Incorrect spelling. The art or practice of writing badly.
example_sentence: His cacography made the notes almost useless. The essay was full of cacography and mistakes. Teachers often complain about students' cacography. Cacography is the opposite of calligraphy.

english_meaning: Producing a harsh, discordant mixture of sounds that is unpleasant to hear. Characterized by a jarring combination of loud and confusing noises. Used to describe an unpleasant, chaotic blend of sounds, often from multiple sources at once. Marked by a lack of harmony, resulting in noise that feels grating or overwhelming.
example_sentence: The construction site was filled with the cacophonous noise of drills and hammers.  A cacophonous mix of horns and shouting filled the busy intersection.  The orchestra's warm-up sounded cacophonous before the conductor brought order.  She found the cacophonous chatter of the crowded restaurant overwhelming.  The cacophonous sounds of the city kept him awake at night.

english_meaning: A harsh, discordant mixture of sounds. A loud, unpleasant and confusing combination of noises. A jarring, unmelodious blend of voices or sounds occurring together. Any disagreeable or chaotic clamour.
example_sentence: A cacophony of car horns filled the busy street. The cacophony of the construction site made it hard to concentrate. We woke up to a cacophony of bird calls at dawn. The orchestra's tuning created a brief cacophony before the concert. Her ears could not bear the cacophony of the crowded market.

english_meaning: A man who behaves in a dishonest or unfair way. A man who acts with deliberate disregard for another's feelings or rights.
example_sentence: He acted like a cad when he ignored her after promising to marry her. Everyone considered him a cad for spreading false rumors. Only a cad would treat his friends so badly. She realized too late that he was a cad who never respected her feelings.

english_meaning: To ask for or get something, especially food, money, or favours, without paying or working for it. To beg or scrounge in a casual or shameless manner. To obtain by imposing on another’s generosity. To live by sponging off others.
example_sentence: He always tries to cadge a cigarette from his friends. She cadged a lift home after the concert. Some students cadge meals from their classmates. Don’t cadge money; earn it through honest work. He cadged a free ticket to the cricket match.

english_meaning: Relating to Julius Caesar or the Caesars of ancient Rome. A surgical operation in which a baby is delivered through an incision in the mother's abdomen. Describing a delivery performed by such an operation.
example_sentence: The doctor advised a Caesarean because of complications. She delivered twins by Caesarean section. Recovery after a Caesarean usually takes several weeks. The term Caesarean is linked in legend to Julius Caesar's birth.

english_meaning: An alternative spelling of Caesarean, meaning delivery of a baby by surgical incision. Relating to such an operation. Of or connected with Julius Caesar and the Roman emperors.
example_sentence: The baby was delivered by Caesarian section. Doctors decided on a Caesarian to protect the mother. Caesarian rates have risen in many countries. The word Caesarian carries an old Roman association.

english_meaning: A natural pause or break in a line of poetry. A pause, break, or stop within a line of poetry, often used to create rhythm, emphasis, or emotional effect. It usually occurs in the middle of a line but can appear elsewhere. The pause may be marked by punctuation or simply by the flow of speech.
example_sentence: The soldier stood firm, then fell as the drums went silent. To be, or not to be, that is the question. The wind was fierce, shaking the trees all night. She spoke softly, yet her words carried power.

english_meaning: A bitter chemical compound that acts as a central nervous system stimulant. It reduces tiredness, increases mental alertness, and is commonly present in coffee, tea, soft drinks, energy drinks, and chocolate. It can also increase heart rate and temporarily raise blood pressure.
example_sentence: I drink coffee every morning because it contains caffeine. Too much caffeine can make you feel nervous. Many students rely on caffeine during exams. Energy drinks often have high levels of caffeine.

english_meaning: Collusion or secret partnership, usually used in the phrase 'in cahoots'. A state of scheming or acting together in secret, often for dishonest purposes.
example_sentence: The detective suspected that the guard was in cahoots with the thieves. They worked in cahoots to rig the local election. The two companies were secretly in cahoots to fix prices. I refuse to be in cahoots with anyone involved in illegal activities.

english_meaning: To persuade someone to do something by using flattery, gentle persuasion, or repeated coaxing. To convince someone gradually through charm, sweet talk, or mild pressure rather than force. To wheedle or coax a person into agreeing to something they were initially reluctant to do. Often implies a degree of manipulation, though usually in a light-hearted or harmless way.
example_sentence: She managed to cajole her brother into helping with the household chores.  The salesman tried to cajole the customer into buying the more expensive model.  He was cajoled into attending the party by his persistent friends.  The teacher gently cajoled the shy student into reading aloud to the class.  They cajoled their parents into letting them stay out late.

english_meaning: A member of a group of people of French descent living in Louisiana, USA. Relating to the culture, language, or spicy cuisine of the Cajun people. A style of cooking from Louisiana that uses strong spices. A French dialect spoken by Cajun communities.
example_sentence: They enjoyed a spicy Cajun gumbo at the New Orleans restaurant. The Cajun band played lively accordion music. His grandparents spoke Cajun French at home. Cajun culture is famous for its food, music, and festivals.

english_meaning: A large gourd whose hard shell is dried and used as a container, bowl, or pipe. The tropical American tree or climbing vine that bears such a fruit. A bowl, bottle, or utensil made from the dried shell of a gourd. A tobacco pipe with a bowl made from a gourd.
example_sentence: The elder poured fresh milk into a carved calabash for the guests. Many African communities use calabashes to store grain and water. He smoked a curved calabash pipe while reading by the fire. The children decorated dried calabashes with bright paint for the festival.

english_meaning: A variety of green sprouting broccoli with large central heads. Relating to Calabria in southern Italy, its people, or its cuisine. A spicy Italian salami from Calabria.
example_sentence: She steamed some calabrese to serve with the grilled fish. Calabrese grows well in cool weather. The restaurant offers a spicy pizza topped with Calabrese salami. He learned several Calabrese recipes from his grandmother.

english_meaning: An event that causes great harm or damage (disaster). A disastrous event marked by great loss and lasting distress and suffering.
example_sentence: The whole calamity, with the falling form of Macey, was plainly descried from the ship. The country suffered a series of calamities during the 1980s. His financial help saved the magazine from total calamity.

english_meaning: A branch of mathematics that deals with rates of change and accumulation of quantities. A particular method or system of calculation or reasoning. A hard stone or concretion formed in a part of the body, such as the kidney. The gradual buildup of mineral deposits on teeth, also known as tartar.
example_sentence: She is studying advanced calculus in her first year of engineering. The political calculus of the election changed after the scandal broke. The doctor discovered a calculus in the patient's gallbladder during the ultrasound. Regular brushing helps prevent the formation of dental calculus on teeth.

english_meaning: A large metal pot or kettle used for cooking or boiling something over an open fire. A big deep round vessel, usually made of iron, with a handle at the top, used for heating or boiling liquids. (Figuratively) A situation or place of intense feelings, conflict, activity, or change. A state in which strong emotions, ideas, or forces are mixed together. Also spelled 'cauldron'.
example_sentence: The witches stirred a bubbling caldron in the old fairy tale. Soup was cooking slowly in a huge iron caldron over the fire. The city has become a caldron of political unrest. His mind was a caldron of conflicting emotions after the news. Workers poured the molten metal from the caldron into the moulds.

english_meaning: A chart or system showing the days, weeks, and months of a particular year. A schedule or list of planned events, appointments, or activities. A system for determining the beginning, length, and divisions of a year. To enter or schedule something in a calendar or appointment book.
example_sentence: She marked the important date on her calendar. The academic calendar runs from September to June. My calendar is full this week with meetings. He calendared the appointment for next Tuesday.

english_meaning: The fleshy muscular part at the back of the lower leg. The rounded muscle between the knee and the ankle. A young cow or bull in its first year. The young of certain large animals such as elephants, whales, and deer.
example_sentence: He pulled a muscle in his left calf while running. Climbing stairs daily strengthens the calves. The farmer sold a healthy calf at the market. The whale swam slowly beside her calf.

english_meaning: The quality of someone’s character or the level of their ability. The internal diameter of a tube, especially the barrel of a gun, or the diameter of a bullet or shell. The degree of mental capacity, moral excellence, or professional standard. The standard of excellence or worth of a person or thing.
example_sentence: She is a writer of the highest caliber. The company hires engineers of exceptional caliber. The rifle uses bullets of a small caliber. Few players in the team match his caliber. We need leaders of strong moral caliber.

english_meaning: To mark or adjust the scale of a measuring instrument so that it gives accurate readings. To carefully measure and adjust something so that it works correctly. To compare the readings of a device with a standard to ensure accuracy. To plan or adjust an action carefully according to specific conditions.
example_sentence: The technician will calibrate the thermometer before use. Scientists carefully calibrate their instruments to ensure accuracy. The machine needs to be calibrated every six months. Speakers calibrate their tone according to the audience. The government must calibrate its policies to changing economic conditions.

english_meaning: The act or process of marking or adjusting a measuring instrument so that it gives correct readings. The careful comparison of a device with a known standard to ensure accuracy. The marks or graduations on a measuring instrument. The act of adjusting something carefully to suit a particular purpose or condition.
example_sentence: Regular calibration of laboratory instruments is essential for accurate results. The calibration of the new sensor took several hours. Speedometers require calibration to show the correct speed. The calibration of policies to economic realities is necessary. Engineers checked the calibration of every machine before delivery.

english_meaning: The quality of a person’s character or the level of their ability. The internal diameter of the barrel of a gun, or the diameter of a bullet or shell. A degree or standard of excellence, especially of intellect or moral worth. The capacity or merit of a person or thing measured against a standard.
example_sentence: He is a scholar of the highest calibre. The army uses rifles of various calibres. Few students in the class match her calibre. Companies look for employees of strong moral calibre. The competition attracted players of international calibre.

english_meaning: To measure and set the accuracy of a device by comparing it with a standard. To adjust a plan, response, or judgment carefully according to conditions.
example_sentence: The technician calibrated the thermometer to ensure accurate readings. Scientists must calibrate their instruments before conducting experiments. The company needs to calibrate its strategy according to market changes. Engineers calibrate machines regularly to maintain precision.

english_meaning: The act or process of checking and adjusting a measuring instrument so that it gives accurate readings. The set of marks on a measuring device that indicate units of measurement. Careful adjustment of something according to a specific standard or condition. The comparison of a device or process with a recognized standard to determine accuracy.
example_sentence: The laboratory performs regular calibration of all its instruments. Accurate calibration is essential for reliable test results. The calibration of the weighing scale was off by a few grams. Modern industries depend on precise calibration of machinery. The calibration of the radar system improved its accuracy.

english_meaning: A religious and political leader in Islam, regarded as a successor to the Prophet Muhammad. The chief Muslim civil and religious ruler. The head of an Islamic state. A title for Islamic leaders claiming religious authority.
example_sentence: The first caliph after Muhammad was Abu Bakr. The Abbasid caliphs ruled from Baghdad. The role of the caliph combined spiritual and temporal authority. Some groups seek to establish a new caliphate.

english_meaning: Physical exercises involving rhythmic body movements, usually performed with little or no equipment. Bodyweight training intended to improve strength, flexibility, coordination, and fitness.
example_sentence: The soldiers began each morning with an hour of calisthenics. Push-ups and squats are common calisthenics exercises. She includes calisthenics in her daily fitness routine. The coach designed a calisthenics program to build core strength.

english_meaning: To speak honestly and directly, even if the truth is unpleasant, to say things as they really are.
synonyms: ["Be honest","Speak frankly","Be direct","Tell the truth","Be straightforward"]
example_sentence: She always calls a spade a spade, even if people don’t like it. It’s time to call a spade a spade and admit the plan failed. He is respected because he calls a spade a spade, no matter who is listening. Let’s call a spade a spade, this project needs serious improvement.

english_meaning: To stop at a place for a short time, usually while traveling. To stop briefly as part of an official schedule. To pay a short formal visit. To stop at a port or station during a voyage.
example_sentence: The train will call at Hyderabad before reaching Karachi. The ship called at several ports along the coast. I will call at your office tomorrow to drop the documents. The bus calls at every major town on its way to Sukkur.

english_meaning: To ask someone to leave a place for an urgent reason.
example_sentence: The doctor was called away to an emergency. He was called away from the meeting. She got called away for urgent work. I was called away just as dinner started.

english_meaning: To return a phone call that someone made earlier. To ask someone to return after they have left. To recall someone for a job, audition, or duty.
example_sentence: I’ll call you back later. The company called back the defective items. Please call me back when you can. The manager called him back for another interview. I missed his call, so I’ll call him back later.

english_meaning: To demand, require, or need something.
example_sentence: This situation calls for action. The recipe calls for two eggs. His illness calls for rest. The moment calls for celebration.

english_meaning: To cause something to appear, exist, or happen, to bring out a reaction, response, or quality in someone or something.
example_sentence: His speech called forth many emotions. The book called forth memories. The accident called forth emergency teams. The situation called forth courage.

english_meaning: To stop doing something, usually because the work is finished or because you are tired. To decide that no further effort is needed for the time being.
example_sentence: Let’s call it a day and go home. We have done enough cleaning for today, let’s call it a day. After working twelve hours straight, he decided to call it a day. It’s getting dark, let’s call it a day and continue in the morning.

english_meaning: To stop what one is doing for the rest of the evening and go to bed or go home. To end an activity, work, or social gathering for the night. To decide that enough has been done and it is time to rest.
synonyms: ["Turn in","Retire","Wrap up","Finish up","Go to bed","Stop for the day","Knock off","Close up","End the evening","Head home"]
antonyms: ["Carry on","Continue","Stay up","Keep going","Persist","Start","Begin","Resume","Press on","Work through the night"]
example_sentence: We finished the report at midnight and decided to call it a night. After three hours of practice, the team called it a night. I'm exhausted, so let's call it a night. They danced until two o'clock before calling it a night.

english_meaning: To cancel or stop something that was planned, such as a meeting, event, or arrangement.
example_sentence: They called off the meeting. The game was called off due to rain. The strike was called off after talks. She called off the wedding.

english_meaning: To visit someone, usually formally or briefly. To ask someone to speak, answer, or participate. To formally request help, support, or action from someone. To appeal to someone for assistance or support.
example_sentence: She called on the government to hold a vote. She called on her Representative to help her. I will call on my friend tomorrow. The teacher called on me to answer the question. The committee called on the government to take action. He called on his neighbors to help with the project.

english_meaning: To shout, summon, or criticize someone openly.
example_sentence: He called out for help. The teacher called out the names. The protestors called out for justice. The captain called out orders.

english_meaning: To loudly proclaim the Islamic call to prayer that announces the time for prayer. To recite the azan aloud, inviting Muslims to gather for worship. To make the public announcement summoning believers to prayer. To deliver the traditional call from the mosque before each prayer.
synonyms: ["Recite the azan","Give the call to prayer","Announce the azan","Proclaim the call"]
example_sentence: The muezzin called out the azan from the minaret. He calls out the azan five times a day. The boy learned how to call out the azan beautifully. They waited for someone to call out the azan before praying. The man called out the azan as the sun began to set.

english_meaning: To challenge or confront someone publicly or directly about their behavior or mistake. To confront or criticize someone openly.
example_sentence: She called him out on his lies. The teacher called the student out on cheating. The journalist called the minister out on corruption. Don’t call me out on this in front of everyone.

english_meaning: To challenge someone to prove a claim or threat that you believe is false. To force a person to act on what they have only pretended they would do. To expose someone's pretence by refusing to back down.
example_sentence: She called his bluff and asked him to show the documents. When they threatened to resign, the board simply called their bluff. He kept boasting until someone finally called his bluff. I called her bluff by agreeing to every condition she demanded.

english_meaning: To challenge a person to carry out a threat you believe they will not carry out. To ask someone to prove a claim that you think is false. To expose another person's pretence by calling for action.
example_sentence: I called his bluff and told him to file the complaint. She called her brother's bluff about moving out. The teacher called the student's bluff by asking him to explain the topic. Nobody expected the tenants to call the landlord's bluff.

english_meaning: To challenge a threat or claim in order to show that it is not genuine. To demand proof from someone who is only pretending. To refuse to be frightened by an empty warning.
example_sentence: The union decided to call the bluff and continue the strike. Investors called the bluff when the figures did not add up. Someone had to call the bluff before the rumour spread further. He called the bluff by asking for written proof.

english_meaning: To be in control and make decisions. To have the authority or power to decide what will happen, especially in a group, organization, or situation. The person who calls the shots directs others and sets rules or plans.
synonyms: ["Be in charge","Make decisions","Run the show","Have authority"]
example_sentence: In this company, the manager calls the shots. Parents usually call the shots at home. The funding agency calls the shots in the project. Whoever controls the budget calls the shots.

english_meaning: To telephone or contact someone by phone. To summon someone for duty, especially in the army. To remember or recall something. To bring something onto a computer screen or display.
example_sentence: She called up her best friend. The army was called up for duty. He called up the report on his computer. They called up new recruits. The picture called up many childhood memories.

english_meaning: To formally ask someone to do something or to request help or support. To visit someone, usually for a short time or for a specific purpose. To appeal to or invoke a power, principle, or feeling. To require someone to perform a duty or task.
example_sentence: The teacher called upon Ali to answer the question. We should call upon our friends when they are in need. The president called upon the nation to remain united. They called upon the doctor for advice.

english_meaning: The art of beautiful and decorative handwriting. The artistic practice of writing letters and words in a beautiful, stylish, and decorative manner using pens, brushes, or digital tools. It is often used in religious texts, invitations, certificates, logos, and artwork.
example_sentence: She practiced calligraphy to design beautiful wedding cards. The museum displayed ancient Arabic calligraphy on the walls. His calligraphy skills impressed the art teacher. Many students learn Chinese calligraphy as a traditional art form.

english_meaning: A hardened, thickened area of skin. A callus formed on the body due to friction or pressure. Emotional hardness or lack of feeling. Insensitivity to the suffering of others. A state of being unfeeling or harsh in nature.
example_sentence: Years of hard labor caused callosity on his hands. The doctor examined the callosity on the patient's foot. His callosity toward the poor shocked everyone. She could not bear the callosity of his remarks.

english_meaning: Showing or having an insensitive and cruel disregard for others. Emotionally hardened and unsympathetic. Indifferent to the suffering or feelings of others. Of skin: hardened and thickened.
example_sentence: His callous remarks about the victims shocked everyone. It was callous of her to ignore her friend in need. The dictator was known for his callous treatment of opponents. Years of hard labour had made his hands callous. He showed a callous disregard for human life.

english_meaning: Having an area of skin made thick and hard by repeated pressure or friction. Covered with or affected by calluses. Emotionally hardened and insensitive because of repeated exposure or experience. Made less responsive to suffering, criticism, or feeling. Past tense and past participle of callous.
example_sentence: Years of farm work had left his hands calloused. The guitarist’s fingertips were calloused from practice. Repeated violence had calloused him to suffering. Her calloused feet needed rest after the long walk.

english_meaning: In an insensitive, cruel, or emotionally hardened manner. Without sympathy for the pain or feelings of others. With careless disregard for suffering or harm. In a way that shows a lack of compassion or concern.
example_sentence: He callously ignored the injured man’s request for help. The workers were callously dismissed without warning. She spoke callously about people who had lost their homes. The company callously placed profit above public safety.

english_meaning: A hard or thickened area of skin caused by friction or pressure. An insensitive and cruel disregard for the feelings or suffering of others. Emotional hardness that prevents sympathy or compassion. The quality of being unfeeling or indifferent to pain and hardship. A tough, uncaring attitude developed over time.
example_sentence: The callousness of his remarks shocked everyone at the meeting. She was surprised by the callousness with which the manager fired the workers. His callousness toward the poor made people dislike him. Years of war had left the soldiers with a certain callousness.

english_meaning: An instance of publicly criticizing or drawing attention to someone's unacceptable actions or behavior. A summons for a worker, like a doctor or plumber, to come and perform a task, often in an emergency. In design, a piece of text that points to and explains a specific part of an illustration.
example_sentence: The activist's social media callout of the company for its environmental record went viral. We had to make an emergency callout for a plumber when the pipe burst. Her blog post was a direct callout to politicians who ignored the issue. The diagram included a callout to highlight the engine's new feature. The fee for an engineer's callout after midnight is quite high.

english_meaning: Young, inexperienced, and lacking in maturity or judgement. Not yet fully developed or wise because of young age. (Of a bird) Young and without feathers, not yet able to fly. Used to describe people, especially young men, who are immature in behaviour or thinking.
example_sentence: He was just a callow youth when he joined the army. The manager did not trust the callow new recruits with such an important task. Her callow remarks showed she had little experience of the world. As a callow writer, he made many mistakes in his early work. The nest was full of callow chicks waiting for their mother.

english_meaning:
Not excited, nervous or upset. Peaceful, quiet, and without worry. Without hurried movement or noise. To stop someone feeling upset, angry, or excited. 
Become quite, relax, peaceful after strong emotion, excitement.
example_sentence: Her previous calm way to terror. The policemen appealed for calm. We waited inside until thing calmed down. The city is calm again. He always stays calm under pressure. Try to remain calm.

english_meaning: A quiet or peaceful period just before a difficult, chaotic, or dangerous situation begins. A temporary moment of silence, peace, or normality that happens just before trouble, conflict, or intense activity starts. It is often used when people sense that something big or bad is about to happen, even though everything currently
synonyms: ["Peace before trouble","Lull before chaos","Quiet before disaster","Temporary calm","Suspicious calm"]
example_sentence: The classroom was unusually quiet before the teacher announced the surprise test, it was the calm before the storm. The sea looked peaceful in the morning, but sailors knew it was the calm before the storm. Everyone was smiling at the party, but it felt like the calm before the storm because an argument started later. The office was silent on Monday, but the manager’s meeting turned it into chaos, showing it was the calm before the storm.

english_meaning: To become or make someone less angry, anxious, or excited, to relax emotionally or mentally.
example_sentence: Please calm down and explain what happened. It took him a while to calm down after the argument. The teacher calmed the students down. A walk helped her calm down.

english_meaning: Making a loud, confused, and continuous noise. Expressing demands or complaints in a noisy and insistent way. Full of loud voices or shouting. Expressing strong feelings, opinions, or demands in a forceful and disturbing manner.
example_sentence: A clamorous crowd gathered outside the parliament. The children were clamorous for ice cream after the match. Journalists became clamorous when the minister refused to answer. The market was clamorous with traders shouting prices. Citizens are clamorous in their demand for justice.

english_meaning: A unit of energy often used to measure the nutritional value of food. The amount of heat required to raise the temperature of one gram of water by one degree Celsius. A kilocalorie, which is a common unit for measuring energy intake in diets. Any of several units of heat energy in the metric system. The energy potential contained in chemical bonds of food items. A measure of the work or effort required to perform physical activity. A standard metric unit of energy equal to approximately 4·184 joules.
synonyms: ["Energy Unit","Thermal Unit","Heat Unit","Kilocalorie","Kcal","Joule Equivalent","Nutritional Energy","Food Energy","Fuel Value","Metabolic Unit","Thermal Measure","Power Unit","Caloric Value","Diet Unit"]
example_sentence: She carefully counted every calorie in her daily meal plan to lose weight. This chocolate bar contains over two hundred calories per serving size. Burning a calorie requires a specific amount of physical movement or metabolic work. The scientist measured the heat release in calories during the chemical reaction.

english_meaning: Relating to the amount of heat or energy produced by something, especially food or fuel. Producing a large amount of heat. Containing many calories. Used to describe the energy value of substances.
example_sentence: Coal has a high calorific value compared to wood. Sweets and oily foods are highly calorific. The calorific content of the fuel is measured in joules. Athletes need calorific meals to maintain their energy. Nutritionists check the calorific value of each ingredient.

english_meaning: To make false and harmful statements about someone in order to damage their reputation. To slander or defame a person through untrue accusations. To spread malicious lies about another person. To attack the good name of someone with false charges.
example_sentence: His opponents tried to calumniate him during the election campaign. It is sinful to calumniate honest people for personal gain. The newspaper was sued for calumniating the businessman. Do not calumniate your colleagues behind their backs. She refused to calumniate her former friend despite their quarrel.

english_meaning: A branch of Protestant Christianity based on the teachings of John Calvin, emphasizing predestination and God's absolute authority.
example_sentence: Their religious philosophy is grounded in Calvinism. He feels other people often focus only on the restrictions that Calvinism imposes. Calvinism glorified entrepreneurial virtues but kept them under strict watch. American Protestants largely abandoned harsh Calvinism.

english_meaning: A follower of the Christian teachings and theological ideas of John Calvin, especially the belief in predestination.
example_sentence: He was one of five sons born to a Calvinist preacher and his wife. Her parents have very Calvinist attitudes. Driven by a deeply ingrained Calvinist work ethic, he is notorious for his hatred of holidays. He continued to spread Calvinist theology around Scotland, preaching from Edinburgh.

english_meaning: To convert someone to the religious beliefs of John Calvin or to make ideas strict and disciplined according to Calvinist principles.
example_sentence: The ruler attempted to Calvinize his subjects by enforcing strict moral laws. The community was gradually Calvinized, adopting stricter religious discipline.

english_meaning: A feeling of friendship, trust, and mutual support among a group of people who spend a lot of time together. A spirit of good fellowship and loyalty between companions. The warm relationship that develops among colleagues, teammates, or soldiers. A close bond formed through shared experiences and common goals.
example_sentence: There is great camaraderie among the players of this team. Soldiers develop a strong camaraderie during long missions. The office picnic helped build camaraderie among the staff. The camaraderie between the two old friends was clear to everyone. A spirit of camaraderie keeps the workers motivated.

english_meaning: To hide or disguise something by making it blend with its surroundings. To conceal or disguise a person, object, or feeling so that it is not easily noticed. A disguise or pattern that helps something blend with its surroundings. It can refer to physical hiding using colors or patterns, or to hiding emotions, intentions, or facts.
example_sentence: The soldiers camouflaged themselves with leaves. The vehicles were all well camouflaged. He pulled the camouflage net over the entrance to the tent. The whiteness of polar bears and arctic foxes provides camouflage. Predators make as much use of camouflage as their prey do. Her angry words were camouflage for the way she felt.

english_meaning: A planned series of activities organized to achieve a particular goal, especially in politics, business, or social matters. A series of military operations intended to achieve a particular objective in a war. An organized effort by a group of people to promote a cause or idea. To work in an organized and active way towards a particular aim.
example_sentence: The party launched a nationwide campaign before the elections. A new advertising campaign boosted the sales of the product. Health workers ran a campaign against polio in remote villages. Many citizens campaigned for clean drinking water. The general led a successful military campaign in the north.

english_meaning: A person who spends a holiday living in a tent or camp. A recreational vehicle equipped for camping out. A participant in a summer camp or similar organized outdoor program. Someone who enjoys the outdoors and setting up temporary shelter in nature.
example_sentence: The experienced camper easily started a fire without matches. We rented a large camper for our family road trip across the country. Every summer, the camp welcomes hundreds of enthusiastic young campers. She considers herself a dedicated camper who prefers tents over hotels.

english_meaning: Unable to understand something at all. To find something completely confusing or unclear. Not being able to make any sense of a situation or matter. To be totally puzzled by what someone says or writes. To fail to grasp the meaning of something.
example_sentence: I can't make head nor tail of these instructions. She couldn't make head nor tail of his strange behavior. The report was so complex that I couldn't make head nor tail of it. He tried to read the map but couldn't make head nor tail of it.

english_meaning: A long artificial waterway built for boats, irrigation or drainage. A channel dug to carry water from a river to fields. In anatomy, a tube-like passage inside the body. To build a canal or provide an area with canals.
example_sentence: Farmers depend on the canal for irrigation. The old canal is now used for boat trips. The dentist cleaned the root canal carefully. Engineers plan to canal the eastern district.

english_meaning: An unfounded rumor or story. A false report or piece of news that is intentionally fabricated and spread. It often implies an element of deception aimed at misleading the public or damaging someone's reputation.
example_sentence: The report about the CEO resigning was a complete canard. He was forced to resign after entirely fabricated canards were published in the press. This canard about the election being rigged has been debunked multiple times. The news of his sudden death turned out to be nothing but a vicious canard.

english_meaning: To remove or neutralize the effect of something, to make something ineffective.
example_sentence: The benefits cancel out the risks. His kindness cancels out his past mistakes. One vote canceled out another. The two forces canceled each other out.

english_meaning: A disease caused by uncontrolled growth and spread of abnormal cells. A malignant tumor that can invade and destroy surrounding tissue. A group of diseases characterized by cellular mutations and proliferation. A serious illness requiring treatment like surgery, chemotherapy, or radiation.
example_sentence: Early detection increases cancer survival rates. She was diagnosed with breast cancer. Cancer treatment has improved significantly. Smoking increases the risk of lung cancer.

english_meaning: Saying what you think openly and honestly, not hiding your thoughts. Honest and telling the truth, especially about something difficult or painful. Free in expressing one's true feelings and opinions.
example_sentence: You must be absolutely honest and candid. His responses were remarkably candid. It is better to let the photographer mingle among the guests and take candid shots

english_meaning: In a honest and straightforward way, frankly. In a way that is open and honest, saying what you really think.
example_sentence: He candidly discussed his efforts to find employment. She candidly admitted her mistakes. Candidly, I have sympathy for both positions. I find she is easy to speak to candidly. He candidly admitted that he was surprised and disappointed. We created a neutral space where everyone could speak candidly about race issues and also work side-by-side in "co-designing" solutions.

english_meaning: The quality of being open, honest, and sincere in what one says. Freedom from bias or prejudice; fairness in expressing opinions. Frankness or openness of expression, even when the truth may be uncomfortable. Straightforward and truthful behaviour without hidden motives.
example_sentence: She spoke with great candor about her past mistakes. I appreciate the candor of your honest opinion. The minister answered the journalists’ questions with surprising candor. Such candor is rare in modern politics. He explained the situation to his parents with complete candor.

english_meaning: Relating to dogs or the dog family. A pointed tooth between the incisors and the premolars, used for tearing food. A dog, especially in formal or scientific use. Having qualities or characteristics similar to those of a dog.
example_sentence: The police use canine units to search for missing people. His sharp canine was chipped during the accident. Canine behaviour can be improved with regular training. The vet specialises in canine health and nutrition.

english_meaning: A large semiaquatic reptile of the alligator family, native to Central and South America, with a long snout and a heavy armoured body. Carpe diem is a Latin phrase that encourages people to live in the present moment and take advantage of opportunities without worrying too much about the future. It suggests enjoying life, acting boldly, and not delaying important actions.
synonyms: ["Seize the moment","Live for today","Make the most of now","Enjoy the present","Act now","Live in the moment"]
example_sentence: She decided to travel the world, believing in carpe diem. Carpe diem inspired him to start his own business without fear. Instead of worrying about tomorrow, he lived by carpe diem. They celebrated every moment of life with a true carpe diem attitude.

english_meaning: A person who makes and repairs wooden objects and structures. A skilled worker who builds furniture, doors, and frames from wood. Someone whose trade is woodwork. To work as a maker of wooden items.
example_sentence: The carpenter built a strong wooden bookshelf for us. We called a carpenter to repair the broken door. Her father worked as a carpenter for thirty years. The carpenter measured the frame before cutting the wood.

english_meaning: The work or skill of making and repairing wooden things. The trade of a carpenter. Woodwork produced by a carpenter. The craft of shaping timber into useful structures.
example_sentence: He learned carpentry from his uncle as a boy. The school offers courses in carpentry and welding. The carpentry in this old house is remarkably fine. Good carpentry requires patience and accurate measurement.

english_meaning: A wheeled vehicle pulled by horses, used for carrying passengers. A passenger car of a railway train. The way a person holds and moves their body; posture. The act or cost of transporting goods. A moving part of a machine that supports or carries something.
example_sentence: The queen arrived at the palace in a golden carriage. We traveled in a first-class railway carriage. Her upright carriage showed her confidence. The typewriter carriage moved smoothly across the page.

english_meaning: The decaying flesh of a dead animal. Dead and rotting bodies eaten by certain animals or birds. Something regarded as worthless or repulsive.
example_sentence: Vultures feed mainly on carrion. The smell of carrion filled the air. Hyenas often scavenge carrion left by lions. Crows gathered around the carrion in the field.

english_meaning: The decaying flesh of dead animals. Dead and rotting animal bodies, often eaten by scavengers. The remains of a dead creature left in the open. Something disgusting, decayed, or corrupt in nature. Flesh unfit for human consumption due to decomposition.
example_sentence: Vultures circled above the carrion in the desert. The hunters left the carrion behind for wild animals. A foul smell rose from the carrion beside the road. Crows quickly gathered around the carrion in the field.

english_meaning: A tapering orange-colored root eaten as a vegetable. It is known for its crisp texture and sweet flavor when eaten raw. The vegetable is highly nutritious and a good source of vitamin A. It is widely used in salads, stews, and even desserts like cakes.
example_sentence: Bugs Bunny is famous for constantly chewing on a carrot. She grated a fresh carrot into the salad bowl. Drinking carrot juice is very good for your eyesight. He added chopped celery and carrot to the chicken soup.

english_meaning: Having the orange color of a carrot. Having bright red or orange-red hair. Resembling a carrot in color or appearance.
example_sentence: The boy had carroty hair that everyone noticed. The sky turned a carroty orange at sunset. She dyed her hair a bright carroty shade. His carroty beard gleamed in the sunlight.

english_meaning: To become so excited or involved that you lose control of your feelings or actions.
example_sentence: She got carried away with the music. Don’t get carried away by promises. The crowd was carried away by his speech. I got carried away and spent too much money.

english_meaning: To move something to the next stage, especially figures, plans, or ideas.
example_sentence: The balance will be carried forward to next month. They carried forward the project to next year. Let’s carry forward his legacy. The unused funds were carried forward.

english_meaning: To manage something successfully, especially when it seems hard. To win a prize, award, or victory. To carry something or someone away from a place. To perform or present something well.
example_sentence: She managed to carry off the role perfectly despite her nervousness. The team carried off the championship after a tough match. Thieves carried off valuable jewelry from the house. He carried off the speech with great confidence.

english_meaning: To continue doing something, to behave in an excited or emotional way.
example_sentence: Please carry on with your work. She carried on talking despite the noise. They carried on after the interruption. Stop carrying on and calm down.

english_meaning: To talk continuously and annoyingly about something. To talk too much or complain repeatedly about something.
example_sentence: He keeps carrying on about his new car. Stop carrying on about the same topic. She carried on about her problems for hours. They were carrying on about the weather.

english_meaning: To continue a relationship or activity, to behave improperly. To continue doing something.
example_sentence: He’s been carrying on with his studies. She carried on with another colleague. They carried on with their plan. Stop carrying on with that attitude.

english_meaning: To perform, complete, or execute something. To perform a task, complete a duty, fulfill an order, conduct an activity, or put a plan into action.
example_sentence: The team carried out the experiment successfully. Orders must be carried out carefully. They carried out the plan as instructed. Police carried out an investigation.

english_meaning: To transfer or move something from one time, place, or situation to another. To continue to have an effect or influence into another period or situation.
example_sentence: The tension carried over into the next meeting. Unused leave can be carried over. His anger carried over to his work. They carried over the rules to the new system.

english_meaning: To bear a heavy burden of suffering or responsibility patiently. To endure long-lasting hardship without complaint. To accept a duty that brings pain or sacrifice.
synonyms: ["Bear a burden","Endure","Suffer patiently","Shoulder responsibility","Put up with","Sustain hardship"]
example_sentence: She carried the cross of her family's debts for years. After his father's death he had to carry the cross alone. Every leader must carry the cross of criticism. He carried the cross of that mistake all his life.

english_meaning: Complete freedom to act as one thinks best. Unconditional authority; full discretionary power.
example_sentence: The new manager was given carte blanche to reorganize the department. The designer had carte blanche to create the most luxurious interior. She was given carte blanche to decorate the house as she wished. The government gave the military carte blanche to deal with the crisis. He used his carte blanche to implement radical changes.

english_meaning: Firm, whitish, flexible connective tissue found in various forms in the larynx and respiratory tract, in structures such as the external ear, and in the articulating surfaces of joints. It is more widespread in the infant skeleton, being replaced by bone during growth.
example_sentence: The human nose and ears are supported by cartilage. A torn cartilage in the knee can be very painful. Sharks have skeletons made of cartilage, not bone. The doctor explained that the damage to his cartilage was severe. Cartilage allows for smooth movement between joints.

english_meaning: The science and art of making maps. The study of maps and their design. The practice of representing geographical areas graphically.
example_sentence: Digital tools have transformed modern cartography. He studied cartography before joining the survey department. Ancient cartography relied on travellers' reports. The exhibition displayed the history of cartography.

english_meaning: To cut something into a shape, design, or pieces. To cut or shape a material such as wood, stone, or meat using a sharp tool. To make distinct marks, lines, or designs on a surface. To create or establish something with effort (for example: a career or path).
example_sentence: The piece of wood has been carved out into the shape of flower. They carved their initials on the desk. She carved a place for herself in the fashion world. People should remember that our proposals aren't carved in stone.

english_meaning: To establish a unique place or position for oneself in a field, market, or society where one can be acknowledged, successful, or influential. It often implies effort, strategy, and skill in standing out from others.
synonyms: ["Establish oneself","Create a space","Make a mark","Gain recognition"]
antonyms: ["Blend in","Be lost","Fail to stand out","Be unnoticed"]
example_sentence: She carved a niche for herself in the fashion industry with her innovative designs. Small businesses can carve a niche by serving unique local needs. He carved a niche in history as a pioneering scientist. The author carved a niche in literature by writing stories about

english_meaning: Something that is fixed, permanent, or cannot be changed. Rules, decisions, plans, or statements that are permanent or very difficult to change. It suggests certainty and finality, like something engraved into stone that cannot be erased or modified easily.
example_sentence: The deadline for the project is not carved in stone, so we can extend it if needed. Our plan is not carved in stone; we can adjust it later. Company policies are not carved in stone and may change over time. The schedule is carved in stone, so no changes are allowed now.

english_meaning: To create your own way in life instead of following others; to make independent choices and build your own future. To live life according to one’s own decisions, ideas, and goals rather than copying others or following a fixed tradition. It shows independence, originality, and self-direction in career, study, or life choices.
synonyms: ["Follow one’s own way","Make one’s own way","Forge one’s own path","Go one’s own route","Be independent"]
antonyms: ["Follow the crowd","Conform to others","Copy others","Depend on others","Go with the flow"]
example_sentence: She decided to carve her own path instead of joining the family business. Many young artists carve their own path in the world of music. He left a stable job to carve his own path as an entrepreneur. Despite pressure from society, she carved her own path in science.

english_meaning: To establish, create, or achieve something with effort and determination. To cut or shape something literally (but most often used metaphorically in careers, lives, or spaces). To create or obtain something that helps you by skillful activities.
example_sentence: I want to carve out the name for myself around the global. Finally carved out a niche for the sport in the school's athletic program. The new start-up company carved out a large chunk of the market within a year. She carved out a reputation among her male colleagues. She carved out a reputation for herself as a high-powered lawyer. He carved out a career in law. She carved out time for her family.

english_meaning: To build a successful career with effort, skill, and determination, often in a competitive field. To create a place for yourself in a profession or industry through hard work, persistence, and talent. It often suggests starting from nothing or a difficult position and gradually achieving recognition or success.
synonyms: ["Build a career","Establish a career","Make a name in a profession","Rise in profession","Develop a career path"]
antonyms: ["Fail in career","Lose direction in profession","Remain unemployed","Struggle without progress","Stagnate professionally"]
example_sentence: She worked hard to carve out a career in medicine. After many struggles, he carved out a career in journalism. They carved out a career in the IT industry through dedication. He moved to a big city to carve out a career in acting.

word: Carve out a name for oneself
english_meaning: To stand out from others. To become distinguished. To earn respect in a profession. To create personal identity. To become famous, respected, or successful through your own effort. To build a reputation, recognition, or success by working hard and showing talent, especially in a competitive field. It suggests achieving distinction independently.
synonyms: ["Make a name for oneself","Build a reputation","Establish oneself","Gain recognition","Rise to prominence"]
antonyms: ["Remain unknown","Lose reputation","Fade into obscurity","Stay unnoticed","Fail to gain recognition"]
example_sentence: She worked hard to carve out a name for herself in the medical field. The young artist carved out a name for himself with unique paintings. He moved to another city to carve out a name for himself. With dedication, she carved out a name for herself as a journalist.

english_meaning: To create a special position for yourself in a particular field. To successfully establish yourself in a unique or specialized area, especially where there is competition, by using your skills, ideas, or qualities.
synonyms: ["Establish yourself","Find your place","Specialize","Stand out","Create a position","Make a name"]
antonyms: ["Blend in","Lose identity","Follow the crowd","Remain ordinary","Fail to stand out"]
example_sentence: She carved out a niche in digital marketing for small businesses. The company carved out a niche by offering eco friendly packaging. He carved out a niche as a freelance translator. The app carved out a niche among language learners.

word: Carve out a place for oneself
english_meaning: To find a unique role by effort. To create a successful position or reputation through effort. To work hard and gradually build a recognized role, identity, or success in a particular field, society, or group. To achieve recognition through hard work. To build one's own opportunity.
synonyms: ["Establish oneself","Make a name for oneself","Build a reputation","Create a niche","Secure a position","Gain recognition"]
antonyms: ["Lose one's position","Fade into obscurity","Remain unnoticed","Fail to establish oneself","Fall behind"]
example_sentence: She carved out a place for herself in the tech industry through innovation. The young writer carved out a place for himself among famous authors. With dedication, he carved out a place for himself in the competitive market. They carved out a place for themselves in the community by helping others.

english_meaning: To deliberately set aside or create time in a busy schedule for a specific activity, person, or task. It means making space in your day even when you are busy.
synonyms: ["Make time","Set aside time","Allocate time","Schedule time","Free up time"]
example_sentence: I try to carve out time every morning for exercise. She carved out time from her busy schedule to meet her friend. Parents should carve out time for their children despite work pressure. He carved out time to learn English after his job.

english_meaning: To divide something into parts, often in a way that is unfair or for sharing. To divide land, territory, or resources among people or groups. To split profits, responsibilities, or assets. To cut food into pieces (literal use). To divide something in a way that may be unfair or competitive.
example_sentence: The company was carved up between the two investors after the merger. The politicians carved up the land for their own benefit. They carved up the cake and shared it among the children. After the war, the country was carved up by foreign powers.

english_meaning: A man who is charming and loves many women. A man known for being a smooth talker and often romantically involved with many women.
example_sentence: He acted like a Casanova at the party. The novel’s hero was a Casanova. Everyone knows him as the office Casanova. He tried to impress her like a Casanova.

english_meaning: A small waterfall, typically one of several that fall in stages down a steep rocky slope. A mass of something that falls or hangs in copious or graceful quantities. A process whereby something, typically information or knowledge, is successively passed on or distributed through different levels. To fall, pour, flow, or hang in large amounts. To arrange or pass down through a series of stages, usually from top to bottom.
example_sentence: Water cascaded down the rocky stairs during the heavy rainstorm. The new company policies will cascade down to all employees by next week. We discovered a beautiful cascade of water falling into the serene pool below. Her shiny dark hair cascaded down her back in elegant curls.

english_meaning: Something that brings a lot of money. A steady source of income or profit. A business, product, or investment that regularly earns a lot of money for a company with little effort or cost.
example_sentence: That new app is a real cash cow for the company. The company’s old software is still a cash cow, generating millions every year. The luxury car segment became the firm’s cash cow. Their smartphone app is a cash cow that funds new projects. Tourism is a cash cow for many developing countries.

english_meaning: To exchange chips, shares, or assets for cash, especially after gambling or investment. To withdraw money from an account, investment, or pension. To sell one's holdings to take profits. Informally, to take money out and end one's involvement in something. In slang, sometimes used to mean dying.
example_sentence: He decided to cash out his shares before the market dropped. After winning at the casino, she went to cash out her chips. Many early investors cashed out when the company went public. He cashed out his savings to buy a new house. They cashed out their pension fund early.

english_meaning: The kidney-shaped edible seed of the cashew tree. A popular dry fruit eaten roasted, salted, or used in cooking. A nut rich in healthy fats, protein, and minerals. The seed that grows attached to the bottom of the cashew apple.
example_sentence: She added roasted cashew nuts to the rice. Cashew nuts are a good source of protein. He is allergic to cashew nuts. The shopkeeper sells cashew nuts by the kilogram.

english_meaning: A long starchy root vegetable with brown skin and firm white flesh. A tropical crop used to make flour, tapioca, and starch. The shrubby plant that produces this root. A staple food that must be cooked before it is safe to eat.
example_sentence: Cassava is a staple food in many tropical regions. Tapioca pearls are made from cassava starch. She peeled and boiled the cassava roots. Raw cassava should never be eaten.

english_meaning: To throw or hurl something forcefully. To cause light or a shadow to appear on a surface. The group of actors who take part in a play, movie, or other production. A solid object made by pouring a liquid substance into a mold and letting it harden, such as a plaster cast for a broken limb.
example_sentence: The fisherman cast his net into the sea. The lamp cast a warm glow over the room. The play has a cast of twenty actors. She had to wear a cast on her arm for six weeks. The tree cast a long shadow on the ground.

english_meaning: To untie a moored boat and allow it to float free. To discard or get rid of something no longer needed. To throw off something that has been constraining. In knitting, to remove stitches from the needle at the end.
example_sentence: The fishermen cast off at dawn and headed out towards the open sea. She cast off her inhibitions after moving to the city and found a confidence she had never known before. He cast off the ropes and the boat drifted slowly away from the pier. She cast off the last row of stitches and the scarf was finally complete. It is time to cast off the outdated attitudes that have held this community back for so long.

english_meaning: To be the first to criticize, accuse, or punish someone. Often used as a warning against judging others if you are not free from fault yourself.
example_sentence: Don’t cast the first stone unless you’re innocent. She cast the first stone during the argument. He was quick to cast the first stone at his rival. People love to cast the first stone online.

english_meaning: To vomit, to throw up the contents of the stomach, usually because of sickness, disgust, or overeating.
example_sentence: He drank too much and cast up his accounts. After eating spoiled food, he cast up his accounts all night. The sailor cast up his accounts during the rough sea voyage. The child cast up his accounts after eating too many sweets. She felt dizzy and nearly cast up her accounts during the long bus ride.

english_meaning: A social class or group into which a person is born, especially in Hindu society. A rigid social system that divides people based on birth, occupation, or heritage. A hereditary class distinguished by relative wealth, rank, or profession. Any exclusive social group with distinctions of hierarchy.
example_sentence: The caste system has been part of Indian society for centuries. He belongs to a well-known caste in his village. Discrimination based on caste is illegal in many countries. Marriages often take place within the same caste in traditional families.

english_meaning: To reprimand or criticize severely. To punish or rebuke harshly. To scold strongly for a fault or mistake. To express strong disapproval through words. Often used in formal contexts such as journalism, courts, or official statements to indicate sharp and public criticism of a person, institution, or action.
example_sentence: The judge castigated the lawyer for misleading the court. Newspapers castigated the minister over the corruption scandal. The coach castigated the players for their poor performance. She was castigated by her parents for staying out late. The report castigates the company for ignoring safety rules.

english_meaning: Giving something valuable, wise, or beautiful to people who cannot understand or appreciate it. Offering valuable advice, knowledge, kindness, art, or opportunities to people who do not recognize their worth. It is often used when someone wastes effort on an ungrateful or ignorant audience.
synonyms: ["Wasting wisdom on the ungrateful","Offering value to the undeserving","Speaking to deaf ears","Wasting good advice","Giving treasure to fools"]
example_sentence: Explaining advanced poetry to students who were not interested felt like casting pearls before swine. She spent hours giving sincere advice to people who mocked her, which was like casting pearls before swine. Offering rare books to careless readers is casting pearls before swine. The scientist felt he was casting pearls before swine when the audience ignored his important research.

english_meaning: A large building or group of fortified buildings usually built for protection by a king or noble. A heavy chess piece that can move any number of unoccupied squares horizontally or vertically, also known as a rook. To make a special move in chess involving the king and a rook.
example_sentence: The ancient castle stood high on the hill overlooking the valley. Tourists gathered to explore the grand stone towers of the royal castle. In chess, it is often wise to castle early to protect your king. The knight led his troops back to the castle grounds before sunset.

english_meaning: The removal of the testicles of a male animal or man. The act of rendering an individual incapable of reproduction by removing the gonads. The process of removing the stamens from a flower to prevent self-pollination. A metaphorical deprivation of power, vitality, or effectiveness. The surgical or chemical procedure used to eliminate hormonal influence for medical or punitive reasons.
example_sentence: The farmer scheduled the castration of the young bulls for early spring. Historically, castration was sometimes used to create soprano singers known as castrati. The critic argued that the censorship of the film was a symbolic castration of the director's vision. Medical castration may be recommended as a treatment for certain types of advanced prostate cancer.

english_meaning: Relaxed and informal in manner or dress. Happening by chance without planning. Not regular or permanent, especially of work. Showing little concern or attention. Suitable for everyday use rather than formal occasions.
example_sentence: He wore casual clothes to the party. Their meeting was purely casual, not planned. She works as a casual employee at the shop. He gave a casual glance at the menu.

english_meaning: A thief who breaks into upper stories of buildings by stealthily climbing walls, pipes, or roofs. A burglar characterized by agility, quiet movement, and covert entry skills.
example_sentence: The cat burglar managed to scale the high mansion wall without triggering any alarms. Police are hunting for a notorious cat burglar who stole priceless paintings from the top floor apartment. The jewelry was taken so silently that everyone suspected a professional cat burglar. Wearing dark clothes, the cat burglar slipped through the skylight in the dead of night.

english_meaning: Referring to a sudden, violent, and disastrous event that causes great destruction or change. Something extremely significant and life-altering, often used for natural disasters, social upheavals, or major crises.
example_sentence: The cataclysmic earthquake destroyed the entire city within minutes. Climate change could lead to cataclysmic floods and droughts in the future. The war had cataclysmic effects on the nation’s economy and people. The fall of the empire was a cataclysmic event that reshaped history.

english_meaning: An underground cemetery consisting of tunnels or passages with recesses for tombs. A subterranean burial place with galleries or chambers. An underground complex used for burial purposes. A network of underground tunnels used as graves.
example_sentence: The ancient catacombs beneath Rome hold thousands of graves. Tourists explored the dimly lit catacombs. Early Christians were buried in the catacombs. The catacombs stretch for miles underground.

english_meaning: A complete list of items, typically arranged systematically and often with descriptions. A publication or booklet containing details of goods, products, or services for sale. A list of books, works of art, or other items in a library, museum, or collection. To make a systematic list of items. To enter something in a register or record.
example_sentence: The library keeps a detailed catalogue of every book in its collection. She flipped through the clothing catalogue looking for a winter coat. Researchers must catalogue each specimen before storing it. The museum has begun to catalogue its ancient artifacts online.

english_meaning: To cause or accelerate a reaction by acting as a catalyst. To precipitate or bring about an event or change. To act as a catalyst in a chemical process.
example_sentence: Enzymes catalyse metabolic reactions inside the human cell. Her passionate speech helped to catalyse a nationwide movement for reform. High temperatures can catalyse the chemical reaction much faster. The government hopes the new tax incentives will catalyse investment.

english_meaning: The acceleration of a chemical reaction by a catalyst. An increase in the rate of a chemical reaction due to the participation of an additional substance called a catalyst. A process in which a reaction rate is changed by a substance that is not consumed during the reaction.
example_sentence: Enzymes are protein molecules that perform catalysis in biological systems. Industrial catalysis is essential for the production of synthetic fertilizers. Platinum is widely used for catalysis in automobile exhaust systems. The discovery of a new form of catalysis revolutionized organic chemistry.

english_meaning: Something that causes a change or speeds up a process without itself being affected. A  substance or an agent that accelerates a chemical reaction or brings about significant change in a situation or process without undergoing permanent change itself. It can be literal, in chemistry, or metaphorical, in social, economic, or personal contexts.
example_sentence: The new manager was a catalyst for positive changes in the company. Enzymes act as catalysts in many biological reactions. The invention of the internet was a catalyst for global communication. Her speech served as a catalyst for social reform.

english_meaning: Relating to, acting as, or involving a catalyst. Causing, accelerating, or facilitating an action, change, or event without itself undergoing any permanent chemical change.
example_sentence: The catalytic converter helps lower the amount of toxic gas emitted by automobiles. Her inspiring speeches played a catalytic role in sparking the social reform movement. Complex chemical reactions often rely on catalytic agents to proceed smoothly at lower temperatures. The new investment acted as a catalytic force for local economic development.

english_meaning: To cause or accelerate a reaction by acting as a catalyst. To cause an action or process to begin. To bring about; to inspire.
example_sentence: The enzyme catalyzes the breakdown of the protein. The new law catalyzed a wave of protests across the country. His speech catalyzed the crowd into action. Technology has catalyzed significant changes in the workplace. A single event can catalyze major social reform.

english_meaning: To throw or launch something with great force, or to move someone suddenly into a new position or situation. A simple machine used to hurl stones or other objects, especially in ancient warfare.
example_sentence: The soldiers used a catapult to launch stones over the wall. His viral video catapulted him to international fame. The strong winds catapulted debris across the road. The invention catapulted the company into the global market.

english_meaning: A sudden event that causes very great trouble or destruction, A bad situation, An event causing great and usually sudden damage or suffering, a disaster, Something very unfortunate or unsuccessful
example_sentence: The attempt to expand the business was a catastrophe for the firm. Early warnings of rising water levels prevented another major catastrophe. We have had a few catastrophes with the food for the party.

english_meaning: Extremely harmful, disastrous, or causing great damage. Something that results in severe destruction, loss, or failure. It refers to events or situations that have extremely negative consequences, often unexpected or sudden.
example_sentence: The earthquake had a catastrophic impact on the city. Poor planning led to a catastrophic failure of the project. Climate change could have catastrophic effects on agriculture. A catastrophic storm destroyed many homes along the coast.

english_meaning: In a way that causes great damage or disaster. Describes actions, events, or outcomes that result in extreme misfortune, failure, or destruction. Often used to emphasize severity or disastrous consequences.
example_sentence: The bridge collapsed catastrophically during the storm. The company failed catastrophically after mismanaging funds. His decision to ignore warnings ended catastrophically. The wildfire spread catastrophically through the dry forest.

english_meaning: The belief that the Earth has been shaped by sudden, violent events such as floods, earthquakes, or volcanic eruptions. A scientific theory in geology which states that major changes in the Earth's surface were caused by sudden natural disasters rather than slow and gradual processes. It suggests that events like massive floods, volcanic eruptions, earthquakes, or asteroid impacts played a key role in shaping landscapes and causing extinction of species.
example_sentence: Catastrophism explains mass extinction as the result of sudden natural disasters. Early geologists supported catastrophism to describe changes in Earth's history. The asteroid impact theory supports aspects of catastrophism. Catastrophism contrasts with the idea that geological changes happen slowly over time.

english_meaning: To publicly shout, whistle, or comment at someone in a rude or sexual way, often to annoy or attract attention. A loud, often rude or suggestive whistle, shout, or comment aimed at someone to express disapproval, ridicule, or sexual attraction.
example_sentence: He catcalled the passerby, which was rude and inappropriate. The crowd catcalled the politician during his speech. Teenagers catcall at drivers for fun. The actor ignored the catcalls from the crowd. Catcalls from the audience interrupted the speaker. Women often face catcalls while walking on the street.

word: Catch a tiger by the tail
english_meaning: To take on a task or challenge that turns out to be much harder than expected. To become involved in something dangerous or difficult to control. To gain something powerful but risky. To face unexpected trouble after a bold move. To handle a situation that is difficult to release or manage.
synonyms: ["Bite off more than one can chew","Get in over one's head","Take on trouble","Court disaster"]
antonyms: ["Play it safe","Take a small step","Avoid risk"]
example_sentence: By accepting the deal, he caught a tiger by the tail. The company caught a tiger by the tail with the new project. She realized she had caught a tiger by the tail after signing the contract. Sometimes, ambition makes you catch a tiger by the tail.

english_meaning: To achieve something very rare, special, or hard to repeat. To succeed in doing something extraordinary that usually happens only once. It refers to a unique moment of luck, creativity, or timing that cannot easily be recreated. It is often used for artists, businesses, or events that become unexpectedly successful.
synonyms: ["Achieve rare success","Strike gold","Have a once in a lifetime success","Hit the jackpot"]
example_sentence: The band caught lightning in a bottle with their first album. The company knows it cannot easily catch lightning in a bottle again. That movie was a hit, but the sequel failed to catch lightning in a bottle. She caught lightning in a bottle when her first novel became a bestseller.

english_meaning: A Singaporean and Malaysian English slang expression meaning to not understand something at all. To be completely confused or unable to follow what is being said. Used colloquially to express total incomprehension.
example_sentence: I completely catch no ball when she explains the technical details of the project. He sat through the entire lecture and still caught no ball about what the professor was teaching. She admitted she caught no ball the first time she heard the new team's jargon. When they switched to coding language, I just catch no ball at all. He looked at the instructions and said honestly that he caught no ball.

english_meaning: To attract someone’s attention or interest. To attract someone’s interest or liking suddenly. When something “catches one’s fancy,” it appeals to a person’s taste, imagination, or preference. It means the person feels drawn to it.
example_sentence: The colorful painting caught her fancy immediately. That new phone model caught his fancy at the store. Traveling abroad caught their fancy after watching the documentary. The music band caught the audience’s fancy with their performance.

english_meaning: A well-known sentence or phrase associated with a particular person, group, or advertisement. A memorable expression that is repeated often and becomes popular. A short striking phrase used to attract attention.
example_sentence: The actor's catch phrase became popular all over the country. Every brand needs a strong catch phrase for its advertisement. The politician's catch phrase was printed on every banner. Children often imitate the catch phrase of their favourite cartoon character. The new catch phrase of the campaign attracted millions of viewers.

english_meaning: To surprise someone when they are not prepared. To catch someone at a moment of weakness or confusion. To make someone physically lose their balance by a sudden movement.
example_sentence: The reporter's unexpected question caught the minister off balance. The sudden gust of wind caught him off balance and he nearly fell. Her direct criticism caught me off balance during the meeting. The boxer caught his opponent off balance with a quick left hook.

english_meaning: To attract someone’s attention or interest, often because something or someone is noticeable, beautiful, or unusual. It can also mean to make eye contact with someone.
example_sentence: The bright dress caught everyone’s eye. A new painting in the gallery caught my eye. His talent caught the teacher’s eye during the competition. While walking in the market, a golden necklace caught her eye.

english_meaning: To complete tasks, study, reading, rest, or other activities that you did not finish earlier. It is used when someone wants to reach the current level after falling behind.
example_sentence: I need to catch up on my homework after being absent from school. She spent the weekend catching up on her emails. He is trying to catch up on the latest news. During the holidays, I like to catch up on my reading.

english_meaning: A no-win situation or paradox. A situation where a person cannot escape because of contradictory rules or conditions. It describes a paradoxical problem with no satisfactory solution. A dilemma in which every choice leads to a negative outcome. A problem where trying to solve it creates another problem that makes it unsolvable. A circular situation where the condition for success contradicts the condition for eligibility.
example_sentence: He wanted to get experience to apply for the job, but he couldn’t get the job without experience, that was a Catch-2. The company wouldn’t lend money to new businesses, and without a loan, starting a business was impossible, it was a Catch-2. To join the university, she needed a recommendation, but to get the recommendation, she had to already be enrolled, a true Catch-2. You can’t get health insurance without a pre-existing condition check, but you need insurance to afford the check, that’s a Catch-22.

english_meaning: An area of land from which rainfall flows into a river, lake, or reservoir. The action of collecting water, especially rain, for later use. The geographical area served by a school, hospital, or other public institution. The total amount of water collected in such an area.
antonyms: ["Outflow","Discharge area","Drainage outlet","Desert","Dry land","Runoff zone","Wasteland","Barren area","Outside area","Periphery"]
example_sentence: Heavy rain in the catchment area raised the level of the dam. The school admits children living within its catchment. Deforestation has damaged the river's natural catchment. Engineers are studying the catchment to improve water supply.

english_meaning: Pleasant and easily remembered. Tending to catch the interest or attention. Likely to attract attention. Requiring exceptional skill or caution in performance or handling. Having concealed difficulty.
