The phrase can also imply a sudden, forceful departure from something.
example_sentence: The children love to jump off the swing at the highest point. We decided to jump off the project with a brainstorming session. He had to jump off the moving train carefully. The artist hopes this grant will help her career jump off. Don't jump off to conclusions so quickly.

english_meaning: To criticize someone quickly and severely for something they have said or done. To take immediate advantage of an opportunity. To get onto a moving vehicle or object.
example_sentence: The boss jumped on him for being late again. She jumped on the new business idea immediately. He jumped on the bus just as it was leaving. Critics jumped on the minister for his careless remarks. Investors jumped on the opportunity to buy shares.

english_meaning: To join others in doing something that is currently popular or fashionable, especially after it has become successful or widely accepted. It often implies that a person supports something only because it’s trendy or successful, not because they truly believe in it.
example_sentence: Everyone is jumping on the bandwagon of social media trends. After the team started winning, many new fans jumped on the bandwagon. When online business became profitable, everyone jumped on the bandwagon and started their own stores. Politicians often jump on the bandwagon of popular movements to gain votes. He didn’t believe in the cause at first, but he jumped on the bandwagon when it became popular.

english_meaning: To leave a place or vehicle quickly by leaping. To be very noticeable or striking. To appear suddenly and surprise someone.
synonyms: ["Leap out","Spring out","Stand out","Catch the eye","Emerge suddenly"]
example_sentence: He jumped out of the car and ran into the house. Her red dress really jumped out at the party. The mistake jumped out at me as soon as I read the page. A cat jumped out from behind the bush. His name jumped out from the list of winners.

english_meaning: To leap across or above something in order to get to the other side. To skip or omit a step, section, or part.
example_sentence: The horse jumped over the fence gracefully. He jumped over the puddle to keep his shoes dry. She jumped over the introduction and started with chapter two. The dog jumped over the wall easily. You should not jump over important safety steps.

english_meaning: To do something too soon or before the proper time, often without enough preparation or before it is allowed. It originally comes from runners starting a race before the starting gun is fired.
example_sentence: He jumped the gun by announcing the results early. He jumped the gun and submitted his application early. He jumped the gun and announced the project before it was officially approved. Don’t jump the gun, wait until we get all the data before making a decision. The students jumped the gun and submitted their reports before the teacher’s instructions.

english_meaning: To pass through something by leaping. Used often in the idiom to indicate doing many difficult tasks to please someone or achieve something.
example_sentence: The tiger jumped through the ring of fire. Applicants had to jump through many stages of testing. The dog was trained to jump through a hoop. She had to jump through a lot to get the visa. They made him jump through several procedures.

english_meaning: To go through a long series of difficult or annoying tasks or procedures in order to achieve something or please someone. To make great efforts, often unnecessarily, to satisfy a demand.
synonyms: ["Go to great lengths","Struggle","Bend over backwards","Make great efforts"]
example_sentence: I had to jump through hoops to get my documents verified. Employees are forced to jump through hoops for a small pay rise. She jumped through hoops to please her boss. Getting a bank loan makes you jump through hoops. Do not make customers jump through hoops for a simple refund.

english_meaning: To move quickly and suddenly from one place or topic to another. It implies a rapid transition, often without much warning or smooth progression. This phrase can be used literally for physical movement or figuratively for shifts in conversation, thought, or action.
example_sentence: She tends to jump to conclusions without considering all the facts. He jumped to his feet when he heard the alarm. Let's not jump to any decisions before we've discussed all options. The conversation kept jumping to different topics, making it hard to follow. I had to jump to action when I saw the child fall.

english_meaning: To suddenly or quickly rise from a sitting or lying position or to move upwards rapidly. It often implies a swift, energetic, and sometimes unexpected movement. It can also refer to an increase in quantity, value, or level.
example_sentence: He had to jump up quickly when his name was called. The child jumped up and down with excitement. Prices for essential goods are expected to jump up again next month. The dog will jump up on you if you encourage it. We saw the stock market jump up after the positive news.

english_meaning: A place where two or more roads or railroad lines meet or cross. The act or process of joining two or more things together. A point at which two things are joined or connected in a physical structure. The interface or boundary between two different regions within a semiconductor device. A state of being joined or combined into one unit.
example_sentence: The train stopped at a busy junction where three different lines intersected. Scientists studied the junction of the two tectonic plates to predict earthquakes. The junction of their talents resulted in a spectacular performance. In electronics, a p-n junction is essential for the operation of a diode.

english_meaning: A particular point in events or time. A critical moment or turning point. A place where things join or connect. A crisis or decisive period. A moment of significant change or decision.
example_sentence: At this juncture, we need to reconsider our strategy. The negotiations reached a critical juncture last night. The juncture between the two rivers formed a beautiful delta. This is a crucial juncture in the company's history. The juncture of the two roads was marked by an old signpost.

english_meaning: A group of military officers or a small group of people who take control of a government, especially after a coup. It can also mean a committee or council in a general sense.
example_sentence: The military junta took control of the country after the coup. Citizens protested against the oppressive junta. A junta of local leaders decided on the community's rules. Scholars often study historical juntas to understand political instability.

english_meaning: Relating to law or the administration of justice. Concerned with legal matters, the judicial system, or the authority of courts. It describes anything that has a legal or formal judicial aspect.
example_sentence: The lawyer explained the juridical implications of the new law. Juridical decisions must be respected by all citizens. The committee examined the juridical framework of the contract. His argument was strong from a juridical standpoint.

english_meaning: The official power or authority to make legal decisions and judgments. The territory or area within which such authority can be exercised. The range or scope of an organization's control or influence. The right to interpret and apply the law. Authority in general over any area of activity.
example_sentence: The case falls outside the court's jurisdiction. Local police have no jurisdiction beyond the city limits. Tax matters come under the jurisdiction of the federal government. The tribunal claimed jurisdiction over the dispute.

english_meaning: The theory, philosophy, and science of law. The study of the principles on which legal systems are built. A particular system or body of law of a country or area. The branch of knowledge dealing with the interpretation, application, and development of legal rules.
example_sentence: He is studying jurisprudence at a well-known university. Islamic jurisprudence has a long and rich history. Modern jurisprudence covers human rights and constitutional law. The judge is well versed in international jurisprudence. Students of law must understand the basics of jurisprudence.

english_meaning: Able to be defended or explained as reasonable, fair, or acceptable. Supported by a valid reason or evidence.
example_sentence: The decision was justifiable under the circumstances. Her anger was justifiable after the unfair accusation. The expense is justifiable because it improved safety. The officer gave a justifiable explanation for the delay.

english_meaning: To stick out or extend beyond something. To project outward or forward from a surface, edge, or line. It is often used to describe physical objects like rocks, balconies, chins, or buildings that extend out noticeably. The word suggests something that is prominent and not flat or even.
example_sentence: Sharp rocks jut out from the side of the mountain. His chin juts forward when he speaks confidently. A wooden balcony juts over the narrow street.

english_meaning: A young person or something related to youth. A child or young person who is not yet an adult. It can also describe behavior that is childish, immature, or not appropriate for adults.
example_sentence: The court handles juvenile cases separately from adult crimes. Juvenile animals depend on their parents for survival. His juvenile behavior made the meeting unprofessional. The program focuses on rehabilitating juvenile offenders.

english_meaning: To place two or more things side by side, especially for the purpose of comparison or contrast. To position contrasting elements close together so their differences or similarities become more apparent. Used in art, writing, and design to create meaning by placing unlike things next to each other. To arrange items in close proximity to highlight a relationship between them.
example_sentence: The exhibition juxtaposed modern sculptures with ancient artifacts to highlight contrasts across eras.  The director juxtaposed scenes of wealth and poverty to emphasize social inequality.  The article juxtaposed two opposing viewpoints on the same issue.  Designers often juxtapose bold colors with neutral tones for visual impact.  The photographer juxtaposed images of nature and industry in his latest collection.

english_meaning: The fact of putting things that are not similar next to each other. Placing two or more things side by side, often to compare, contrast, or highlight differences, similarities. The fact of putting people or things together, especially in order to show a contrast or a new relationship between them.
example_sentence: The juxtaposition of modern buildings beside ancient ruins highlights the city’s history. What an interesting juxtaposition of fledgeling popular culture only metres away from chanting mobs of protesters. It was an interesting juxtaposition. Still, many of her paintings contain unusual subject matters and interesting juxtapositions.

english_meaning: An extreme or irrational fear of novelty, newness, or change. Very similar to neophobia, it specifically relates to an overwhelming dread of anything new or different.
example_sentence: Kainophobia prevented him from moving to a new city. Her kainophobia was triggered by the announcement of a new school curriculum. He struggled with kainophobia after returning from war. Kainophobia can make life in a rapidly changing world very difficult.

english_meaning: A system of government run by the worst, least qualified, or most unscrupulous citizens. The opposite of a meritocracy.
synonyms: ["Government by the worst","rule of incompetents","corrupt regime","ineptocracy"]
example_sentence: Critics described the corrupt regime as a kakistocracy. The satirist wrote that the nation had slipped into kakistocracy. In a kakistocracy, incompetence rises to the top. Many feared the election would entrench a kakistocracy.

english_meaning: A leafy green vegetable with tough, curly, dark green leaves. A nutritious vegetable eaten cooked, in salads, or as crisps. The plant grown for these edible leaves. A hardy winter crop rich in vitamins.
example_sentence: She added chopped kale to the lentil soup. Kale survives well in cold weather. Baked kale crisps are a healthy snack. Kale is packed with vitamins and minerals.

english_meaning: An unfair or unofficial court that ignores proper legal procedures. A trial in which the outcome is decided in advance. A mock or illegitimate legal proceeding. A court that disregards justice and fairness. Any judgment given without a fair hearing.
example_sentence: The trial was nothing but a kangaroo court. Human rights groups condemned the kangaroo court proceedings. He said the disciplinary hearing was a kangaroo court. Many dictators use kangaroo courts to silence opponents.

english_meaning: Broken, no longer working, or completely useless. Ruined, destroyed, or beyond repair. Finished, defeated, or having failed entirely. Informal word used to describe something that has stopped functioning.
example_sentence: My old laptop is finally kaput. The washing machine went kaput last night. Their business plan seems to have gone kaput. After the accident, the car was completely kaput.

english_meaning: A ten-line stanza form developed by the poet John Keats for his great odes. A stanza of ten iambic pentameter lines combining a Shakespearean quatrain (ABAB) with a Petrarchan sestet (CDECDE or a variation of it). A fixed poetic pattern used in odes such as 'Ode to a Nightingale' and 'Ode on a Grecian Urn'. A hybrid English stanza that blends sonnet elements into ode form. A term used in prosody to describe Keats's characteristic ode structure.
synonyms: ["Ode stanza","Ten-line stanza","Decastich","Keatsian stanza","Ode form","Lyric stanza","Verse form","Strophe"]
example_sentence: The professor explained how the Keatsian ode stanza combines a quatrain with a sestet. Students were asked to write a poem using the Keatsian ode stanza. The Keatsian ode stanza gives the poem a slow, meditative rhythm. Critics admire the balance and music of the Keatsian ode stanza.

english_meaning: Having a sharp edge or point. Intense or strong, as a desire or interest. Eager and enthusiastic about something. Highly developed or sensitive. A British informal term for a funeral lament.
example_sentence: The keen blade of the knife cut through the rope easily. She has a keen interest in ancient history. He is keen to learn new languages. The dog had a keen sense of smell. The keen wind blew through the narrow streets.

english_meaning: To control something or someone strictly. To manage with strict discipline. To carefully limit or restrict. To maintain firm control over a situation. To keep something under close supervision.
example_sentence: The manager keeps a tight rein on the office expenses. Parents should keep a tight rein on their teenagers. She keeps a tight rein on her emotions in public. The government keeps a tight rein on the media.

english_meaning: To stay informed and up to date about something. To regularly follow information, changes, or developments so that you do not fall behind. It is often used for news, technology, education, work trends, or current events.
synonyms: ["Stay informed","Stay updated","Keep up with","Remain aware of","Follow closely"]
example_sentence: Teachers must keep abreast of new teaching methods. Journalists work hard to keep abreast of current events. It is important to keep abreast of changes in climate policy. She reads daily to keep abreast of developments in her field.

english_meaning: To watch carefully, monitor, or pay close attention to someone or something especially to make sure nothing goes wrong.
example_sentence: Can you keep an eye on my bag while I go inside? The teacher kept an eye on the students during the trip. We need to keep an eye on the weather; it might rain soon. Keep an eye on the soup while it’s cooking so it doesn’t burn.

english_meaning: To keep something or someone nearby because it may be useful or needed later. It suggests holding on to an item or maintaining contact with a person instead of throwing it away or letting them go.
example_sentence: I keep a notebook around for ideas. Keep your umbrella around. She keeps snacks around the house. We should keep good friends around.

english_meaning: To continue doing something with determination. To persist with a task or activity despite difficulty, delay, or discouragement until it is completed or progress is made.
example_sentence: She kept at her studies even when the course became difficult. If you keep at the practice, your skills will improve. He told the team to keep at the project until it was finished. Despite many failures, she kept at her goal.

english_meaning: Continue doing something with effort and determination, even if it is difficult or slow. To encourage someone not to stop trying. It means to persist with a task, activity, or goal despite challenges, failures, or slow progress. It emphasizes consistency, patience, and determination until success is achieved.
synonyms: ["Keep going","Persevere","Carry on","Stick with it","Keep trying","Stay with it","Don’t give up"]
example_sentence: You are improving in math, just keep at it and you will succeed. Learning a new language is hard, but keep at it every day. The task is difficult, but if you keep at it, you will finish it. He didn’t understand the lesson at first, but he kept at it until he got it right.

english_meaning: To stay at a distance from someone or something. To avoid going near a person, place, or thing because it may be dangerous, harmful, unwanted, or restricted. It is often used as a warning or advice.
example_sentence: Keep away from that fire. The doctor said to keep away from sweets. A fence keeps animals away. Please keep away from private property.

english_meaning: To stay behind or to stop something or someone from moving forward or being revealed. To remain at a distance, delay movement, or prevent something from being shown, shared, or released.
example_sentence: He kept back the truth. Don’t keep back your emotions. The teacher kept back some marks. I couldn’t keep back my laughter.

english_meaning: To survive or manage to stay alive, especially when one has very little money, food, or resources. It means doing just enough to sustain life, maintaining basic needs like food, shelter, or health.
example_sentence: He worked hard to keep body and soul together. After losing his job, he could hardly keep body and soul together. The poor old man sells fruits just to keep body and soul together. In the desert, the travelers struggled to keep body and soul together until help arrived. During the famine, many families barely managed to keep body and soul together.

english_meaning: To continue working hard despite obstacles or fatigue. Keep working hard and consistently, even when it’s difficult or tiring.
example_sentence: Keep grinding and success will come. Even when tired, he kept grinding through the project. Athletes keep grinding to improve their skills. She keeps grinding day and night for her dream.

english_meaning: To talk about something repeatedly in an annoying way. To nag about something continuously. To keep reminding someone of a mistake or issue. To repeatedly stress the same point. To dwell on a topic without moving forward
synonyms: ["Nag about","Go on about","Dwell on","Repeat constantly","Keep talking about"]
example_sentence: He keeps harping on about my late arrival. Stop harping on the same issue and let us move forward. She was harping on about the budget cuts during the entire meeting. My brother keeps harping on about healthy eating habits.

english_meaning: To continue doing something without stopping. To persist or carry on an action, even if it is difficult or tiring.
example_sentence: She kept on talking despite interruptions. He kept on talking even when no one was listening. Keep on trying, and you will succeed.

english_meaning: To stay confident and hopeful despite challenges or sadness. To remain positive, confident, or courageous in difficult or challenging situations, without showing fear or discouragement.
example_sentence: Despite losing the match, he kept his head up. She kept her head up while dealing with workplace stress. Keep your head up; better days are coming. He kept his head up even when everyone doubted him.

english_meaning: To stay out of trouble. To avoid doing anything illegal, wrong, or morally questionable. To behave properly so no one can blame you.
example_sentence: He tries to keep his nose clean and avoid trouble. He just got out of prison, so he’s trying to keep his nose clean. If you want to succeed in this job, keep your nose clean and work hard.

english_meaning: To remain cheerful, brave, and confident, especially in a difficult or challenging situation.
example_sentence: Even after losing his job, he tried to keep his pecker up. Life can be tough sometimes, but you must keep your pecker up. She told her friend to keep his pecker up during the exam stress. Though the team lost several matches, their coach told them to keep their peckers up.

word: Keep ones nose to the grindstone
english_meaning: To work hard and steadily without stopping. To stay focused on a difficult or tedious task. To apply oneself diligently over a long period. To keep working without allowing distractions.
example_sentence: If you keep your nose to the grindstone, you will finish on time. She kept her nose to the grindstone all through college. He tells his staff to keep their noses to the grindstone before the audit. Keeping your nose to the grindstone pays off in the long run.

english_meaning: To hope strongly that something will happen as desired. To wish for good luck for oneself or someone else. To remain hopeful about an uncertain outcome.
synonyms: ["Hope for the best","Wish for luck","Pray","Be hopeful","Touch wood"]
example_sentence: I am keeping my fingers crossed for your interview tomorrow. We kept our fingers crossed until the results were announced. Keep your fingers crossed that the weather stays clear. She kept her fingers crossed hoping for good news from the hospital.

english_meaning: To do what one has promised, or to fulfill a commitment.
synonyms: ["Honor one’s commitment","Be true to one’s word","Stand by one’s promise"]
antonyms: ["Break one’s word","Go back on one’s promise","Betray trust","Fail to keep a promise"]
example_sentence: He promised to help me, and he kept his word. A true leader always keeps his word to his people. If you keep your word, people will trust you more. She said she would be there on time, and she kept her word.

english_meaning: To prevent something from increasing or becoming too great. To maintain constant control over a situation or feeling. To ensure that something stays within manageable bounds. To regulate or monitor something to avoid excess.
example_sentence: She struggled to keep her laughter in check during the meeting. Natural predators help keep the insect population in check. We need to keep our spending in check this month. Regular exercise helps keep blood pressure in check.

english_meaning: To remain motionless without moving any part of the body. To stay quiet and silent, without speaking. To not disturb or interfere with something. To stay calm and composed in a situation.
example_sentence: Please keep still while I take your photograph. The doctor asked the child to keep still during the examination. Keep still and listen to what I am saying. It was hard for the puppy to keep still for even a moment.

english_meaning: Stay positive and strong during difficult times. To encourage someone not to lose hope or confidence when facing problems, failures, or sadness. It suggests staying emotionally strong and maintaining a positive attitude even when things are not going well.
synonyms: ["Stay positive","Stay strong","Don’t lose hope","Be optimistic","Keep going"]
antonyms: ["Lose hope","Give up","Feel discouraged","Be pessimistic","Break down emotionally"]
example_sentence: Keep your chin up, things will get better soon. Even after failing the exam, he told himself to keep his chin up. Keep your chin up and don’t lose hope during hard times. She kept her chin up after losing her job and started looking for new opportunities.

word: Keep your eye on the ball
english_meaning: To stay focused on the main task or goal and not get distracted. It means maintaining attention, awareness, and consistency, especially during important work or situations.
antonyms: ["Lose focus","Get distracted","Ignore the task","Be careless","Lose track"]
example_sentence: If you want to succeed in your exams, you must keep your eye on the ball. The manager told his team to keep their eye on the ball during the project. Even under pressure, she kept her eye on the ball and completed the task on time. It is easy to lose progress if you do not keep your eye on the ball.

word: Keep your feet on the ground
english_meaning: To remain sensible, practical, and realistic. To stay humble despite success, praise, excitement, or wealth. To maintain a balanced judgment and proper perspective
example_sentence: She advised her son to keep his feet on the ground after his promotion. It is important to keep your feet on the ground when dealing with sudden wealth. He kept his feet on the ground despite becoming an overnight sensation. Coaches remind young athletes to keep their feet on the ground after early victories.

english_meaning: To hope strongly that something good will happen. To wish for good luck for oneself or someone else. To express hopeful anticipation while waiting for a result. A superstitious gesture of crossing one finger over another to bring good fortune.
synonyms: ["Hope for the best","Wish for luck","Pray","Stay hopeful","Cross one's fingers","Await hopefully"]
example_sentence: Keep your fingers crossed for my interview tomorrow. We are keeping our fingers crossed that the weather stays clear. She kept her fingers crossed while the results were announced. Let's keep our fingers crossed and hope for the best.

english_meaning: To stay confident and hopeful despite challenges or sadness. To remain positive, brave, or confident in difficult situations and not let problems or failures make you feel defeated.
example_sentence: Keep your head up; things will get better. Even in tough times, she keeps her head up. Keep your head up—you’ve done your best. He told his friend to keep his head up after the loss.

english_meaning: To do what one has promised to do. To fulfill a promise or commitment. To remain true to a spoken agreement. Being reliable and honest about what one says. Not breaking a promise, no matter the circumstances.
synonyms: ["Honor a promise","Fulfill","Stay true","Be reliable","Follow through","Stand by","Deliver","Commit"]
example_sentence: He always keeps his word, no matter how difficult the task is. She promised to help and kept her word. A true leader must keep his word to gain trust. If you keep your word, people will respect you.

english_meaning: A person who guards, manages, or takes care of something. A goalkeeper in sports. A person in charge of a museum, park, or animals. Something worth keeping, informal.
example_sentence: The lighthouse keeper lived alone for years. The keeper saved three goals in the match. The zoo keeper feeds the lions daily. This photograph is definitely a keeper.

english_meaning: A small item kept in memory of the person who gave it or originally owned it. An object preserved as a reminder of an event or experience.
example_sentence: She gave him a silver locket as a keepsake before he left for the war. I bought this beautiful shell as a keepsake of our tropical vacation. The old pocket watch serves as a precious keepsake of his late grandfather. Guests were given personalized mugs as a keepsake of the wedding celebration.

english_meaning: To prevent something from increasing or to stay in a low position. To control or limit something so it does not rise or grow. It can refer to costs, noise, emotions, or numbers. It also means to stay low or not be seen or noticed, especially to avoid trouble or danger.
example_sentence: Keep your voice down. The medicine keeps the fever down. Prices were kept down by the government. Try to keep down your anger.

english_meaning: To prevent oneself or someone from doing something. To avoid doing something oneself. To withhold something from someone. To protect or shield someone or something from harm or trouble. To refrain from expressing a feeling or action.
example_sentence: I couldn’t keep from laughing. Keep from touching the hot stove. She kept herself from crying. We must keep from wasting time.

english_meaning: To remain inside or to continue having something such as contact, control, or possession. To hold back feelings or speech. To include or keep something in mind. To not share information.
example_sentence: The teacher kept the students in after class. I kept in my anger. Keep the cat in during the night. He kept in his feelings. Please keep in touch while you are abroad. The news was kept in to avoid panic.

english_meaning: To stay away from something or not touch or step on it. (Used especially on warning signs to protect property, plants, or unsafe areas.)
example_sentence: Keep off the grass. Please keep off spicy food. He kept off the subject of politics. Keep your hands off my things.

english_meaning: To prevent entry; not allow someone to enter a place. To stay away from something; avoid participation or involvement. To exclude from participation or influence. To resist or prevent something from affecting.
example_sentence: Keep out of the restricted area for your safety. He tried to keep out of the argument between his friends. Please keep out strangers from the private garden. She keeps out of trouble by following the rules.

english_meaning: To follow, stick with, or stay on something. To continue doing something consistently, follow a rule, plan, schedule, or path, or to restrict oneself to a particular topic, route, or routine.
example_sentence: Keep to the path. Try to keep to your budget. He kept to the topic. Please keep to your word.

english_meaning: To maintain or continue at the same level. To continue doing something at the same rate, pace, or standard; to remain informed about something. To not fall behind.
example_sentence: Keep up the good work!. She can’t keep up with the others. Keep up your studies. Prices are kept up by demand.

english_meaning: The base unit of temperature in the international system of units, written as K. A temperature scale that begins at absolute zero, the lowest possible temperature. A unit equal in size to one degree Celsius but starting from a different zero point. Widely used in science and engineering.
example_sentence: Absolute zero is zero kelvin, or minus 273.15 degrees Celsius. The star's surface temperature is about six thousand kelvin. Scientists usually record temperature in kelvin. Room temperature is roughly 293 kelvin.

english_meaning: Neat and well-groomed. Refers to someone or something that is clean, tidy, orderly, and well-maintained in appearance.
example_sentence: She always looks kempt, even after a long day at work. The kempt garden showed the gardener’s dedication. His kempt appearance impressed the interview panel. The hotel rooms were kempt and ready for guests.

english_meaning: The eerie atmosphere of a place that is usually busy but is now empty. The strange feeling caused by abandoned or silent familiar spaces. A coined word describing emptiness that feels haunting. The mood of a deserted school, station or street.
example_sentence: The empty airport at midnight filled him with kenopsia. There is a strange kenopsia in a school during the holidays. Photographers often capture the kenopsia of closed malls. She felt kenopsia walking through the silent office.

english_meaning: An abnormal or intense love and fascination for thunder and lightning. A psychological attraction to or emotional connection with thunderstorms. Feeling a sense of peace or joy during electric storms. Seeking out or admiring the aesthetic beauty of lightning bolts. A paraphilia or specific preference involving atmospheric electricity. A deep emotional bond with the power and sound of the elements during a storm.
example_sentence: As a person with keraunophilia, he always sits by the window during a storm to watch the lightning. Her keraunophilia makes the loud crashes of thunder feel like music rather than something to fear. Most people run for cover during a heavy storm, but his keraunophilia drives him to stand out on the porch. The photographer's keraunophilia led him to travel across the country chasing the most violent thunderstorms.

english_meaning: The extreme or irrational fear of thunder and lightning. A specific phobia in which a person experiences intense fear, anxiety, or panic when they hear thunder or see lightning. The fear may occur during storms or even at the thought of stormy weather. It can lead to avoidance behavior, stress, and physical symptoms like sweating or trembling.
example_sentence: She suffers from keraunophobia and hides in a closed room during thunderstorms. His keraunophobia became worse after he experienced a severe lightning strike as a child. People with keraunophobia often check weather reports frequently to avoid storms. Despite his keraunophobia, he tries to stay calm when thunder starts at night.

english_meaning: A situation in which people become upset, confused, or angry over something, usually something minor. It often involves loud disagreement, disorder, or unnecessary excitement about a small issue.
example_sentence: There was a kerfuffle in the office after the email was sent to the wrong person. The children caused a kerfuffle when they started arguing over the toy. A small pricing error created a huge kerfuffle among customers. The politician tried to calm the kerfuffle caused by his statement.

english_meaning: The softer, usually edible part inside a nut or seed. The central or essential part of something. A small grain or seed. The core idea or most important element of a concept. In computing, a central component of an operating system.
example_sentence: The kernel of the corn was sweet and juicy. The kernel of his argument was that education should be free. She found a kernel of truth in his long speech. The kernel of the operating system manages memory and processes. A single kernel of wheat can grow into a full plant.

english_meaning: A metal or plastic container with a lid, spout, and handle used for boiling water. A large metal pot used for cooking over an open fire. A confined area where a police tactic is used to contain a crowd.
example_sentence: She put the kettle on the stove to make some tea. The campers cooked a stew in a large iron kettle over the fire. The electric kettle boils water much faster than the old one. Police decided to kettle the protesters in the main square to prevent rioting.

english_meaning: The correct explanation or solution to a mystery, problem, or puzzle. Something that allows entry, control, or access to a place, system, or opportunity. A guide that explains symbols, signs, or codes in a chart, map, or text.
example_sentence: The witness gave the key to the mystery. Communication is the key to a healthy relationship. Education is the key to a better future. Practice is the key to mastering any skill. Confidence is the key to public speaking. Use the key to understand the map symbols.

english_meaning: To make someone more alert, focused, or energetic. To increase tension or anticipation in a situation. To enter data or information into a system (less common, in computing context). To stimulate emotions or reactions in a group or individual.
example_sentence: The speaker keyed up the audience with an inspiring story. The tension in the courtroom keyed up as the verdict was announced. He keyed up all the customer orders into the system before lunch. The trainer keyed up the athletes before the championship.

english_meaning: A person who makes aggressive or abusive comments online while avoiding confrontation in real life. Someone who argues bravely on the internet but is passive in person. An informal, disapproving term for an internet ranter.
example_sentence: He is just a keyboard warrior who never speaks up in meetings. The post attracted dozens of keyboard warriors within an hour. Keyboard warriors filled the comment section with insults. Ignore the keyboard warriors and focus on real feedback.

english_meaning: To discuss or talk about an idea informally before making a decision. To move or travel from one place to another without a clear purpose. (British informal) To spend time aimlessly or casually.
example_sentence: We kicked about the idea of moving abroad. They kicked about some business plans. The topic was just kicked about at lunch. Let’s not just kick about, let’s decide.

english_meaning: To resist or protest something. Relax after hard work. To react strongly or forcefully. Can also mean to return money illegally (bribe).
example_sentence: He always kicks against authority. They kicked against the unfair decision. Children often kick against strict rules. She kicked against her parents’ expectations.

english_meaning: To sit comfortably and rest without stress. Money given secretly in return for favor or business. To react suddenly or violently (machine/gun). To respond strongly or aggressively.
example_sentence: After work, I just want to kick back and watch TV. The horse kicked back when someone touched it. The manager was accused of kicking back money to suppliers. Let’s kick back and enjoy the weekend.

english_meaning: To begin to take effect or start working (often used for medicines, plans, systems, or reactions). To contribute or add something, especially money or effort.
example_sentence: The painkillers kicked in after ten minutes. The law will kick in next month. The new system kicked in smoothly. His training kicked in during the emergency.

english_meaning: To begin or start something. To indicate the start of an event, activity, process, or action. It can also mean to remove something by kicking, or in informal contexts, to get angry.
example_sentence: The football match will kick off at 7 PM. Let’s kick off the meeting with a quick introduction. He kicked off his shoes as soon as he got home. She kicked off when she heard the unfair decision.

english_meaning: To expel someone or something from a place or organization.
example_sentence: He was kicked out of school. They kicked out the rude customer. The tenant was kicked out for not paying rent. She kicked him out of the car. The teacher kicked the noisy students out of the class.

english_meaning: To overturn or knock something down accidentally. En relax after hard work. To react strongly or forcefully. Can also mean to return money illegally (bribe).
example_sentence: He kicked over the bucket of paint by mistake. The child kicked over his toys. The engine kicked over but didn’t start. She kicked over the stool while dancing.

english_meaning: To die. A very informal idiom used to say that someone has died. It is often used in a humorous or indirect way instead of saying “die” directly.
example_sentence: My old neighbor finally kicked the bucket at the age of ninety. The car was so old that it looked like it would kick the bucket any day. He joked that his phone would kick the bucket after years of use. Many soldiers kicked the bucket during the war.

english_meaning: To cause trouble or anger by doing or saying something that upsets many people. To create a situation full of problems, anger, or conflict that is difficult to control afterward.
example_sentence: When he criticized the management during the meeting, he really kicked the hornet’s nest. The new policy kicked the hornet’s nest among the employees. By questioning the leader’s decision, she kicked the hornet’s nest. Posting that controversial comment online was like kicking the hornet’s nest.

english_meaning: To cause trouble or start a disturbance. Du relax after hard work. To react strongly or forcefully. Can also mean to return money illegally (bribe).
example_sentence: The students kicked up a fuss about the new rules. The wind kicked up a lot of dust. The kids kicked up when asked to go to bed early. Prices kicked up after the announcement.

english_meaning: To give a strong or energetic start to a process, activity, or project, often to overcome inertia or delay. It can also mean jump-starting something to make it function efficiently.
example_sentence: The manager tried to kick-start the new marketing campaign with a big launch event. I need a strong cup of coffee to kick-start my day. The government launched a program to kick-start economic growth in rural areas. A short motivational speech helped kick-start the team’s energy before the match.

english_meaning: An illegal payment made to someone in return for a favour or contract. A bribe given as a share of profits from a corrupt deal. A sudden backward movement or recoil of a machine or tool. An unwanted reaction or resistance to an action.
example_sentence: The officer was arrested for accepting kickbacks from suppliers. Investigators uncovered a network of kickbacks in the ministry. The saw gave a violent kickback and injured his wrist. Kickbacks inflate the cost of public projects.

english_meaning: To take a person away illegally by force or deception. To abduct someone and hold them captive. To seize a person for ransom, pressure, or another unlawful purpose. The act of unlawfully carrying someone away.
example_sentence: The criminals planned to kidnap a wealthy businessman. Police rescued the child before the kidnappers could leave the city. The story is about a plot to kidnap a scientist. They were arrested for trying to kidnap a witness.

english_meaning: One of a pair of bean-shaped organs located at the back of the abdomen. An organ that filters waste products from the blood to form urine. An organ that regulates the body's water, salt, and mineral balance. An organ that helps control blood pressure and red blood cell production. The kidney of an animal used as food.
example_sentence: Each kidney filters the blood many times a day. He needs a kidney transplant to survive. Drinking enough water helps keep your kidneys healthy. The scan showed a small stone in her right kidney.

word: Kill the goose that lays the golden eggs
english_meaning: To destroy a valuable source of income or benefit through greed or foolishness. To ruin something that continuously provides advantages. To act shortsightedly and lose long-term profit. To sacrifice future gains for immediate ones. To harm the very thing that supports one’s success.
synonyms: ["Ruin one’s luck","Destroy the source","Squander wealth","Self-sabotage","Short-sighted greed","Waste opportunity","Cut off one’s livelihood","Bite the hand that feeds","Undermine success","Spoil the prospects"]
antonyms: ["Nurture the source","Protect one’s assets","Invest wisely","Preserve wealth","Sustain growth","Reward loyalty","Cherish resources","Cultivate benefits","Safeguard income","Value the giver"]
example_sentence: By overworking his best employees, he killed the goose that laid the golden eggs. Cutting research funding would kill the goose that lays the golden eggs. Don’t raise prices too high or you’ll kill the goose that lays the golden eggs. Overfishing killed the goose that laid the golden eggs for the coastal town.

word: Kill two birds with one stone
english_meaning: To achieve two goals or solve two problems with a single action or effort. Doing one thing that brings double benefit.
example_sentence: He killed two birds with one stone by shopping and visiting friends. By driving my friend to the airport and doing some shopping on the way back, I killed two birds with one stone. She improved her English and made new friends at the same time, killing two birds with one stone. Walking to work helps me exercise and save money on transport, it’s like killing two birds with one stone.

english_meaning: A furnace or oven used for burning, baking, or drying things, especially pottery or bricks. An enclosed chamber for firing ceramics. A high-temperature oven for processing materials. A structure for heating substances to alter their properties. A device used in metallurgy and manufacturing.
example_sentence: The potter placed the clay bowls in the kiln to harden them. The kiln reached temperatures of over a thousand degrees. Bricks are baked in a large kiln for several days. The glassblower used a small kiln to keep the glass molten. Archaeologists discovered an ancient kiln near the ruins.

english_meaning: A short and informal word for a kilogram. A unit of mass equal to 1,000 grams. Also used informally for a kilometre in some contexts. A metric prefix meaning one thousand.
example_sentence: She bought half a kilo of tomatoes. A kilo of rice costs less in the village. The prefix kilo means one thousand. He lost three kilos after changing his diet.

english_meaning: A unit of digital information equal to 1,024 bytes, or about one thousand bytes. A small measure of computer memory or file size. The amount of storage roughly needed for a short page of plain text.
example_sentence: This text file is only a few kilobytes in size. One kilobyte equals 1,024 bytes. Old computers had memory measured in kilobytes. The image was compressed to about ninety kilobytes.

english_meaning: A unit of energy equivalent to one thousand calories. The amount of heat energy required to raise the temperature of one kilogram of water by one degree Celsius. A measure typically used to quantify the energy value of food. Commonly referred to in everyday language simply as a calorie when discussing nutrition. A metric unit of heat equal to 4·184 kilojoules. A standard unit for expressing metabolic rates in biology.
synonyms: ["Large Calorie","Food Calorie","Kcal","1000 Calories","Thermal Unit","Energy Unit","Nutritional Unit","Heat Energy Measure","Kilogram Calorie","Metabolic Unit","Caloric Value","Fuel Value","Energy Content"]
example_sentence: The label indicates that one serving of this snack contains two hundred kilocalories. An average adult male requires approximately two thousand five hundred kilocalories per day. Scientists use the kilocalorie to measure the heat produced during a chemical reaction. You can burn roughly one hundred kilocalories by walking briskly for twenty minutes.

english_meaning: The base unit of mass in the metric system, equal to 1,000 grams. A standard unit used to measure the weight of people, food, and goods. A unit commonly abbreviated as kg.
example_sentence: She bought two kilograms of mangoes from the market. One kilogram equals 1,000 grams. The baby was born weighing three kilograms. Please weigh the parcel in kilograms.

english_meaning: A unit of energy, work, or amount of heat in the International System of Units (SI). Equal to one thousand joules. Approximately equivalent to 0·239 calories or 0·737 foot-pounds of force. Used commonly in nutrition to measure the energy value of foods and beverages. A derived unit representing the work done by a force of one thousand newtons acting through one meter. Represents a practical measurement for physical activity and metabolic rates.
synonyms: ["Energy Unit","Thousand Joules","KJ","Heat Measure","Metric Energy Unit","Work Unit","Power Metric","Caloric Equivalent","Nutritional Unit","SI Unit","Derived Unit","Physics Measurement"]
example_sentence: The nutrition label lists the energy content in both kilojoules and calories. Running for thirty minutes burns several hundred kilojoules of energy. One kilojoule is exactly one thousand times the energy of a single joule. Scientists calculated the heat released during the chemical reaction in kilojoules.

english_meaning: A metric unit of volume equal to one thousand liters. A large measure of capacity equal to one cubic meter of liquid. A unit used to measure bulk liquids such as water supply, fuel storage, and industrial output.
example_sentence: The tank at the factory stores fifty kiloliters of water. Water usage in the town is measured in kiloliters. One kiloliter is exactly one thousand liters. The tanker delivered three kiloliters of diesel to the site.

english_meaning: A metric unit of length equal to 1,000 metres. A unit used to measure long distances such as roads and journeys. A unit written in short as km.
example_sentence: The village is ten kilometers from the city. One kilometer equals 1,000 meters. He runs five kilometers every morning. The speed limit is eighty kilometers per hour.

english_meaning: A composite unit of energy equivalent to one kilowatt of power sustained for one hour. A common billing unit used by electrical utilities to measure domestic and commercial consumption. A physical quantity equal to 3·6 million joules or 3,600 kilojoules. A measure of work performed or energy converted over a specific duration of time. A standard metric for battery capacity and electrical storage systems. The product of power in kilowatts multiplied by time in hours.
synonyms: ["Board Of Trade Unit","3.6 Megajoules","Electrical Energy Unit","Power Consumption Measure","Energy Metric","Billing Unit","B.O.T. Unit","KWh","3600 Kilojoules","Power Units","Work Unit","Quantity Of Electricity","Energy Usage Unit"]
example_sentence: The monthly electricity bill showed a consumption of five hundred kilowatt-hours. Replacing old appliances can significantly reduce the total kilowatt-hour usage per year. Most electric vehicle batteries are rated by their capacity in kilowatt-hours. The utility company charges a fixed rate for every kilowatt-hour consumed during peak times.

english_meaning: To set something on fire or start it burning. To catch fire or begin to burn. To arouse or inspire a feeling, interest, or emotion. To make something bright or glowing, as the face or eyes. To stir up trouble or conflict.
example_sentence: He kindled a small fire using dry twigs. Her teacher kindled her lifelong love of poetry. The dry leaves kindled quickly in the summer heat. His speech kindled anger among the crowd.

english_meaning: The quality of being kind, warm-hearted, gentle, and considerate. Friendly, sympathetic, or generous behavior toward others. A kindly disposition.
example_sentence: Her kindliness toward strangers made her beloved in the neighborhood. The nurse treated every patient with remarkable kindliness. His kindliness never wavered under pressure. The old teacher was known for her patience and kindliness.

english_meaning: Small dry sticks, twigs, or other easily burned material used to start a fire. The act of lighting or causing a fire to begin. The act of arousing a feeling, interest, or activity. The present participle of kindle.
example_sentence: He gathered dry twigs for kindling before lighting the campfire. The kindling caught fire quickly in the autumn air. Her speech was kindling for the growing debate. Without proper kindling, the fireplace would not light.

english_meaning: In a kind, gentle, helpful, or friendly manner. Having a kind, warm-hearted, or benevolent nature. Pleasant and comforting. Used politely to make a request or instruction.
example_sentence: The old man kindly offered his seat to the tired traveler. She has a kindly face that puts everyone at ease. Kindly close the door on your way out. He spoke kindly to the frightened child.

english_meaning: A group of related people or things. Having similar qualities or character. Related by blood or family ties. A natural affinity or connection. Similar in nature or type.
example_sentence: The kindred spirits shared a love for literature and art. She felt a kindred connection with her distant cousins. The kindred languages evolved from a common ancestor. He found kindred souls among the members of the club. The kindred tribes lived in harmony for centuries.

english_meaning: A person who has the same ideas, feelings, interests, or nature as another person. A person who feels very similar to you in thoughts, emotions, values, interests, or attitude. It is used for someone with whom you feel a natural connection, understanding, or closeness because both of you think or feel in much the same way.
synonyms: ["Like minded person","Soulmate","Kindred soul","Kindred mind","Kindred heart","Kindred being","Kindred companion","Kindred friend","Bosom friend","Kindred one"]
example_sentence: When I met Sara, I felt I had found a kindred spirit because we both loved books and quiet places. He saw his grandfather as a kindred spirit who shared his respect for honesty and hard work. The two artists became kindred spirits after discovering their similar views on beauty and life. In a new city, finding a kindred spirit made her feel less lonely and more understood.

english_meaning: Relating to motion, especially the motion of bodies without reference to force or mass. Concerning the geometry of movement. Pertaining to kinematics, a branch of mechanics dealing with pure motion.
example_sentence: The engineer studied the kinematic properties of the robot arm. Kinematic equations help solve physics problems. The car's kinematic performance was tested on the track. Animators use kinematic principles to create realistic motion. The kinematic model showed how the joints moved.

english_meaning: The fear of zombies or fear of the dead moving. It is a specific phobia where a person feels extreme anxiety or panic at the thought or sight of zombies or animated corpses. Fear of zombies or moving dead.
example_sentence: He could not watch horror movies because of his kinemortophobia. Kinemortophobia made her avoid Halloween events with zombie costumes. Even a cartoon with zombies triggered his kinemortophobia. The documentary on ancient burial practices worsened his kinemortophobia.

english_meaning: Related to motion or movement. Something that is produced by movement or is connected with physical motion. It is commonly used in science, especially physics, to describe energy that an object has because it is moving.
example_sentence: A moving car has kinetic energy. The ball gains kinetic force as it rolls downhill. Wind turbines convert kinetic energy into electricity. The dancer performance was full of kinetic motion.

english_meaning: Having twists or curls, especially in hair. Involving unusual or unconventional sexual practices. Informal term for something strange or eccentric. Full of kinks or twists. Odd or peculiar in behavior or appearance.
example_sentence: Her kinky hair was styled into beautiful braids. The movie explored kinky themes that shocked some audiences. He had a kinky habit of collecting rare bottle caps. The kinky rope was difficult to untangle. Some people consider his fashion sense a bit kinky.

english_meaning: A small booth or stand used to sell items or provide information. A small, separate structure or booth, often found in public places such as streets, malls, airports, or parks. It is used to sell newspapers, food, tickets, or to provide digital services and information through screens.
example_sentence: He bought a newspaper from the kiosk near the bus stop. A digital kiosk helps visitors find their way in the mall. The food kiosk sells snacks and cold drinks. Tickets can be printed from the self service kiosk at the airport.

english_meaning: A light frame covered with paper or cloth, flown in the wind on a string. In geometry, a quadrilateral with two pairs of adjacent sides of equal length. A bird of prey with long wings and a forked tail. To fly or move quickly and lightly through the air.
example_sentence: The children flew a red kite in the park. A kite has two pairs of equal adjacent sides. A kite circled slowly above the fields. Papers kited across the yard in the strong wind.

english_meaning: Friends and family; all your relatives and close acquaintances. People you are closely connected to by blood or friendship.
example_sentence: He invited all his kith and kin to the wedding ceremony. During the festival, people love to celebrate with their kith and kin. She moved to the city, leaving her kith and kin behind in the village. In times of trouble, your kith and kin are the ones who stand by you.

english_meaning: Art or objects considered to be in poor taste, overly sentimental, or excessively decorative. Mass-produced decorative items regarded as lacking artistic value. Tacky or garish aesthetic style. Cheap, sentimental, or low-quality art. Popular culture artifacts that are ironically appreciated.
example_sentence: The souvenir shop was full of kitsch, including plastic snow globes. She decorated her apartment with vintage kitsch from the 1950s. Critics dismissed the painting as mere kitsch. The hotel lobby was a perfect example of overdone kitsch. Some people genuinely love kitsch while others mock it.

english_meaning: A small oval fruit with brown fuzzy skin and bright green flesh dotted with tiny black seeds. A tangy-sweet fruit rich in vitamin C. A flightless bird native to New Zealand. An informal term for a person from New Zealand.
example_sentence: She sliced a kiwi over her breakfast cereal. Kiwi fruit contains more vitamin C than an orange. The kiwi is the national bird of New Zealand. His neighbour is a friendly Kiwi from Auckland.

english_meaning: A government or state in which those in power use their authority to steal public money and resources for personal gain.
example_sentence: International observers accused the regime of being a kleptocracy. The kleptocracy drained the national treasury for decades. Journalists exposed how the kleptocracy laundered stolen wealth abroad. Fighting corruption is essential to ending kleptocracy.

english_meaning: A natural ability to do something well. A special skill or talent that someone has, often learned easily or done naturally without much effort. It usually describes practical abilities rather than academic knowledge.
example_sentence: She has a knack for explaining difficult ideas clearly. He has a natural knack for fixing machines. Teaching requires more than knowledge, it needs a knack for communication. Some people have a knack for making others feel comfortable.

english_meaning: Someone who buys old, worn-out animals (especially horses) for slaughter or disposal. A person who deals in old or worn-out animals, typically buying them to kill for meat or to sell parts like hides, bones, or other materials. Informally, it can also mean someone who is tired out or worn down.
example_sentence: The farmer sold his old horse to the knacker. After years of hard work, he felt like a complete knacker. Knackers often supply leather to tanneries. The village knacker bought the worn-out ox for a small price.

english_meaning: Dishonest, deceitful, or unprincipled behavior. A trick or act performed by a dishonest person. Cunning or roguish conduct intended to cheat others. The quality of being a knave or scoundrel. Mischievous or fraudulent dealings.
example_sentence: His knavery was finally exposed when the documents were reviewed. The old story warns readers against the knavery of dishonest merchants. She could not tolerate the knavery of her business partner. Such knavery has no place in a fair society.

english_meaning: To press, fold, and stretch dough with the hands to make it smooth. To massage a part of the body firmly with the hands. To work a substance into a soft mass by pressing and squeezing. To manipulate or shape by squeezing.
example_sentence: She kneaded the dough for ten minutes before baking. The masseur kneaded the muscles of his back. Knead the clay until it becomes soft and pliable. Grandmother kneads flour every morning to make fresh bread.

english_meaning: The joint between the thigh and the lower leg. The middle joint of the leg that allows bending and straightening. The area of a garment that covers this joint. To hit or push someone with the knee.
example_sentence: He fell and scraped his knee on the pavement. She knelt down and rested her hands on her knees. The trousers were worn out at the knees. He accidentally kneed the chair in the dark.

english_meaning: An automatic or reflexive response. A response that is automatic, instinctive, or done without careful thought. It is usually a quick reaction triggered by emotion, habit, or impulse rather than reason. A response made without analysis or reflection. A habitual or predictable reaction. Often carries a negative connotation implying lack of control.
example_sentence: His criticism was just a knee-jerk reaction to the new policy. She had a knee-jerk reaction of anger when she saw the mistake. Politicians often give knee-jerk responses to public outrage. Don’t let a knee-jerk reaction ruin a thoughtful discussion.

english_meaning: The small flat movable bone at the front of the knee joint. The bone that protects the front of the knee, also called the patella. A rounded bone that slides as the knee bends and straightens. To shoot or injure someone in the knee, especially as a punishment.
example_sentence: He dislocated his kneecap while playing football. The kneecap protects the delicate joint underneath. She felt a sharp pain just below her kneecap. Cyclists often strengthen the muscles supporting the kneecap.

english_meaning: Past tense of knee, meaning to hit or push someone or something with the knee. To press dough with the knee, though usually spelled knead for dough. Struck by the knee.
example_sentence: The player kneed his opponent by accident. He kneed the door to push it open. She kneed the intruder in self defense. The wrestler kneed his rival in the stomach. He accidentally kneed the table and hurt himself.

english_meaning: A man given a rank of honor by a king or queen because of his service, especially in medieval times a mounted armed soldier serving a lord. A chess piece shaped like a horse's head. To confer a knighthood upon.
example_sentence: The brave knight defended the castle from invaders. She was made a knight for her services to medicine. In chess the knight moves in an L shape. Stories of knights and dragons fascinated the children. The queen knighted him at a royal ceremony.

english_meaning: A person who appears at the right moment to help, save, or rescue someone. Often used for someone who protects or supports another in a difficult situation.
example_sentence: He was her knight in shining armour. She waited for a knight in shining armour. Don’t expect a knight in shining armour to fix things. He became the knight in shining armour for his family.

english_meaning: A rounded handle on a door or drawer. A round control on a machine for adjusting settings. A small rounded lump or protuberance. A rounded hill.
