antonyms: ["Remain unknown","Lose reputation","Stay unnoticed","Fade into obscurity","Be ignored"]
example_sentence: She worked hard to make a name for herself in the medical field. The young artist moved to the city to make a name for himself. He made a name for himself by writing inspiring books. With determination, she made a name for herself in business.

english_meaning: To act in a foolish or embarrassing way in public. To behave in a way that attracts unwanted attention and makes a person look silly, embarrassed, or foolish in public. It usually describes actions that cause shame or public embarrassment.
synonyms: ["Embarrass oneself","Make a fool of oneself","Humiliate oneself","Act foolishly","Cause a scene"]
example_sentence: He made a spectacle of himself by shouting loudly in the meeting. She made a spectacle of herself by arguing in the restaurant. Don’t drink too much or you will make a spectacle of yourself. He made a spectacle of himself at the party by dancing on the table.

english_meaning: To attract a great deal of attention or public notice. To make a strong, impressive first appearance or debut. To create excitement or a strong impression quickly.
synonyms: ["Create a sensation","Attract attention","Cause a stir","Make an impact","Make waves","Hit the headlines"]
antonyms: ["Go unnoticed","Pass unnoticed","Fade into obscurity","Make no impression"]
example_sentence: The young singer made a splash with her very first album. The startup made a splash at the technology fair. His controversial speech made a splash in the media. The new restaurant made a splash with its grand opening.

english_meaning: To make a bad decision or incorrect judgment. To choose or decide something incorrectly after judging a situation. It is often used when someone misunderstands facts, misreads a situation, or takes an action that later proves to be a mistake. It can be used in everyday decisions, business, sports decisions, or personal judgment.
synonyms: ["Misjudge","Miscalculate","Misread the situation","Err in judgment","Make a bad decision"]
antonyms: ["Make the right call","Judge correctly","Decide wisely","Make an accurate decision","Think correctly"]
example_sentence: The manager made a wrong call by hiring the inexperienced candidate. I made a wrong call trusting him without checking the facts. The referee made a wrong call during the final minutes of the match. She admitted she made a wrong call by investing all her savings in one project.

english_meaning: To chase, pursue, or follow someone or something, usually in order to catch or attack them.
example_sentence: The police made after the thief. The dog made after the cat. He made after his brother to catch him. The guards made after the suspect.

english_meaning: To escape, run off, or in older usage, to kill or destroy.
example_sentence: The thief made away before the police arrived. He tried to make away with the money. The rebels made away after the attack. The boy made away quietly into the night.

english_meaning: To take something secretly or illegally (to steal), to remove something, or sometimes to kill or dispose of someone. The phrase is often used in crime or theft-related contexts, as well as in figurative expressions meaning to get rid of something.
example_sentence: The thief made away with the jewels. They made away with all the money. Someone made away with my wallet. He made away with company funds.

english_meaning: To unite or join with a person or group in order to achieve a shared aim. To cooperate with someone toward a common goal or against a common opponent. To form an alliance for a mutual purpose.
synonyms: ["Unite with","Ally with","Join forces with","Team up with","Cooperate with","Side with","Band together"]
example_sentence: Several small parties made common cause with the opposition. The two rivals made common cause to defeat a stronger competitor. Environmental groups made common cause with local farmers. During the crisis, neighbors made common cause to protect their community.

english_meaning: To manage with something that is not ideal or sufficient. To use something less than perfect because you have no better option at the moment.
example_sentence: We’ll have to make do with what we have. They made do with a small meal. We can make do with less money this month. She made do with an old computer until she got a new one.

english_meaning: To earn and manage just enough money to cover one’s basic needs and expenses, not rich, but surviving financially. To have just enough income to pay for food, rent, and other daily necessities.
example_sentence: It’s hard to make ends meet with low income. After losing his job, he struggled to make ends meet. They both work two jobs just to make ends meet. With rising prices, it’s becoming harder for families to make ends meet. Despite her small salary, she somehow manages to make ends meet.

word: Make hay while the sun shines
english_meaning: Use a good opportunity while it lasts. This idiom means taking advantage of favorable conditions before they change. Just like farmers dry hay when the sun is shining, people should act quickly when circumstances are beneficial, because opportunities may not last long.
synonyms: ["Strike while the iron is hot","Seize the opportunity","Make the most of the moment","Take advantage of the situation"]
example_sentence: The market is booming, so investors should make hay while the sun shines. She worked extra hours during the busy season to make hay while the sun shines. If you get a scholarship, make hay while the sun shines and complete your studies. Freelancers often make hay while the sun shines when they get high-paying projects.

english_meaning: To change or transform something into something else. To convert one thing into another (either physically, emotionally, or functionally).
example_sentence: She made the old dress into a skirt. Hard work can make you into a better person. They made the garage into a workshop. He made his hobby into a career.

english_meaning: To succeed or achieve something. To arrive or attend. To survive or recover. To become successful in life or career
example_sentence: I hope we make it to the airport on time. She finally made it as a lawyer. We didn’t think he’d make it through the night. Congratulations, you made it!. She worked hard to make it as a doctor. Against all odds, they made it to the top of the mountain.

english_meaning: To compensate or do something kind after causing trouble. (It expresses the idea of repaying an emotional or moral debt.)
example_sentence: I’ll make it up to you for being late. How can I make it up to her?. He made it up to his friend with a gift. She promised to make it up to. You hurt her feelings; you should try to make it up to her. He missed the meeting, so he promised to make it up to his boss.

english_meaning: To make a situation more serious or difficult. To do or say something that increases the severity, difficulty, or unpleasantness of an already bad situation.
example_sentence: His rude reply only made matters worse. Don’t lie—it will make matters worse. The rain made matters worse for travelers. Yelling at him will only make matters worse. She made matters worse by ignoring the warning signs.

english_meaning: To speak plainly and honestly about something. To have no hesitation in stating one's opinion. To express something openly without embarrassment. To be frank and direct about a matter. To not conceal one's views.
synonyms: ["Be frank","Be blunt","Speak openly","Be candid","Not hesitate","Be direct"]
example_sentence: She made no bones about her dislike of the new policy. He made no bones about wanting the promotion. The teacher made no bones about her disappointment. They made no bones about their support for the decision.

english_meaning: To understand, interpret, or form an opinion about something. Used when expressing what you think, feel, or conclude about a person, situation, or thing. It reflects interpretation, evaluation, or judgment.
example_sentence: What do you make of this news? I don’t know what to make of her attitude. What do you make of his silence? He didn’t know what to make of the offer. She didn’t know what to make of his sudden apology. What do you make of the new manager?

english_meaning: To leave quickly, often secretly or after doing something wrong. To run away fast, especially to avoid being caught. To depart quickly without notice. To steal something and run away with it.
example_sentence: The robbers made off before police arrived. He made off with her purse. They made off into the forest. The kids made off laughing. He made off with my wallet during the crowd. The dog made off when it saw the stick. The students made off as soon as the bell rang.

english_meaning: To succeed in life by one’s own efforts, without relying on others. To build a successful life, career, or position through personal effort, determination, and independence. It often implies overcoming difficulties without depending heavily on support from others.
synonyms: ["Be self-made","Be independent","Carve out a path","Stand on one’s own feet"]
example_sentence: She worked hard to make her own way in the business world. After leaving home, he made his own way without financial support. Many successful people had to make their own way from humble beginnings. He believes that everyone should make their own way in life.

english_meaning: To create or form something from another material or situation.
example_sentence: The sculpture was made out of clay. This table is made out of recycled wood. He made a toy out of paper. She made a cake out of leftover ingredients.

english_meaning: To create space or provide opportunity for something new.
example_sentence: Please make room for the new furniture. The company made room for younger employees. We need to make room for innovation. They made room for the guests at the table.

english_meaning: To understand or find meaning or logic in something.
example_sentence: I can’t make sense of this message. Can you make sense of what he’s saying? It all makes sense now after his explanation. She tried to make sense of the puzzle.

english_meaning: To understand, interpret, or achieve success from something. To use an opportunity effectively.
example_sentence: What do you make of this rumor? He’s trying to make something of his life. I didn’t know what to make of her behavior. She made something of her talent in music.

english_meaning: To deliberately find or allocate time to do something important.
example_sentence: I always make time for reading every day. You should make time for your family. She made time for a quick coffee. We need to make time for relaxation.

english_meaning: To improve one's position after falling behind. To recover lost time, distance, progress, or advantage. To move closer to a competitor or leading position
example_sentence: The runner made up ground quickly in the final lap. The company is making up ground lost to competitors last year. She had to make up ground after missing the first week of classes. The team made up ground in the second half and won the match.

english_meaning: To decide something after considering different options. To reach a decision or conclusion after considering different choices or possibilities.
example_sentence: She finally made up her mind to study abroad. I can’t make up my mind about which dress to wear. He made up his mind to quit his job. Make up your mind before it’s too late.

english_meaning: To make someone feel extreme fear or horror. To frighten a person so badly that they feel cold inside. To cause a sudden sensation of dread. To shock someone with something terrifying or gruesome. Used of experiences that leave a person paralysed with fear.
example_sentence: The sound of the door creaking at midnight made my blood freeze. Her calm confession made his blood freeze. Reading the letter made her blood freeze with fear. The sight of the burning building made everyone's blood freeze.

english_meaning: To move in the direction of a place or object. To result in or cause a particular situation or effect. To be suitable or contribute positively to a situation.
example_sentence: He made for the exit. The rain made for a difficult journey. Honesty makes for good friendship. She made for the door when she heard noise. The soldiers made for the camp before sunset.

english_meaning: To understand something clearly. To manage or succeed. To fill out or write (a document, check, or form). To kiss or embrace passionately.
example_sentence: I can’t make out what he’s saying. Can you make out that figure in the distance? He made out a check to her. She made out that she was happy. He made out a list of all the people to invite.

english_meaning: To transfer ownership or transform the appearance of something. To transform or redesign something or someone, either physically (like giving a new look to a person or room) or legally (like transferring property ownership).
example_sentence: She made over the house to her daughter. The room was completely made over. He made over his business before retiring. The show made her over into a star. The company plans to make over its brand image to attract young customers.

english_meaning: To combine parts or elements to form a whole. To create something false or imaginary. To become friends again after a quarrel. To do something to correct a mistake or loss.
example_sentence: They made up after the argument. She made up a story about her trip. Women make up with cosmetics. Our team is made up of five players. They had a fight, but later they made up. Can I make up for my mistake?. Don’t make up lies!. Women make up 60% of the workforce.

english_meaning: To do something good to balance or compensate for something bad, unpleasant, or lacking. It is used when one tries to restore a loss, mistake, or disadvantage by taking corrective or positive action.
example_sentence: He worked hard to make up for lost time. I’ll make up for my mistake. She made up for being late by bringing flowers. Nothing can make up for his loss. The government is trying to make up for the economic losses. He gave her flowers to make up for forgetting her birthday.

english_meaning: Done in bad faith and with dishonest intention. Describing an act carried out with the purpose of deceiving. Not genuine or sincere in a legal or moral sense.
example_sentence: The court held that the transfer was mala fide. His mala fide conduct cost him the contract. The petition was dismissed as a mala fide attempt to delay proceedings. Officials must not act in a mala fide manner.

english_meaning: Bad, dishonest, or inefficient management of public or official affairs. Failure to carry out official duties properly or fairly. Careless or corrupt handling of an organization or department. Poor governance that causes injustice or loss to people.
example_sentence: The report blamed years of maladministration in the department. Citizens complained of maladministration in the housing scheme. Maladministration of funds delayed the entire project. An inquiry was set up to investigate the alleged maladministration.

english_meaning: Done with dishonest intent or bad faith. Actions or intentions that are deliberately dishonest, deceitful, or intended to mislead someone. It implies acting in bad faith, often for personal gain or to harm others.
example_sentence: He made a malafide claim to gain access to the funds. The contract was challenged because of malafide intentions. She accused him of malafide conduct in the workplace. Filing a malafide complaint can have legal consequences.

english_meaning: A general feeling of discomfort, illness, or unease whose exact cause is difficult to identify. A vague sense of mental or moral depression. A condition of society or an organization that causes general anxiety or dissatisfaction. A feeling of being unwell without specific symptoms. An atmosphere of unease or discontent.
example_sentence: After the flu, she experienced a lingering malaise for weeks. There was a general malaise in the office after the layoffs. The economic malaise affected the entire region. He complained of a vague malaise that no doctor could diagnose. A social malaise had spread through the community.

english_meaning: A serious disease transmitted by mosquitoes carrying parasites. A tropical illness caused by Plasmodium parasites. An infectious disease characterized by recurring fever, chills, and sweating. A preventable and treatable disease still affecting millions worldwide.
example_sentence: Malaria is transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes. She contracted malaria while traveling in Africa. Malaria prevention includes using mosquito nets. Antimalarial drugs can treat and prevent malaria.

english_meaning: A Dravidian language spoken predominantly in the Indian state of Kerala and the union territories of Lakshadweep and Puducherry. The official language of Kerala. One of the twenty-two scheduled languages of India. It has its own script derived from the ancient Brahmi script. The language has a rich literary tradition spanning many centuries.
example_sentence: Malayalam is known for its complex script and rich vocabulary. She learned to speak Malayalam during her stay in Kerala. Malayalam cinema has produced many internationally acclaimed films. The poet wrote his verses in beautiful Malayalam. Malayalam literature has a history stretching back over a thousand years.

english_meaning: Filled with or dominated by males. A place, group, or situation where males are overwhelmingly present or dominate, often implying a negative or challenging environment for others.
example_sentence: Her brother forbad her to go the male-infested market. The club was male-infested, making it uncomfortable for women. The meeting was male-infested, so she felt out of place. The office seemed male-infested, with hardly any female employees. The gym was male-infested, making her hesitant to join the weight section.

english_meaning: A curse or the utterance of a wish that harm may befall someone. Words spoken to invoke evil upon a person. The act of cursing or speaking evil of someone. Slander or abusive speech directed at another.
example_sentence: The old woman muttered a malediction as they passed. He believed a malediction had ruined his fortunes. Her speech was full of maledictions against the government. Ancient tablets often carried a malediction against thieves.

english_meaning: Causing or capable of causing harm, evil, or misfortune. Having a harmful or destructive influence, especially in a supernatural sense. Wicked in nature or intention. Regarded in astrology as bringing bad luck.
example_sentence: The novel describes a malefic force haunting the old mansion. Astrologers once considered Saturn a malefic planet. His malefic intentions were obvious to everyone present. A malefic silence settled over the abandoned village.

english_meaning: The state or quality of being male. The set of characteristics associated with men or male animals. Masculinity as a biological or social condition. The male nature or male identity of a person or thing.
example_sentence: The study examined how maleness is defined in different cultures. His maleness was emphasised by the role he played. Hormones influence the development of maleness in the embryo. The poem questions traditional ideas of maleness.

english_meaning: The wish to do evil or harm to others. Hatred or ill will directed at someone. A hostile and spiteful attitude. The quality of having an evil influence or intention.
example_sentence: There was clear malevolence in his tone. The novel explores the malevolence hidden behind polite manners. She felt the malevolence of the crowd around her. His malevolence towards his rivals was well known.

english_meaning: A person, intention, or force that has a desire to cause harm, suffering, or trouble to others. It refers to ill will, hostility, or evil intent. Wishing harm or evil to others.
example_sentence: The villain had a malevolent smile that frightened the children. His malevolent plans were exposed before he could harm anyone. The rumor was spread with malevolent intent. She sensed a malevolent presence in the abandoned house.

english_meaning: In a way that shows a wish to harm others. With evil intent or spite. In a hostile and threatening manner. With obvious ill will.
example_sentence: He smiled malevolently as he read the letter. The character stares malevolently at his victims. She spoke malevolently about her former partner. The dog growled malevolently at the stranger.

english_meaning: Wrongdoing or misconduct, especially by a public official or person in a position of trust. Illegal or dishonest behaviour while performing official duties. An unlawful act that causes harm to others. The word is formal and most often used in legal, governmental, or corporate contexts.
example_sentence: The minister was dismissed for malfeasance in office. The auditor uncovered serious malfeasance in the department. He was charged with malfeasance and misuse of public funds. Several officers were investigated for malfeasance. The committee took strict action against corporate malfeasance.

english_meaning: A failure to work or operate normally or satisfactorily. It can refer to a technical glitch in a computer, machine, or a physiological failure in a bodily organ. Generally, it suggests an interruption in the expected performance of a system.
example_sentence: A technical malfunction caused the entire power grid to shut down. The pilot managed to land the plane despite a serious engine malfunction. If the software continues to malfunction, we will have to reinstall it. Doctors detected a minor malfunction in the patient's heart valve.

english_meaning: The intention to harm someone or strong ill will toward another person. A deep feeling of hatred, spite, or desire to hurt another person. It refers to acting with harmful intent rather than by accident or misunderstanding. In legal and moral contexts, it shows that harm was done deliberately and with bad intention.
example_sentence: She spoke without malice, even though she strongly disagreed with him. The rumor was spread out of pure malice. The judge ruled that the act was done with clear malice. Despite the argument, he held no malice toward his friend.

english_meaning: Having or showing a desire to harm somebody or hurt their feelings, caused by a feeling of hate. Showing hatred & a desire to harm or hurt feeling
example_sentence: He took malicious pleasure in telling me what she had said. It is maliciously motivated to harass opponents.

english_meaning: In a way that shows a desire to cause harm or suffering to others. With ill intent. Spitefully. In a manner intended to hurt or damage.
example_sentence: He acted maliciously toward his coworker. The rumor was maliciously spread. She smiled maliciously as she watched him fail. The property was maliciously damaged. He was maliciously accused of a crime he did not commit.

english_meaning: To speak about someone in a spitefully critical or disparaging manner. It describes the act of telling lies or spreading rumors to damage someone's reputation. It means evil in nature, influence, or effect.
example_sentence: She was accused of trying to malign her rival's character during the election. It is unfair to malign a person who is not present to defend themselves. The disease had a malign effect on the elderly patient’s overall health. He felt that the news report was designed solely to malign his business.

english_meaning: A cancerous growth or tumour that spreads and threatens life. The quality of being very harmful or dangerous, especially in disease. Strong feelings of hatred, spite, or ill will towards others. The state of being evil or intending harm.
example_sentence: The tests confirmed a malignancy in the left lung. Early detection of malignancy improves survival rates. There was clear malignancy in the tone of his letter. Doctors are monitoring the patient for signs of malignancy.

english_meaning: (Of a disease, especially a tumour) Very harmful, dangerous, and likely to cause death if not treated; cancerous. (Of a person or behaviour) Full of hatred, evil, or strong desire to harm others. Showing intense ill will or wishing serious harm to others.
example_sentence: The doctors confirmed that the tumour was malignant. She has a malignant form of cancer that requires immediate treatment. He gave her a malignant look full of hatred. There were malignant rumours spreading about the new manager. His malignant intentions were soon exposed.

english_meaning: To pretend to be ill or injured in order to avoid work or duty. To exaggerate or fake an illness to escape responsibilities. To shirk duty by feigning sickness.
example_sentence: Some soldiers tried to malinger to avoid being sent to the front. The manager suspected that he was malingering to skip work. Doctors can usually tell when a patient is malingering. He was caught malingering and was suspended from duty. She never malingers, even when she feels unwell.

english_meaning: The quality of being able to be shaped, hammered, or pressed out of shape without breaking or cracking. It refers to the physical property of certain metals or the psychological flexibility of a person's character. Often used to describe how easily someone can be influenced or controlled by others.
example_sentence: The malleability of gold makes it an ideal metal for creating intricate jewelry. Investors appreciated the malleability of the young entrepreneur's business plan. Because of the malleability of lead, it was once used for making water pipes. The teacher admired the psychological malleability of his young students.

english_meaning: Capable of being shaped or extended by hammering, forging, or rolling. It describes a substance that can be altered or influenced easily by external forces. In a figurative sense, it refers to a person who is easily controlled or trained.
example_sentence: Gold is one of the most malleable metals found in nature. The sculptor used a malleable clay to create the intricate portrait. Children have malleable minds that are highly receptive to new ideas. He was a malleable young man who followed his mentor's advice without question.

english_meaning: The outermost of the three small bones of the middle ear, shaped like a hammer. The bone that is attached to the eardrum and receives sound vibrations first. A hammer-shaped ossicle that passes vibrations to the incus.
example_sentence: The malleus is attached directly to the eardrum. Sound vibrations first reach the malleus. The malleus is named after its hammer-like shape. A fractured malleus may reduce a person's hearing.

english_meaning: A proper noun used as a surname or place name in English-speaking regions, most notably Ern Malley, a famous fictional Australian poet created as a literary hoax in 1944. Also occurs as a family name of Irish origin, derived from the Gaelic 'O Maille'.
antonyms: ["(No direct antonym as it is a proper noun)"]
example_sentence: Ern Malley remains one of the most famous literary hoaxes in history. Mr Malley joined the team as a new manager. The Malley family has lived in this town for generations. Critics still debate the poetry attributed to Malley. She read a biography of Ern Malley last summer.

english_meaning: A condition resulting from an unbalanced diet in which certain nutrients are lacking, in excess, or in the wrong proportions. It can lead to poor health, weight loss, stunted growth, and weakness. It affects both physical and mental development.
example_sentence: Millions of children in the famine-struck region suffer from severe malnutrition. The hospital treated the rescued animals for dehydration and malnutrition. A poor diet consisting only of junk food can lead to malnutrition. Educating mothers about balanced diets helped reduce child malnutrition. Prolonged malnutrition severely stunted the physical growth of the orphans.

english_meaning: Improper, illegal, or negligent professional activity or treatment, especially by a medical practitioner, lawyer, or public official. It involves a failure to exercise the degree of skill and care expected of a professional. This often leads to injury, loss, or damage to a client or patient.
example_sentence: The surgeon was sued for medical malpractice after a sponge was left inside the patient. The attorney was disbarred due to professional malpractice and embezzlement. Victims of legal malpractice can seek financial compensation for their losses. Strict regulations are in place to prevent administrative malpractice in government offices.

english_meaning: To treat someone cruelly or violently. To abuse, harm, or neglect a person or animal. To handle someone or something badly. To behave toward someone in an unfair or brutal way.
example_sentence: The law punishes people who maltreat children. No one has the right to maltreat an animal. Workers complained that the supervisor used to maltreat them. The rescued dog had clearly been maltreated.

english_meaning: Animals characterized by the presence of mammary glands which produce milk to feed their young, a backbone, warm-blooded metabolism, and usually body hair or fur. They can live on land, in water, or in air.
example_sentence: Humans are mammals because they give birth to live young and feed them milk. Whales are mammals even though they live in the ocean. Bats are the only mammals capable of true flight. Lions are mammals that live in groups called prides.

english_meaning: A biologist specializing in the study of mammals, their behavior, classification, ecology, and evolution.
example_sentence: The mammalogist studied the behavior of African elephants in the wild. As a mammalogist, she published several papers on bat ecology. The mammalogist discovered a new species of rodent in the forest. Universities often hire mammalogists to conduct wildlife conservation research.

english_meaning: A large extinct elephant-like animal with long tusks and shaggy hair that lived during the Ice Age. Extremely large, Huge in size, amount, or importance.
example_sentence: The company undertook a mammoth project to build a new city. Cleaning up the flood damage was a mammoth task. The museum displayed the skeleton of a mammoth from the Ice Age. He made a mammoth effort to improve the education system.

english_meaning: A very large and difficult job. A huge responsibility requiring great effort. A major undertaking that may take much time and planning. An enormous challenge.
synonyms: ["Huge task","Enormous job","Major undertaking","Large project","Great challenge","Heavy responsibility","Immense effort","Big job"]
antonyms: ["Easy task","Small job","Simple duty","Minor chore","Light work","Quick task","Effortless job"]
example_sentence: Cleaning the entire archive was a mammoth task. Rebuilding the bridge after the flood became a mammoth task. The students faced the mammoth task of organizing all the data. Writing a full dictionary is a mammoth task.

english_meaning: An adult human male. A human being in general, especially in formal or traditional usage. To operate, staff, or supply something with people.
example_sentence: The man waited quietly outside. Every man and woman deserves respect. Two engineers man the control room at night. The crew manned the emergency station.

english_meaning: A loyal and devoted male assistant or servant who can be trusted with any task. A faithful helper or right-hand man, named after the character in Robinson Crusoe. A male employee who performs a wide range of duties.
example_sentence: He has been the manager's Man Friday for ten years. Every busy office needs a reliable Man Friday. The shopkeeper treated his Man Friday like family. As Man Friday, he handled everything from accounts to deliveries.

english_meaning: A phrase used to report that a person has been injured or knocked down. A call for help when someone is hurt.
example_sentence: The medic shouted, “Man down!” when the player collapsed. The radio message reported one man down near the entrance. Everyone stopped when they heard the call of “man down.” In the drill, the team practiced responding to a man-down situation.

english_meaning: A warning that a person is leaving or has left an area. In sports, a call that a player has been put out.
example_sentence: The guard shouted, “Man out!” as the worker left the building. In cricket, the umpire signaled that the batsman was man out. The team yelled “man out” during the fielding drill. The phrase warned everyone that a person had moved beyond the safe area.

english_meaning: Humans make plans, but the final outcome depends on God or fate. Things do not always happen as people expect. Human beings cannot fully control the future. Life is uncertain and unpredictable. Success and failure are not always based only on planning. Divine will is greater than human effort.
example_sentence: Ahmed planned to study abroad, but his visa was rejected, Man proposes, God disposes. They organized a picnic for weeks, but heavy rain ruined the event, Man proposes, God disposes. She worked hard to win the competition, yet she became ill before the final round, Man proposes, God disposes. The businessman invested all his savings in a project, but the market suddenly crashed, Man proposes, God disposes.

english_meaning: To be brave and deal with a difficult situation. To show courage, responsibility, or emotional strength, though the phrase can sound old-fashioned or stereotypical.
example_sentence: You need to man up and apologize for your mistake. She told him to man up and face the consequences. The coach urged the players to man up during the final minutes. Instead of saying “man up,” it is often kinder to say “be brave.”

english_meaning: A metal band, chain, or shackle for fastening someone's hands or ankles. To restrain a person with handcuffs or similar physical bindings. Something that restricts or shackles a person's freedom or progress. The act of placing someone under physical constraint to prevent movement or escape. A device used primarily to secure prisoners during transport.
example_sentence: The guards had to manacle the prisoner before transferring him to the high-security wing. The heavy iron manacle left deep bruises on the captive's wrists. We must work together to break the manacle of poverty that holds back the community. The officer reached for his belt to produce a manacle for the suspect.

english_meaning: To exercise executive, administrative, and supervisory control over an organization or project. To succeed in surviving or attaining one's goals despite having difficult circumstances. To handle or wield a tool or weapon with skill and precision. To maintain control over a person, animal, or situation through influence or authority. To organize and regulate resources or time effectively for a specific purpose.
example_sentence: She had to manage a team of twenty developers to meet the tight deadline. Even with a very small budget, they managed to organize a beautiful wedding. It is important to learn how to manage your time effectively during the exam. The rider was unable to manage the wild horse and was eventually thrown off.

english_meaning: Capable of being controlled, directed, or governed with ease. Possible to deal with or handle without excessive difficulty. Small enough or simple enough to be dealt with successfully. Able to be kept under control or within reasonable limits. Susceptible to being manipulated or influenced effectively.
example_sentence: The project was broken down into manageable tasks to ensure steady progress. Despite the heavy traffic, the commute remained manageable due to the new bypass. The teacher found the smaller class size much more manageable for individual instruction. We need to keep our expectations at a manageable level to avoid burnout.

english_meaning: Successfully controlled or guided something toward a specific outcome. Handled a difficult situation or problem with skill. Supervised or directed a business, organization, or a group of people. Contrived or succeeded in doing something despite obstacles. Administered resources or time efficiently to achieve a goal. Governed or regulated the behavior of individuals or systems.
example_sentence: She managed the project with remarkable efficiency and precision. Despite the heavy rain, he managed to reach the venue on time. The company is managed by a board of experienced directors. He managed his finances carefully to save for a new house.

english_meaning: The process of dealing with or controlling things or people. The responsibility for and control of a company or organization. The group of people who are in charge of a business or enterprise. The act of organizing or handling a situation or task skillfully. The treatment or care of a patient or disease over a period of time.
example_sentence: Effective time management is essential for productivity in the workplace. The management has decided to implement a new policy regarding remote work. We need better management of our natural resources to ensure sustainability. The medical team discussed the long-term management of the patient's chronic condition.

english_meaning: A person who is responsible for controlling or administering an organization or group of staff. Someone who manages the business affairs of a sports team, an actor, or a performer. A computer program or system that organizes and controls data or tasks. An individual who handles money or resources with skill and efficiency. A person whose job is to oversee a particular department or branch of a company.
example_sentence: The project manager lead the team to complete the task ahead of schedule. She is the personal manager for several famous Hollywood actors. The store manager addressed the customer's concerns immediately. He is a very efficient manager of his household finances.

english_meaning: A judicial writ ordering a public official or body to perform a legal duty. A command issued by a higher court to a lower court or authority. A legal remedy used to compel the performance of an official act.
example_sentence: The court issued a writ of mandamus against the department. They filed for mandamus to compel the officer to act. Mandamus cannot be granted for a discretionary decision. The lawyer explained the grounds for seeking mandamus.

english_meaning: An official order or commission to do something. Authority granted by an electorate to act as a representative. To require by law or order. A political authorization.
example_sentence: The government issued a mandate to wear masks. The president has a strong mandate from the people. The law mandates fair treatment of all workers. The committee received a mandate to reform the system. Voters gave her a clear mandate.

english_meaning: Officially required or ordered by law, rule, or authority. Given official permission or authority to act on behalf of others. Made compulsory through a formal decision. Of a territory, placed under the administration of another country by international agreement.
example_sentence: Face masks were mandated during the outbreak. The law mandated equal pay for equal work. The committee is mandated to review all appeals. Mandated territories were administered under international supervision.

english_meaning: Required by law or rule and therefore not a matter of choice. Officially ordered and having to be obeyed. Describing something that must be done as a condition or duty. Relating to a mandate or official command given to a country or authority.
example_sentence: Wearing a seat belt is mandatory in this country. The court imposed a mandatory sentence for the offence. Registration is mandatory for all new students. The company introduced mandatory safety training last year.

english_meaning: The lower jawbone that holds the lower teeth. The largest and strongest bone of the human face. The movable bone of the skull used for chewing and speaking. The jaw or mouthpart of an insect or other animal.
example_sentence: The mandible is the only movable bone of the skull. He fractured his mandible in the accident. The dentist examined the alignment of her mandible. Insects use their mandibles to cut and hold food.

english_meaning: To move something or someone carefully and skillfully, often to achieve a goal or gain an advantage. A planned and controlled movement, especially in a military, driving, or strategic context.
example_sentence: The pilot made a sharp maneuvre to avoid the storm. She tried to maneuvre the car through the narrow street. His clever maneuvre changed the direction of the meeting. The team had to maneuvre quickly to win.

english_meaning: To spoil or damage severely by cutting, tearing, or crushing. To ruin something such as a piece of music or a language through incompetent handling. A machine for pressing laundry with rollers.
example_sentence: The car was mangled in the accident. He mangled the pronunciation of every word. The old machine mangled the linen. She hated when singers mangled classic songs. Wild animals mangled the fence.

english_meaning: A sweet tropical stone fruit with smooth skin and juicy golden-orange flesh. A fruit widely regarded as the king of fruits in South Asia. The large tree that produces this fruit. The pulp of this fruit used in juices, pickles, and desserts.
example_sentence: Sindhi mangoes are famous for their rich sweetness. The whole family sat under the mango tree. She made a thick mango shake for the guests. Raw mangoes are used to prepare tangy pickles.

english_meaning: A small tropical fruit with a thick purple rind and sweet white segments inside. A fruit known for its delicate, slightly tangy flavour. The tree that produces this fruit. A Southeast Asian fruit often called the queen of fruits.
example_sentence: The mangosteen has a soft, snow-white centre. He tasted mangosteen for the first time in Thailand. Mangosteen is often called the queen of fruits. The purple rind of the mangosteen stains clothes easily.

english_meaning: To handle, move, or control someone or something roughly or forcefully. To treat a person harshly or physically.
example_sentence: The guards were accused of manhandling the protesters. Workers manhandled the heavy crates into the truck. Please do not manhandle the fragile equipment. The security officer handled the visitor firmly but did not manhandle him.

english_meaning: Showing wild, uncontrolled, or extreme behavior, often associated with madness or obsession. Behaving in a frenzied, irrational, or excessively enthusiastic manner. Used to describe laughter, behavior, or plans that are excessive to the point of seeming insane. Often used to describe villains or characters with extreme, obsessive determination.
example_sentence: The villain let out a maniacal laugh as his plan came together.  His maniacal obsession with winning destroyed his relationships.  The crowd watched in shock as the man ran through the streets in a maniacal frenzy.  Her maniacal energy on stage left the audience both thrilled and exhausted.  The dictator's maniacal pursuit of power led to widespread suffering.

english_meaning: People who behave in an extremely wild, violent, or uncontrolled way. Persons obsessed with something to an excessive degree. Wildly enthusiastic fans. Individuals suffering from mania.
example_sentence: The maniacs on the road drive too fast. Football maniacs filled the stadium. Doctors treated the maniacs with special care. Those maniacs stayed up all night playing games. History remembers the tyrants as maniacs of power.

english_meaning: To show something clearly or make something obvious. To make something visible or obvious, or to show a quality, feeling, or condition clearly. A document or list of cargo, passengers, or goods carried by a ship, aircraft, or vehicle. Clear, obvious, or easily noticed.
example_sentence: Her talent was manifest from a very early age. The symptoms of the disease began to manifest after three days. The ship's manifest listed all the cargo on board. His anxiety manifested itself through constant nail-biting.

english_meaning: An event, action, or object that clearly shows or embodies something abstract or theoretical. It is the act of demonstrating or showing something clearly to the sight or understanding. In a spiritual context, it refers to the materialization of a spirit or phenomenon.
example_sentence: The protests were a clear manifestation of the public’s frustration with the government. His sudden wealth was the manifestation of years of hard work and saving. Scientists studied the physical manifestation of the virus in the host cells. She believes that positive thinking leads to the manifestation of one's desires.

english_meaning: A public declaration of the intentions, policies, or views of an individual, group, or political party. Often issued before elections or major events to communicate key aims. A manifesto is like a written promise or plan that tells people what someone believes and what they will do in the future.
example_sentence: The party released its manifesto one week before the election. His manifesto called for free education and universal healthcare. The artist published a manifesto outlining his creative philosophy. The environmental manifesto was signed by over a million people.

english_meaning: To handle, control, or influence something or someone cleverly or skillfully. To skillfully operate, manage, or control something, often in a way that influences or changes it. It can be neutral (like handling a machine) or negative (influencing someone unfairly).
example_sentence: She uses her charm to manipulate people. They managed to manipulate us into agreeing to help. Computers are efficient at manipulating information. As a politician he knows how to manipulate public opinion.

english_meaning: To influence or control someone so that they do something, often unfairly or deceptively. To skillfully move or arrange something into a particular position or condition.
example_sentence: The salesperson manipulated him into buying an expensive plan. She was manipulated into signing the document. The technician manipulated the parts into the correct position. Do not let anyone manipulate you into making a rushed decision.

english_meaning: The act of controlling or influencing someone or something, often unfairly or deceptively. Skilled handling or adjustment of an object, system, or information.
example_sentence: The advertisement relies on emotional manipulation. Data manipulation can produce a misleading result. Gentle manipulation of the joint improved movement. The investigation exposed manipulation of the voting records.

english_meaning: Using clever or unscrupulous methods to control or influence others for one's own advantage. Characterised by deceitful and cunning behaviour designed to manage or exploit others. Tending to influence or control people in a dishonest or unfair way.
example_sentence: His manipulative behaviour made it very difficult for his colleagues to trust him. She recognised the manipulative tactics being used and refused to be drawn in. The manipulative character in the novel controls everyone around him through lies and flattery. His manipulative use of the situation to gain personal advantage was widely condemned. She warned her daughter about the manipulative nature of people who constantly seek to control others.

english_meaning: A person who controls or influences others in a clever or unscrupulous way. A device used to handle materials or perform operations, especially in a mechanical or robotic system. One who operates or handles skillfully.
example_sentence: He is a clever manipulator of people. The scientist used a manipulator to handle the radioactive material. Politicians are often accused of being manipulators. A skilled manipulator can perform precise robotic surgery. She recognized him as a manipulator and avoided him.

english_meaning: A way in which a thing is done or happens. A person's outward behavior or way of behaving toward others. Manners refers to polite social behavior. A style or fashion. A kind or sort.
example_sentence: She spoke in a polite manner. Children should learn good manners. He solved the problem in a clever manner. All manner of goods were sold at the market. His rude manner offended everyone.

english_meaning: To move something or someone carefully and skillfully, often to achieve a goal or gain an advantage. A planned and controlled movement, especially in a military, driving, or strategic context.
example_sentence: The driver made a quick manoeuver to avoid the bike. They practiced each manoeuver before the show. He manoeuvered his way through the crowd. The manoeuver required focus.

english_meaning: To move something or someone carefully and skillfully, often to achieve a goal or gain an advantage. A planned and controlled movement, especially in a military, driving, or strategic context.
example_sentence: The soldiers performed a difficult manoeuvre. She manoeuvred around the obstacle with care. His political manoeuvre surprised everyone. The manoeuvre saved the ship.

english_meaning: A large country house with lands. A unit of land in medieval Europe under the feudal system. An estate. In British history, the lord's estate.
example_sentence: The old manor stood on a hill overlooking the village. The manor had been in the family for centuries. Peasants worked on the lord's manor. Tourists visited the historic manor. The manor was surrounded by beautiful gardens.

english_meaning: The number of people available or required for work or service. Human strength or effort. Workforce. Labor available for a task.
example_sentence: The factory needs more manpower to increase production. Modern machines have reduced the need for manpower. The army has significant manpower. Manpower shortages delayed the project. They lack the manpower to run the campaign.

english_meaning: A large, impressive house. A very large, expensive house. A large and imposing house.
example_sentence: The street is lined with enormous mansions where the rich and famous live. The mansion is set in 90 acres of beautiful, unspoilt countryside. He told me he owned a mansion in Spain and I fell for it.

english_meaning: The unlawful killing of another person without the intent to commit murder. A criminal offense involving causing someone's death through recklessness, negligence, or in the heat of the moment without premeditation. Considered less severe than murder under most legal systems because it lacks malicious intent or planning. Often classified as voluntary or involuntary, depending on the circumstances of the act.
example_sentence: The driver was charged with manslaughter after the fatal accident caused by reckless driving.  The jury found him guilty of manslaughter rather than murder due to lack of intent.  The case was reduced from murder to manslaughter after new evidence emerged.  Voluntary manslaughter often involves a sudden loss of self-control.  She received a lighter sentence for involuntary manslaughter caused by negligence.

english_meaning: A traditional lace or silk veil or shawl worn by women over the head and shoulders, especially in Spain and some Latin American countries. A decorative veil or shawl, usually made of lace, silk, or other fine fabric. It is traditionally worn by women during religious ceremonies, cultural celebrations, weddings, and formal occasions, especially in Spain and parts of Latin America. It is also considered a symbol of elegance and cultural heritage.
synonyms: ["Veil","Shawl","Head covering","Lace veil","Headscarf (in some contexts)","Cloak (loosely depending on context)"]
example_sentence: She wore a beautiful black mantilla during the church ceremony. The bride completed her traditional outfit with a delicate lace mantilla. Tourists admired the elegant mantillas worn during the cultural festival. Her grandmother carefully preserved an antique silk mantilla for future generations.

english_meaning: A predatory insect with a long body, powerful forelegs held in a praying position, and a triangular head. Also called praying mantis. Known for its hunting posture.
example_sentence: A green mantis sat still on the leaf. The praying mantis caught a fly in mid air. Children were fascinated by the mantis in the garden. The female mantis sometimes eats the male. Mantis species come in many sizes and colors.

english_meaning: A loose cloak or covering, often worn over the shoulders. A role or responsibility passed from one person to another. The layer of the Earth between the crust and the core. Something that covers, hides, or envelops like a cloak. To spread over like a layer or veil. To cover, cloak, or envelop something, literally or figuratively.
example_sentence: She wore a beautiful silk mantle over her shoulders. The mantle of leadership passed from the father to his son. Scientists study the Earth’s mantle to understand volcanic activity. Darkness spread its mantle across the valley. A soft mist mantled the mountains in the early morning. Her face was mantled with embarrassment.

english_meaning: Relating to or done with the hands rather than using machines. Requiring or using physical effort and strength. A small book giving instructions or information for using a product or performing a task. A keyboard played with the hands on an instrument like an organ or harpsichord. Operated by a human rather than an automatic system or process.
example_sentence: The new staff members were assigned to perform manual labor in the warehouse. Please consult the instruction manual before assembling the furniture. The car has a manual transmission rather than an automatic one. Playing a pipe organ requires coordinating multiple manuals and foot pedals simultaneously.

english_meaning: By hand rather than by machine or automatic process. Using physical effort or direct human control.
example_sentence: The forms must be entered manually. She manually adjusted the camera settings. The workers manually sorted the packages. The gate can be opened manually during a power cut.

english_meaning: To make goods, especially in large quantities using machinery or industrial methods. A product or the process of making products. To invent or fabricate something, sometimes dishonestly.
example_sentence: The factory manufactures medical equipment. This company manufactures bicycles locally. The story was a complete manufacture. Modern methods manufacture products more efficiently.

english_meaning: A person or company that makes goods, usually in large quantities. A producer of products or equipment.
example_sentence: The manufacturer recalled the defective cars. Check the manufacturer’s instructions before use. The phone manufacturer released a new model. The manufacturer guarantees the machine for two years.

english_meaning: The process or industry of making goods from raw materials, especially in factories. Relating to the production of goods.
example_sentence: Manufacturing provides thousands of jobs in the region. The company is investing in advanced manufacturing. Manufacturing costs increased this year. The manufacturing sector needs skilled workers.

english_meaning: The formal act of freeing a slave from slavery. Legal release from forced servitude.
example_sentence: The document recorded the manumission of the family’s servants. Manumission was an important step toward ending slavery. The law required proof of manumission. Historians studied records of manumission in the region.

english_meaning: Animal dung, especially that of cattle or horses, used to fertilize the soil and make crops grow better. Any natural substance applied to land to enrich it. To spread fertilizer or dung on land in order to improve its fertility. Decayed organic matter used in farming and gardening.
example_sentence: Farmers spread manure on the fields before sowing the seeds. Cow manure is considered an excellent natural fertilizer. The garden needs fresh manure to produce healthy vegetables. He uses organic manure instead of chemical fertilizers. They manure the land twice a year for better crops.

english_meaning: A book, document, or piece of music written by hand rather than typed or printed. An author's text that has not yet been published. Any handwritten or unpublished document.
example_sentence: The museum displayed an ancient manuscript. She sent her manuscript to the publisher. Old manuscripts are preserved with great care. Scholars study medieval manuscripts. The composer wrote the manuscript by hand.

english_meaning: A long-distance race (usually 42.195 kilometers or 26 miles). A long activity or event that takes a lot of time and effort.
example_sentence: He trained for months to run the marathon in London. Writing the entire report in one night was a real marathon. The charity organized a marathon to raise funds for hospitals. The meeting turned into a five-hour marathon discussion.

english_meaning: A person who roams around looking for things to steal or destroy. Someone who moves from place to place in search of goods, valuables, or property to steal.
example_sentence: The marauder attacked the small village at night. Farmers protected their crops from marauders. The pirates acted like marauders along the coast. The army defended the border against invading marauders.

english_meaning: To begin something in a strong, bold, or powerful way. To enter a place or situation with confidence and force. Often used to describe March weather starting with harsh conditions. To start an event with impressive energy or authority. To make a striking or forceful beginning.
example_sentence: The new CEO marched in like a lion on his first day. This year, March marched in like a lion with heavy storms. Their campaign marched in like a lion but ended quietly. The team marched in like a lion, determined to win.

word: March to the beat of one’s own drum
english_meaning: A person who is independent-minded and does not feel pressured to follow what others are doing. Such a person prefers to make their own decisions, even if they are unusual or unpopular.
synonyms: ["Be independent-minded","Think outside the box","Go your own way","Follow one’s own path","Nonconformist behavior"]
antonyms: ["Follow the crowd","Conform to others","Copy others","Go with the flow","Be conventional"]
example_sentence: She always dresses differently and marches to the beat of her own drum. Even in school, he marched to the beat of his own drum and chose unique projects.

english_meaning: To push someone or something to the edge of society or importance. To treat a person, group, or idea as less important or powerless, often by excluding them from decision making, resources, or social activities.
example_sentence: Poor communities are often marginalized in urban development plans. The policy marginalized small farmers and favored large corporations. Women were marginalized in leadership roles for many years. Ignoring minority voices can marginalize entire groups.

english_meaning: Relating to the sea or ocean and the life found in it. Connected with shipping, sailing, or naval affairs. A soldier trained to serve on land and at sea, especially a member of the marines. The shipping fleet of a country considered collectively.
example_sentence: Plastic waste is a serious threat to marine life. She is studying marine biology at university. A marine engineer inspected the damaged hull. His brother served as a marine for eight years.

english_meaning: Connected with the sea, especially in relation to shipping, navigation, or trade. Living or found near the sea. Bordering on the sea. Relating to sailing or naval activities. Concerning marine affairs.
example_sentence: Pakistan has a long maritime border along the Arabian Sea. The country signed a new maritime trade agreement. Maritime laws regulate activities on the high seas. He works in the maritime industry. The museum exhibits a rich maritime history.

english_meaning: To reduce a price or score. To lower the price of something or to give someone a lower score or opinion.
example_sentence: The shop marked down all winter clothes. The teacher marked him down for careless mistakes. Prices are marked down during the sale. The judge marked down the performance slightly.

english_meaning: To separate or tick as done. To separate an area or to indicate something as completed on a list.
example_sentence: The police marked off the accident area. She marked off tasks on her to do list. The room was marked off for VIP guests. He marked off each chapter as he finished it.

english_meaning: To identify or separate clearly. To show or draw boundaries or to make someone or something stand out.
example_sentence: The workers marked out the land for construction. Her talent marks her out from others. The teacher marked out key topics. The field was marked out with white lines.

english_meaning: To increase price or add notes. To raise the price of goods or to write notes or corrections on a text.
example_sentence: The store marked up the prices before Eid. The editor marked up the document with comments. They marked up imported items heavily. Please mark up the report before submission.

english_meaning: Able or likely to be sold. Attractive to buyers or suitable for a particular market. In demand because of useful qualities, skills, or commercial appeal. Legally capable of being bought, sold, or transferred. Presentable enough to be promoted successfully.
example_sentence: Her technical skills are highly marketable. The designer changed the packaging to make the product more marketable. Farmers selected fruit of marketable size and quality. A clear legal title makes the property marketable.

english_meaning: A name of a historic literary poem by Sir Walter Scott, published in 1808. Also used as a proper name. Not a common English noun; refers to a chivalric character or the poem itself.
example_sentence: Students study Marmion in English literature classes. Marmion tells a tale of chivalry and betrayal. The name Marmion belongs to a proud knight. Marmion is one of Scott's most famous poems. Critics have long analyzed Marmion.

english_meaning: A dark brownish-red colour. Describing something of this deep reddish-brown shade. To leave a person trapped and alone in a place from which they cannot escape.
example_sentence: The school uniform includes a maroon blazer. She painted the door a rich maroon. The storm marooned the travellers on the island. They were marooned for three days without food.

english_meaning: A brand or make of a product, especially a car. A distinctive emblem or badge on a vehicle. A license granted by a state to a private citizen to attack ships of an enemy nation.
example_sentence: Ferrari is a famous luxury car marque. Each marque has its own reputation for quality. Collectors prefer classic marques. The marque of the ship was well known. Letters of marque were once issued to privateers.

english_meaning: Spoiled, damaged, or made less perfect by something unpleasant. Having lost beauty, quality, or value because of a flaw, mistake, or unwanted event. Past form of the verb 'mar', meaning to spoil or impair.
example_sentence: The beautiful painting was marred by a deep scratch in the middle. Their wedding day was marred by sudden heavy rain. His face was marred by an old scar. The match was marred by the poor behaviour of the spectators. A small mistake marred his otherwise excellent performance.

english_meaning: The fourth planet from the Sun, known as the Red Planet. The Roman god of war. A large chocolate bar brand. To spoil, damage, or impair something, when used as a verb (mar/mars).
example_sentence: Scientists sent a rover to Mars. Mars is often called the Red Planet. In Roman myth Mars was the god of war. A scratch mars the smooth surface of the table. The scandal mars his reputation.

english_meaning: An area of low-lying land that is flooded in wet seasons or at high tide and typically remains waterlogged at all times. A wetland area dominated by grasses, rushes, and reeds. An area of soft, wet ground.
example_sentence: The marsh stretched for several kilometres along the edge of the estuary. The rare bird was spotted nesting in the reed beds at the edge of the marsh. Draining the marsh for agricultural use destroyed a unique and irreplaceable habitat. The conservation team worked to restore the marsh to its natural condition after years of industrial pollution. Marsh plants such as bulrushes and cattails are essential for water filtration and wildlife habitat.

english_meaning: Ground that is soft and wet, like a swamp or bog. Low-lying, wet land often covered with water and filled with grasses, reeds, and small plants. Land where the soil remains soft, muddy, and waterlogged most of the time, usually home to birds, insects, and aquatic life.
example_sentence: Many rare birds live in the coastal marshlands. The road becomes impassable during rain because it crosses a marshland. Scientists are studying how climate change affects marshland ecosystems. The villagers built their homes away from the marshland to avoid flooding.

english_meaning: A person who demands absolute adherence to forms and rules. A strict disciplinarian, especially in the armed forces. Someone who enforces rigid discipline through punishment or authority. A taskmaster who allows no deviations from established procedures. A formalist who prioritizes regulations over individual needs.
example_sentence: The drill sergeant was a notorious martinet who punished the slightest uniform imperfection. Our new manager is a bit of a martinet regarding punctuality and office decorum. While he was a martinet on the field, the coach was surprisingly gentle in private. The school principal was feared as a martinet for his uncompromising stance on the dress code.

english_meaning: A strap or set of straps fastened at one end to the noseband, bit, or reins of a horse and at the other end to the girth, used to prevent the horse from raising its head too high. In sailing, a stay or rope used to hold down the jib-boom. A betting strategy in which the gambler doubles the stake after every loss in the hope of recovering all previous losses with a single win.
example_sentence: The rider attached a standing martingale to keep the young horse's head in the correct position. A running martingale is preferred by many riders because it gives the horse more freedom. The sailors checked the martingale carefully before setting out into the open sea. He lost most of his money trying to apply the martingale system at the casino. Trainers often warn that a martingale should never be used as a substitute for proper training.

english_meaning: A person who is killed because of their religious or political beliefs. To kill somebody because of their religious or political beliefs
example_sentence: He was martyred for his religious beliefs. Many first-century Christians were martyred for their faith.

english_meaning: The state of suffering or dying for a cause, especially a religious or noble belief. The suffering, pain, or death endured by a person who refuses to give up their beliefs, values, or faith. It is often linked with religious devotion, but it can also apply to people who sacrifice their lives for justice, freedom, or a noble cause.
example_sentence: He was remembered for his martyrdom in the struggle for freedom. The story describes the martyrdom of early believers. Many leaders gained respect after their martyrdom for justice. Her martyrdom became a symbol of courage and sacrifice.

english_meaning: To be filled with wonder or astonishment. To feel great surprise or admiration. A wonderful or astonishing person or thing. An object of amazement. To express amazement at something extraordinary.
example_sentence: The children marveled at the size of the elephant. She is a marvel of intelligence and hard work. Tourists marvel at the beauty of the Taj Mahal. The new technology is a marvel of modern science.

english_meaning: A person, animal, or object believed to bring good luck to a team, group, or organization. A symbolic figure used for promotion or team identity.
example_sentence: The school's mascot is a lion. The team wore their mascot on their jerseys. A cartoon character served as the company's mascot. The mascot cheered up the crowd. Children love the friendly mascot at events.

english_meaning: To give something masculine qualities or a masculine appearance. In biology or medicine, to cause male physical characteristics to develop.
example_sentence: Critics said the design masculinized the whole brand. Certain hormones can masculinize the body. The uniform was redesigned to masculinize its look. The condition may masculinize the voice over time.

english_meaning: To crush food into a soft, pulpy mass. A soft mixture produced by crushing. Boiled and crushed potatoes. In brewing, grain mixed with hot water.
example_sentence: Mash the potatoes with butter and a little milk. She served sausages with mash and gravy. Mash the bananas before adding the flour. The brewer stirred the mash slowly.

english_meaning: To press something down firmly until it is flattened or pulped. In informal Caribbean use, to destroy, ruin or crush completely.
example_sentence: Mash down the fruit until the juice runs out. He mashed down the soil around the seedling. The storm mashed down the whole crop. They mashed down the old fence in an hour.

english_meaning: To crush, smash, or break into pieces. To mix different elements together, often creatively. To spoil or ruin something through careless handling. In music, creating a track by blending multiple songs. To heavily criticize or defeat someone. To distort something in a playful or exaggerated way.
example_sentence: He mashed up the vegetables for the soup. The kids mashed up the toy by accident. The DJ mashed up two popular songs into one track. Don’t mash up your report; organize it carefully.

english_meaning: A common spelling variant of muskmelon, a sweet melon with netted skin. A round or oval summer fruit with juicy orange or green flesh. A member of the gourd family grown widely in warm climates. A refreshing fruit eaten fresh, in salads, or as juice.
example_sentence: He bought a ripe maskmelon from the fruit market. Maskmelon is very refreshing in the summer heat. She cut the maskmelon into small cubes. Maskmelon seeds are often dried and eaten.

english_meaning: The tendency to derive pleasure, especially sexual gratification, from one's own pain or humiliation. Willingness to endure painful or unpleasant experiences. The counterpart of sadism.
example_sentence: Psychologists study cases of masochism. His constant self criticism borders on masochism. Some see extreme sports as a form of masochism. The novel explored themes of masochism. Masochism is opposite to sadism in psychology.

english_meaning: To pretend to be someone or something else. A false show or pretense. A costume party where people wear masks. To disguise oneself for deception or fun. An act of hiding one's true identity.
example_sentence: He masqueraded as a doctor to gain their trust. The guests attended a grand masquerade ball. Her kindness was a masquerade to hide her true intentions. He masqueraded under a false name for years.

english_meaning: The widespread or large-scale mistreatment, misuse, or exploitation of people, power, or resources. A situation where many people or things are harmed, mistreated, or violated at the same time. It often involves systematic or organized wrongdoing, such as human rights violations, corruption, or exploitation affecting a large group or community. The term can apply to social, political, or digital contexts.
example_sentence: The report revealed mass abuse of human rights during the conflict. Social media companies were criticized for mass abuse of user data. The organization works to prevent mass abuse of children in poor communities. The dictator was accused of mass abuse of power against his citizens.

english_meaning: To carry out a brutal killing of many people or animals. To destroy completely in a figurative sense. An act of killing a large number of people or animals in a violent and brutal manner. Can also mean overwhelming defeat.
example_sentence: Invaders massacred the entire town. Poachers massacred hundreds of elephants. The massacre left the village in ruins. Thousands were victims of the massacre.

english_meaning: A thick, powerful muscle of the cheek that runs from the cheekbone to the lower jaw. One of the main muscles of chewing, which raises the lower jaw and closes the mouth. The strongest muscle in the human body in terms of the force it can apply for its size.
example_sentence: You can feel the masseter tighten when you clench your teeth. Grinding the teeth at night can enlarge the masseter muscle. The dentist gently pressed the masseter to check for pain. Chewing tough food gives the masseter a real workout.

english_meaning: Very large. Heavy & solid. Extremely large or serious
example_sentence: The explosion made a massive hole in the ground. He suffered a massive heart attack.

english_meaning: A tall upright post on a ship or boat that supports the sails. A flagpole or antenna support. The fruit of beech, oak, and other forest trees, used as food for pigs and wildlife.
example_sentence: The sailors climbed the mast to fix the sail. A tall mast supported the ship's flag. Radio signals travel through a mast antenna. The pigs fed on mast in the forest. Storms broke the ship's mast.

english_meaning: A surgical operation to remove all or part of a breast. A procedure most often performed to treat or prevent breast cancer. The medical removal of breast tissue, sometimes including lymph nodes. An operation that may be followed by reconstructive surgery.
example_sentence: The doctor recommended a mastectomy after the biopsy results. She recovered quickly following her mastectomy. A mastectomy is sometimes performed to prevent cancer in high-risk patients. The hospital offers counselling to women before a mastectomy.

english_meaning: To bite food many times as you eat it. To grind or crush (food) with or as if with the teeth.
example_sentence: Masticate your food thoroughly.

english_meaning: To stimulate one's own genitals for sexual pleasure. To the act of touching or rubbing one's own sexual organs to achieve sexual arousal or orgasm, usually done alone.
example_sentence: He felt embarrassed to talk about how he would masturbate. Many people consider masturbation a normal part of sexual development. She read a book on sexual health that explained how to masturbate safely. Some cultures discourage or stigmatize people who masturbate.

english_meaning: The act of stimulating one's own genitals for sexual pleasure. The self-stimulation of the genital organs, usually to achieve sexual arousal or orgasm, without a partner. It is a natural activity and is often practiced privately.
example_sentence: He was embarrassed to talk about masturbation. Masturbation is considered normal behavior in adolescents. Doctors say masturbation is safe if done in moderation. Some cultures have taboos against masturbation.

english_meaning: A perfect relationship or pairing where two people or things suit each other extremely well. A relationship, partnership, or combination that seems ideally suited, as if destined to be perfect. It is often used for romantic couples, but it can also describe business partnerships, friendships, or even things that work exceptionally well together.
synonyms: ["Perfect match","Ideal pair","Made for each other","Perfect combination","Well-suited pair"]
example_sentence: Their marriage is truly a match made in heaven. This software and your project are a match made in heaven. The chef and his assistant are a match made in heaven in the kitchen. Those two friends are a match made in heaven when it comes to teamwork.

english_meaning: Each of a pair of animals or birds that live or breed together. It also refers to a fellow worker, a partner in marriage, or a close friend. To bring animals together for the purpose of breeding.
example_sentence: The swan spent the entire afternoon searching for its lost mate. They have been lifelong mates since they met in primary school. The biologist observed the lions as they began to mate in the wild. Chess players must protect their king to avoid a checkmate by the opponent’s mate.

english_meaning: The substance from which something is made. Cloth or fabric. Information or ideas used for a book, film, or study. Relating to physical objects rather than the mind or spirit. Important or significant, especially in legal contexts.
example_sentence: The bridge is built from strong material. She chose a soft material for the curtains. He collected material for his new book. The lawyer said the point was material to the case.

english_meaning: A strong interest in money and possessions rather than spiritual values. The tendency to consider material comfort more important than anything else. In philosophy, the belief that only physical matter exists and that everything can be explained by it.
example_sentence: He criticised the materialism of modern city life. Materialism often leaves people feeling empty. The philosopher defended materialism against idealism. Growing materialism has changed family values.

english_meaning: Overly concerned with money, possessions, or physical comfort. Valuing material things more than spiritual, moral, or intellectual matters.
example_sentence: The story criticizes a materialistic lifestyle. He became less materialistic after traveling. Materialistic values can weaken relationships. She disliked the materialistic tone of the advertisement.

english_meaning: Materialistisch is a German adjective meaning materialistic. It describes a person, attitude, or way of thinking that gives too much importance to money, possessions, luxury, and material success, often more than spiritual, emotional, moral, or intellectual values. Concerned mainly with money, possessions, wealth, and physical comforts rather than non-material values.
example_sentence: He described the culture as materialistisch. The character's materialistisch attitude changes by the end. A materialistisch view ignores inner values. She rejected the materialistisch pressure to buy more.

english_meaning: A performance of a play, film, concert, or show held in the afternoon. An afternoon cinema or theater showing. A daytime entertainment event. A cheaper or earlier performance before the evening show.
example_sentence: We bought tickets for the Saturday matinee. The theater was full for the afternoon matinee. Families often prefer a matinee because it ends early. She took her children to a matinee during the school holiday.

english_meaning: A woman who is the head of a family or community. A matriarch is a respected older woman who leads a family, clan, or community. She is often a decision-maker and a source of guidance and support for others.
example_sentence: The grandmother became the matriarch of the family after her husband passed away. She is the matriarch of a large business empire. In many indigenous communities, the matriarch holds significant authority. The family respected her as the wise matriarch who guided everyone.

english_meaning: The killing of one's own mother. The crime of murdering a mother. A person who kills his or her mother.
