example_sentence: He hurt his thumb while hammering the nail. Babies often suck their thumb when they feel sleepy. She thumbed through the magazine while waiting. The travellers thumbed a ride to the next town.

english_meaning: hand gesture in which the thumb is raised upward, commonly used to indicate approval, agreement, encouragement, or that something is good or satisfactory.
example_sentence: The boss gave the project a thumbs up. He gave me a thumbs up before the presentation. Everyone gave a thumbs up to the new policy. That’s a thumbs up from the team.

english_meaning: The loud noise that follows a flash of lightning during a storm. Any very loud, deep, rumbling sound. To make a loud rumbling noise. To speak loudly and angrily. To move heavily and noisily with great force.
example_sentence: The thunder woke the children in the middle of the night. We heard thunder in the distance before the rain began. The crowd thundered its approval as the team scored. He thundered at the workers for arriving late.

english_meaning: People who make a lot of noise, threats, or promises usually do very little in reality. Loud talk often produces little action. People who boast, threaten, or speak dramatically are often less capable than they appear. Just like clouds that thunder loudly but bring little rain, some people create excitement or fear through words but fail to produce real results. Quiet and sincere people are often more effective than loud and boastful ones.
synonyms: ["Empty vessels make the most noise","Barking dogs seldom bite","Actions speak louder than words","Big talk","Little action","All talk and no action"]
antonyms: ["Actions prove words","Practice what you preach","Quiet people achieve more","Deeds match promises"]
example_sentence: The politician made huge promises during the campaign, but people later realized that thundering clouds seldom rain. Ahmed kept threatening to quit the project, yet he never did. Truly, thundering clouds seldom rain. The company advertised revolutionary changes, but nothing improved. Thundering clouds seldom rain. She worried about her manager’s loud warnings, but he never punished anyone because thundering clouds seldom rain.

english_meaning: Extremely loud, like the sound of thunder. Describing loud applause, cheering, or noise made by a crowd. Showing great anger in expression or voice. Powerful and forceful in effect.
example_sentence: The singer received thunderous applause from the audience. There was a thunderous crash as the wall collapsed. He gave the students a thunderous look of disapproval. The stadium erupted in thunderous cheers.

english_meaning: In this way. In the manner just described. As a result of what has just been mentioned. Therefore; consequently. To this degree or extent, as in the phrase 'thus far'.
example_sentence: He mixed the colours slowly, thus avoiding any streaks. The road was blocked, thus we had to take a longer route. Thus far, the project has stayed within budget. She spoke calmly and thus calmed the whole room.

english_meaning: To prevent someone from achieving something, to stop, hinder, block, or frustrate a plan or effort. To stop or prevent someone from carrying out a plan, achieving a goal, or succeeding in an effort. It is often used when an action, obstacle, or person blocks progress intentionally or unintentionally.
example_sentence: The police thwarted the robbery before it could take place. Heavy rain thwarted our plans for a picnic. Security measures helped thwart a cyberattack on the company. His determination allowed him to overcome every obstacle that tried to thwart his success.

english_meaning: A small glandular organ located behind the breastbone. An organ in which T-lymphocytes mature and become active. A gland that plays a key role in the body's immune system. An organ that is large in childhood and shrinks with age.
example_sentence: The thymus helps the immune system fight infection. In children the thymus is relatively large. T-cells mature inside the thymus before entering the blood. The thymus gradually shrinks after puberty.

english_meaning: A butterfly-shaped gland located at the front of the neck. A gland that produces hormones controlling metabolism. An endocrine organ that regulates heart rate, body temperature, and energy use. A gland made up of two lobes joined by a narrow isthmus.
example_sentence: The thyroid gland controls how quickly the body uses energy. An underactive thyroid gland can cause tiredness and weight gain. Iodine is needed for the thyroid gland to work properly. She takes medicine daily for her thyroid gland.

english_meaning: The larger and stronger of the two bones of the lower leg, commonly called the shinbone. The bone that runs from the knee to the ankle along the front of the leg. The bone that carries almost all of the body's weight below the knee. The bone that can be felt as a hard ridge at the front of the shin.
example_sentence: The footballer suffered a painful fracture of the tibia. You can feel the tibia just under the skin of your shin. The tibia bears most of the weight passing through the knee. Runners sometimes develop pain along the inner edge of the tibia.

english_meaning: A bookmaker's assistant at a British racecourse who signals betting odds using hand movements. A person who passes information about changing odds between bookmakers. Someone who communicates silently with gestures across a crowd at races. An old occupation now largely replaced by mobile technology.
example_sentence: The tic-tac man stood on a box waving both arms. Old photographs show a tic-tac man signalling across the racecourse. Bookmakers relied on a tic-tac man before mobile phones arrived. He worked as a tic-tac man for more than twenty years.

english_meaning: A simple game in which two players mark X or O in a grid of nine squares. A game won by placing three of one's own marks in a straight line. A children's pencil-and-paper pastime also known as noughts and crosses. Any situation described as a simple contest with limited possible moves.
synonyms: ["Noughts and crosses","Grid game","Paper game","Board game","Pastime","Puzzle game","Two-player game"]
example_sentence: The children played tic-tac-toe while waiting for the bus. He drew a tic-tac-toe grid on the back of his notebook. Almost every game of tic-tac-toe between adults ends in a draw. She wrote a simple computer program to play tic-tac-toe.

english_meaning: A small blood-sucking parasite that attaches itself to the skin of animals and humans. A parasitic arachnid that can transmit diseases such as Lyme disease. A short, sharp sound made regularly by a clock or similar device. A written mark used to show that something is correct or has been done. To mark an item with a check, or to make a light repeated clicking sound.
example_sentence: The vet removed a tick from the dog's ear. Ticks are common in tall grass during the summer months. Please tick the box if you agree to the terms. We could hear the clock tick in the silent room.

english_meaning: Very pleased or delighted. Feeling extremely happy, pleased, or delighted about something, often because of good news, praise, or a pleasant surprise.
example_sentence: She was tickled pink when she received the award. I felt tickled pink after hearing the good news. He was tickled pink by the surprise party. They were tickled pink with their exam results.

english_meaning: To move finger on sensible part of body in a way that makes laugh. A cutaneous sensation often resulting from light stroking.
example_sentence: Do not tickle me please. Her little brother screamed with laughter as she tickled him.

english_meaning: It means to be extremely pleased, delighted, or entertained. It describes a state of immense happiness and satisfaction regarding a particular situation. It implies a feeling of joy that brings a literal or figurative flush of pleasure to one's face. It is used to express profound appreciation or amusement.
example_sentence: She was tickled pink when she received the surprise bouquet of flowers. I know my grandmother will be tickled pink to see all of us at her party. He was tickled pink by the comedian's hilarious performance. We were tickled pink to find out that we had won the grand prize.

english_meaning: Cheap and poor in quality, especially of buildings and materials. Made in a dull, repetitive way with no character or individuality. Describing suburban houses that all look boringly the same. Shoddy material used in cheap construction.
example_sentence: Rows of ticky-tacky houses lined the new suburb. The furniture was ticky-tacky and fell apart within months. He criticised the ticky-tacky design of the shopping centre. They built the huts out of ticky-tacky wood and plastic.

english_meaning: Relating to or affected by the rise and fall of the sea. Describing water, land, or a river that is influenced by tides. Rising and falling regularly like the tide. Very large or powerful in movement, as in a tidal wave of change.
example_sentence: The tidal currents near the harbour are very strong. Birds feed on the tidal mudflats every morning. A tidal power station has been built along the coast. A tidal wave of protest followed the announcement.

english_meaning: The alternate rising and falling of the sea, usually twice in each lunar day at a particular place, due to the attraction of the moon and sun. A powerful surge of feeling or trend of events. It can also refer to a tendency or current of opinion.
example_sentence: The tide comes in quickly, so hikers must be careful near the cliffs. Fishermen usually go out to sea when the tide is high. A rising tide of anger swept through the crowd during the protest. The tide of public opinion has turned against the proposed tax increase.

english_meaning: Neat and orderly in appearance or habits. Having everything ordered and arranged in the right place, or liking to keep things like this. To make something look neat by putting things in the place where they belong.
example_sentence: Keeping a garden tidy is a full-time job. She likes everything neat and tidy. I've tidied the bedroom and the bathroom.

english_meaning: A piece of string, ribbon, or cord used for fastening something. A long, thin piece of fabric worn around the neck and tied in a knot at the front. A connection or link between people, groups, or things. A result in a game or contest where two or more competitors have the same score. To fasten or secure with a string or cord. To form a knot or bow in something. To restrict or limit someone's freedom of action. To achieve the same score or rank as another competitor. A wooden or concrete beam used to support the rails of a railroad track. A curved line in music indicating that two notes of the same pitch are to be played as one. A structural member such as a rod or beam designed to hold two parts together.
example_sentence: He had to straighten his tie before the important interview began. The two teams ended the match in a two-two tie. You need to tie your shoelaces before you trip over them. Family ties are often the strongest connections we have in life.

english_meaning: To fasten something securely using rope, string, or cord. To bind someone's limbs to restrict their movement. To obstruct or hinder progress or traffic. To invest money in a way that makes it unavailable for other uses. To connect or link two things together conceptually or logically. To bring something to a conclusion or settle final details. To keep someone busy or occupied so they are unavailable for other tasks. To dock or moor a boat or ship to a pier or buoy. To achieve an equal score in a competition or game. To cause a complication or delay in a legal or administrative process.
example_sentence: Please tie up the bundle of old newspapers before the recycling truck arrives. The heavy snowstorm managed to tie up traffic for several hours on the highway. I cannot buy the house now because all my capital is tied up in long-term stocks. We need one more meeting to tie up the loose ends of the contract negotiations.

english_meaning: A final point, game, or additional period of play used to determine a winner when a contest ends in a draw or tie. A question or task at the end of a competition designed to separate contestants who have equal scores. A decisive factor or person that resolves a situation of parity or deadlock. A specific rule in sports like tennis where a set reached at six games all is decided by a special game. Any method used to break an equality between two or more parties.
example_sentence: The tennis match went into a thrilling seventh-game tiebreaker to decide the set. Since both candidates had the same number of votes, the chairman cast the tiebreaker. The quiz ended in a draw, so they had to answer a difficult tiebreaker question about history. We need a clear tiebreaker rule to ensure a winner is declared by the end of the tournament.

english_meaning: One of a series of rows, levels, or layers placed one above another, as in a stadium, a cake, or a shelf. A rank or level in a graded system, indicating quality, importance, or status. To arrange something in tiers.
example_sentence: The wedding cake had four tiers decorated with white icing. The stadium seating was arranged in tiers so everyone could see the field. Companies often offer different pricing tiers for their software. The report divided cities into three tiers based on population size.

english_meaning: Very unwilling to spend money. Extremely stingy or miserly. Careful with money to an excessive degree. Reluctant to share resources. Mean in financial matters.
example_sentence: He is so tight fisted that he never buys gifts. Her tight fisted nature annoys her friends. The tight fisted boss refused to give bonuses. Being tight fisted, he saves every penny.

english_meaning: Unwilling to speak or reveal information. Keeping silent about something deliberately. Showing determination or disapproval by pressing the lips together.
example_sentence: The company remained tight lipped about the merger. He stayed tight lipped throughout the interview. She gave a tight lipped smile and said nothing. Officials were tight lipped when asked about the report.

english_meaning: To make something tighter, firmer, or more secure. To become or cause to become more strict or controlled. To pull or draw taut.
example_sentence: She tightened the screws on the shelf to make sure it was secure before loading books on it. The government decided to tighten border controls in response to the increase in smuggling. He tightened his grip on the handlebars as the road became steeper and narrower. The new policy was designed to tighten financial regulations across the sector. Her muscles tightened with tension as she waited nervously for the announcement.

english_meaning: To hold something more firmly or securely. To increase control, authority, or power over something.
example_sentence: The company tightened its grasp on the market with new policies. He tightened his grasp on the rope to avoid falling. The government tightened its grasp on social media platforms. She tightened her grasp on her dreams, refusing to give up.

english_meaning: To reduce expenses and live economically. To live more carefully and avoid waste, especially when income is reduced.
example_sentence: After losing his job, he had to tighten his belt. After losing his job, he had to tighten his belt and stop eating out. During the economic crisis, families were advised to tighten their belts. We’ll need to tighten our belts until business improves. She tightened her belt and started saving for her children’s education.

english_meaning: A person who is very unwilling to spend money. An informal term for a stingy or miserly person. Someone who saves money in an extreme and mean way.
example_sentence: He is such a tightwad that he never buys a round of tea. The tightwad refused to tip the waiter. Don't be a tightwad on your own birthday. Her uncle had a reputation as the family tightwad.

english_meaning: We will stay together until one of us dies. It expresses lifelong commitment, loyalty, and unbreakable love or partnership. Symbolizes a bond that lasts for a lifetime, no matter what challenges come.
synonyms: ["Forever together","Until the end of time","For life","Eternal bond","Lifelong commitment"]
example_sentence: They promised to love each other till death do us part. The phrase “till death do us part” symbolizes eternal love and loyalty. He stood by his wife through every hardship, truly living by “till death do us part”. Their marriage lasted for decades, a real example of “till death do us part”.

english_meaning: To move or cause to move into a sloping position. To lean or slope in one direction. A slanted or sloping position. An attempt or attack, especially in a contest or debate.
example_sentence: She tilted her head to hear the whisper more clearly. The old table tilts slightly to one side. The balance began to tilt in his favor. Do not tilt the glass or the water will spill. He made a tilt at the championship title last year.

english_meaning: Wood that is prepared for use in building and carpentry. Large standing trees that are suitable for logging and commercial purposes. A term used to describe the structural wood used in construction projects.
example_sentence: The workers stacked the freshly cut timber near the saw mill. Builders used heavy oak timber to construct the framework of the old house. Much of the forest was harvested for timber last year. The carpenter selected a fine piece of timber to carve the mantle.

english_meaning: Workers who cut, prepare, or handle timber, especially in a forest or a mine. Miners responsible for installing wooden supports (timbers) to prevent tunnels from collapsing. Plural of 'timberman'.
example_sentence: The timbermen worked hard to secure the mine tunnels. Experienced timbermen are essential for safe underground mining. The village depends on the skill of its timbermen. Timbermen felled the tall trees at the edge of the forest. The company hired more timbermen for the new project.

word: Time and tide wait for none
english_meaning: Opportunities don’t wait. Time never stops or waits. Time keeps moving forward and does not stop for anyone, no matter who they are. It reminds us that we should make use of time wisely, because lost time can never be regained.
synonyms: ["Time once lost is never found again"]
example_sentence: You should complete your work on time, time and tide wait for none. He missed the train because he was late, time and tide wait for none. If you waste your youth, remember that time and tide wait for none. Success comes to those who value time, for time and tide wait for none.

english_meaning: Time passes very quickly, often without realizing it, especially when you’re busy or enjoying yourself. It expresses how fast moments seem to go by in life.
antonyms: ["Time drags","Time stands still","Time moves slowly","Time crawls"]
example_sentence: Time flies when you’re having fun. I can’t believe it’s already October, time really flies!. It feels like just yesterday we started this project; time flies so fast. Our childhood is gone in the blink of an eye, how time flies!.

english_meaning: Showing a lack of courage or confidence and being easily frightened. Characterized by fear or a nervous disposition. Someone who is hesitant to take risks or speak out in social situations.
example_sentence: The timid child hid behind her mother when a stranger approached. He gave a timid knock on the door, unsure if he should enter. Despite his size, the dog was quite timid and ran away from the cat. She made a timid suggestion during the meeting but was ignored.

english_meaning: A lack of courage or confidence, especially in facing new situations. Shyness or nervousness in the presence of other people. An unwillingness to take risks or act boldly. Cautious behaviour caused by fear of failure or criticism.
example_sentence: His timidity prevented him from speaking at the meeting. She overcame her timidity and joined the debate club. The government was criticised for its timidity in facing the crisis. Timidity in business can cost you valuable opportunities.

english_meaning: A thin, pointed projection or prong, usually found on tools like forks, rakes, or on the antlers of animals such as deer. It is one of the sharp or narrow parts that extend from a main structure.
example_sentence: One tine of the fork was bent after it fell on the floor. The deer broke one tine of its antler during the fight. He cleaned the soil stuck between the rake tines. Be careful, the tines of that old tool are very sharp.

english_meaning: To experience or cause to experience a slight prickling or stinging sensation. To feel a light, sharp thrill of excitement or emotion. A slight prickling or stinging sensation in a part of the body.
example_sentence: Her fingers began to tingle from the cold. A shiver of excitement made his spine tingle. She felt a tingle of anticipation before the results were announced. The cream made his skin tingle for a while. I still get a tingle when I hear that old song.

english_meaning: To make small changes to something in order to repair or improve it, especially in a way that may not be helpful.
example_sentence: He’s in the garage tinkering with his bike. The password will prevent others from tinkering with your data. The government is merely tinkering at the edges of a much wider problem. He spends every weekend tinkering (around) with his car. I wish the government would stop tinkering with the health service.

english_meaning: To make or cause to make a light, clear ringing sound. A light, clear ringing sound like that of a small bell. An informal expression for a telephone call in British English.
example_sentence: The bells above the door tinkled as a customer entered. She could hear the tinkle of glasses from the party downstairs. Give me a tinkle when you reach home safely. The wind chimes tinkled softly on the veranda. Ice tinkled pleasantly in the cold drinks.

english_meaning: A shade or variety of a color. A slight coloring or trace of a color. To give a slight color to something. A dye used to color the hair.
example_sentence: The sky had a pink tint at sunset. She used a tint to cover her grey hair. The artist added a tint of blue to the painting. The windows of the car had a dark tint. His words carried a tint of sarcasm.

english_meaning: To make a ringing or tinkling sound like bells. To produce a light, musical, bell-like sound.
example_sentence: The crystal glasses began to tintinnabulate when touched lightly. Wind chimes tintinnabulate beautifully in the breeze. The little bells on her anklet tintinnabulated as she walked. The coins in his pocket would tintinnabulate with every step.

english_meaning: A ringing or tinkling sound, especially the sound of bells. The word evokes the light, musical, resonant sound of small bells or similar objects.
example_sentence: The tintinnabulation of church bells filled the morning air. She loved the tintinnabulation of wind chimes on her porch. The poem describes the tintinnabulation of sleigh bells. The soft tintinnabulation of the temple bells brought peace.

english_meaning: The pointed or rounded end of something. A small sum of money given to someone as a reward for a service. A useful piece of practical advice. To cause to overbalance or tilt. To give a small extra payment to someone.
example_sentence: The tip of the pencil broke while she was writing. He gave the waiter a generous tip after the meal. Let me give you a useful tip for the exam. Do not tip the chair backwards. The boat began to tip dangerously in the strong wind.

english_meaning: A small visible part of a much larger hidden problem. The first sign of something far bigger. Only a fraction of the whole matter that is known so far.
example_sentence: These complaints are just the tip of the iceberg. The arrests were only the tip of the iceberg in the fraud case. What we see on the surface is the tip of the iceberg. Officials fear the losses are the tip of the iceberg.

english_meaning: A traditional outdoor game played with a small piece of wood, called a cat, which is struck with a stick to make it spin or fly into the air, after which it is hit again for distance. A children's game popular historically in Britain and other countries, similar in concept to games like cricket or gilli danda. The small wooden object used in this game, tapered at both ends so it spins when struck.
example_sentence: Children in the village still play tip-cat during their school holidays.  The rules of tip-cat are quite simple but require good hand-eye coordination.  Tip-cat was a popular pastime for boys in nineteenth-century England.  He carved his own tip-cat from a piece of seasoned wood.  Tip-cat is considered an early ancestor of modern bat-and-ball games.

english_meaning: Refers to the very best part, the highest point, or the topmost level of quality or rank. Describes something excellent, perfect, or in the best possible condition. Used for people, objects, performance, or situations that are of the highest quality.
example_sentence: She arrived in tip top shape for the interview. The car looked tip top after the service. He keeps his room in tip top condition. The event went ahead in tip top style. The equipment is in tip top condition. His work is consistently tip top.

english_meaning: Slightly drunk or feeling light-headed from alcohol. Feeling mildly intoxicated, unsteady, or light-headed due to consumption of alcohol. It can also describe someone who behaves a little silly or giddy because of drinking.
example_sentence: After two glasses of wine, she felt a little tipsy. He was tipsy and kept laughing at everything. The party got lively, and soon many guests were tipsy. She walked carefully, tipsy from the champagne.

english_meaning: To walk quietly on the tips of one's toes to avoid being heard. To move in a cautious or stealthy manner. Often used figuratively to describe approaching a sensitive subject with great care.
example_sentence: I had to tiptoe past the baby's room so I wouldn't wake him up. She began to tiptoe across the cold kitchen floor at midnight. The spies had to tiptoe through the hallway to avoid the guards. It is best to tiptoe around the boss when he is in a bad mood.

english_meaning: A long, angry speech criticizing someone or something. An extended, forceful, and often angry verbal attack against a person, idea, or situation. A verbal outburst expressing frustration or irritation.
example_sentence: The coach went on a tirade after the team lost the match. She launched into a tirade against unfair workplace practices. His tirade about traffic made everyone uncomfortable. The politician faced a tirade of questions from journalists.

english_meaning: A group of similar cells that work together to perform a specific function in a living organism. A piece of soft, absorbent paper used for cleaning or wiping. A thin, translucent paper used for wrapping delicate items or making decorations. An intricate network or web of something, often used figuratively to describe a complex structure or collection of lies. A fine, gauze-like fabric often woven with silk or gold threads.
example_sentence: The scientist examined the muscle tissue under a powerful microscope. She reached for a tissue to wipe away her tears during the movie. Please wrap the glass ornament in white tissue paper to prevent it from breaking. The entire testimony was a tissue of lies designed to mislead the jury.

english_meaning: Equal revenge. An action done in return for another action usually revenge or retaliation of the same kind. It means responding to someone’s behavior with similar behavior, whether good or bad.
example_sentence: When he insulted her, she gave him tit for tat. Their argument became a tit-for-tat exchange of harsh words. He helped me last time, so I helped him today — just tit for tat. The two countries continued their tit-for-tat trade restrictions.

english_meaning: A small diacritic mark, such as a dot over a lowercase 'i' or 'j'. A tiny or infinitesimal amount of something. A very small part or particle of a substance. The smallest detail or particular of a matter. To add a small mark to a letter or document.
example_sentence: He didn't care a tittle about the consequences of his actions. Make sure you place the tittle precisely over the letter i. Every jot and tittle of the law must be strictly followed. There is not a tittle of evidence to support these wild claims.

english_meaning: Casual or trivial conversation usually about other people's personal lives. Idle gossip or rumors that carry little substance or importance. The act of talking casually about insignificant matters or local affairs.
example_sentence: She spent the entire afternoon engaging in harmless tittle-tattle with her neighbors. Don't pay any attention to the office tittle-tattle about the upcoming changes. The local magazine is full of harmless tittle-tattle about local celebrities. They would sit on the porch for hours and tittle-tattle about everyone in town.

english_meaning: To make a bad situation even worse by doing or saying something that makes the person affected feel even more upset or disrespected. To compound an already unfortunate experience with something additional that worsens the harm.
synonyms: ["Rub salt in the wound","Make matters worse","Compound the problem"]
example_sentence: To add insult to injury, the airline lost his luggage after already delaying the flight by six hours. She was already upset about being overlooked for the promotion, and to add insult to injury, a less qualified colleague was chosen. The car broke down on the motorway, and to add insult to injury, it started to rain heavily. He was charged a cancellation fee, and to add insult to injury, was told he could not rebook. To add insult to injury, the company publicly blamed the error on him when it was clearly their fault.

word: To bark up the wrong tree
english_meaning: To pursue a mistaken or misguided course of action. To direct effort, suspicion, or blame toward the wrong person or thing. To make a wrong assumption about something or someone.
synonyms: ["Follow the wrong lead","Pursue the wrong course","Be mistaken"]
antonyms: ["Be on the right track","Look in the right place"]
example_sentence: If you think I am responsible for the missing funds, you are definitely barking up the wrong tree. The detective spent weeks barking up the wrong tree before the real culprit was identified. She realised she had been barking up the wrong tree when she discovered the real cause of the problem. You are barking up the wrong tree if you expect him to approve that request. The investigation was barking up the wrong tree for months before a breakthrough finally came.

english_meaning: To be completely unintelligible or beyond one's understanding, as in 'it is all Greek to me'. To speak or write in a way nobody can follow. Something confusing, obscure, or full of unfamiliar terms.
example_sentence: This legal document is all Greek to me. When he explains physics, it becomes Greek to the whole class. The instructions were Greek to anyone without technical training. Her accounts were Greek to me until the auditor explained them.

english_meaning: Losing physical control because of alcohol. Being unable to think clearly. Being unconscious from drinking. Being intoxicated beyond normal limits
example_sentence: He was so dead drunk that he could not walk properly. After the party, a few guests were completely dead drunk. The man looked dead drunk and fell asleep on the sofa. She warned her brother not to come home dead drunk again.

english_meaning: To be in a depressed, unhappy, or unmotivated state. To feel low in mood or stuck in a period of gloom, sadness, or lack of energy.
example_sentence: She has been in a funk ever since she lost her job. He spent the whole week in a funk after the breakup. Being in a funk is normal but it is important to seek help if it lasts long. The rainy weather put the whole office in a funk.

word: To be rushed off one’s feet
english_meaning: To be extremely busy. To be so busy with work or tasks that there is no time to rest, often moving constantly from one task to another.
example_sentence: The hospital staff were rushed off their feet during the emergency. I have been rushed off my feet all day preparing for the meeting. Shopkeepers are rushed off their feet before Eid. She was rushed off her feet handling calls and emails at work.

english_meaning: To be shocked, surprised, or startled by something unexpected, usually in a sudden or emotional way. To lose composure because of surprise, shock, or confusion. It’s used for emotional or mental reactions, not physical ones.
example_sentence: I was taken aback when he suddenly apologized to me. She was taken aback by his rude behavior. They were taken aback to hear about the company’s closure. The teacher was taken aback when the quiet student spoke so confidently.

english_meaning: Used to introduce the first point or reason in a discussion or argument. At the start or in the first place. Initially or originally. As the first consideration or factor.
synonyms: ["First of all","Firstly","Initially","In the first place","Originally","At the outset","At first"]
example_sentence: To begin with, we need to understand the problem clearly. The plan was flawed to begin with. To begin with, let me introduce the team members. She should never have accepted the offer to begin with.

word: To bring grist to the mill
english_meaning: To provide something useful or profitable. To supply material or experience that can be turned to advantage. To add to one's resources or benefit.
example_sentence: Every new client brings grist to the mill for the young firm. His travels brought grist to the mill for his next novel. Even small donations bring grist to the mill of the charity. Local gossip brings grist to the mill of the columnist.

english_meaning: Humans naturally make mistakes. Making mistakes is a natural part of being human. Everyone makes errors, no matter how careful, intelligent, or experienced they are.
synonyms: ["Nobody is perfect","Humans make mistakes","Everyone makes mistakes","It is human to make mistakes","Mistakes are natural"]
antonyms: ["Perfection is expected","Never make mistakes","Absolute accuracy","Flawless behavior"]
example_sentence: I accidentally sent the wrong email to the client, but to err is human. The teacher forgave the student’s mistake, saying that to err is human. Even great scientists make mistakes because to err is human. We should not insult people for small errors since to err is human.

word: To have egg on your face
english_meaning: To look foolish or embarrassed because of a mistake. To feel embarrassed or look silly in front of others because something you said or did turned out wrong, incorrect, or unsuccessful. It is often used when someone confidently makes a claim or decision but is proven wrong later.
synonyms: ["To be embarrassed","To be humiliated","To be proven wrong","To lose face","To look foolish"]
antonyms: ["To be confident","To be respected","To be proven right","To gain respect","To succeed publicly"]
example_sentence: He claimed the project would fail, but when it succeeded, he had egg on his face. She argued loudly that she was right, but later she had egg on her face. The manager had egg on his face after the system he praised crashed. If you make false promises, you may end up with egg on your face.

word: To let the grass grow under one’s feet
english_meaning: To waste time or delay taking action. To be idle and miss opportunities through inactivity. To move slowly when prompt action is needed.
example_sentence: He never lets the grass grow under his feet when there is work to do. Do not let the grass grow under your feet; apply for the job today. She let the grass grow under her feet and lost the contract. Successful people rarely let the grass grow under their feet.

english_meaning: To cause a strong desire for food or something attractive. To create appetite. To make someone eager. To arouse desire. To look extremely tempting.
example_sentence: The smell of fresh biryani made my mouth water. The bakery window was full of cakes that made everyone’s mouth water. The pictures of juicy mangoes made his mouth water. That new sports car is enough to make anyone’s mouth water.

english_meaning: To exploit or take advantage of a situation for as much benefit as possible.
synonyms: ["Exploit","Take advantage of","Capitalize on","Make the most of"]
example_sentence: He milked the opportunity for all it was worth. They’re milking the situation to gain sympathy. The media milked the scandal for weeks. Don’t milk this excuse anymore!.

english_meaning: To restore a friendly relationship after a disagreement or quarrel. To resolve a dispute and make peace. To fix or repair a damaged situation. To reconcile with someone after a fight.
example_sentence: After weeks of silence, the two friends finally patched things up. They argued at dinner but managed to patch things up before leaving. He hopes to patch things up with his brother soon. The couple decided to patch things up for the sake of their children.

word: To poke one’s nose into others’ affairs
english_meaning: To interfere in other people’s matters without invitation. To interfere unnecessarily. To pry into private matters. To become involved without invitation. To meddle in someone else’s business.
example_sentence: He always pokes his nose into other people’s affairs. You should not poke your nose into matters that do not concern you. She became unpopular because she kept poking her nose into everyone’s business. My neighbor loves to poke his nose into family matters.

english_meaning: To pay a required amount of money, especially when one is reluctant to do so. To hand over money or resources, often under obligation or pressure.
example_sentence: Everyone had to pony up fifty dollars for the farewell party. He finally ponied up the money he owed after months of delay. The investors were asked to pony up more capital. She reluctantly ponied up for the repairs.

english_meaning: To pretend to be sad or sorry without feeling real sorrow. This idiom is used for a person who pretends to cry or show sadness only to deceive others or gain sympathy. The emotions are not genuine.
example_sentence: The thief shed crocodile tears after being caught by the police. She cried at the meeting, but everyone knew she was shedding crocodile tears. The politician shed crocodile tears for the poor during the election campaign. He apologized with crocodile tears only to avoid punishment.

word: To shoot oneself in the foot
english_meaning: To ruin one’s own chances. To harm oneself through foolish actions. To create problems for oneself. To sabotage one’s own success. To damage one’s own interests. To do something that causes problems for yourself because of your own mistake or poor decision.
synonyms: ["Self sabotage","Ruin one’s chances","Harm oneself","Backfire on oneself","Make a foolish mistake"]
antonyms: ["Help oneself","Make a wise decision","Improve one’s position","Act wisely","Benefit oneself"]
example_sentence: He shot himself in the foot by insulting his manager during the meeting. The company shot itself in the foot by increasing prices too quickly. She shot herself in the foot when she ignored the customer’s complaints. I really shot myself in the foot by missing the interview.

english_meaning: To remain neutral, avoid choosing a side, or delay making a decision between two opposing views or options. Not taking a clear position in a disagreement, debate, competition, or decision. A person who sits on the fence prefers to remain neutral, waits for more information, or avoids commitment to either side.
synonyms: ["Remain neutral","Stay undecided","Be impartial","Waver","Hesitate","Hold back","Avoid commitment","Keep an open mind"]
example_sentence: He refused to sit on the fence and openly supported the proposal. During the election, many voters sat on the fence until the final week. The manager cannot sit on the fence when two teams are in conflict. She is still sitting on the fence about which university to attend.

english_meaning: To live a carefree and adventurous life in youth. To engage in reckless or irresponsible activities. To pursue temporary pleasures rather than responsibilities. To experiment with life before becoming mature. To have many romantic relationships before settling down. To enjoy freedom without serious commitments.
synonyms: ["Live recklessly","Live carefree","Indulge oneself","Party hard","Chase pleasure","Have fun in youth","Live irresponsibly","Enjoy youthful freedom"]
antonyms: ["Settle down","Act responsibly","Be mature","Live sensibly","Focus on responsibilities","Lead a disciplined life","Be committed","Practice self control"]
example_sentence: Before getting married, he spent several years sowing his wild oats and traveling around the world. His parents hoped he would stop sowing his wild oats and focus on his career. Many young people sow their wild oats before settling into family life. After sowing her wild oats during college, she became a successful businesswoman.

english_meaning: To speak about something without knowing the facts. To talk nonsense or make claims that are not true. To speak foolishly or without proper understanding.
example_sentence: He was talking through his hat about the new tax law. Do not believe him; he is simply talking through his hat. She talks through her hat whenever the subject is science. The critics were talking through their hats without reading the report.

english_meaning: Very deeply or thoroughly. Down to the innermost part or essence. Completely, without anything remaining. Extremely cold or affected. Cut to the essential level.
example_sentence: I was chilled to the bone after walking in the rain. The budget has been cut to the bone. She was soaked to the bone by the storm. His criticism cut me to the bone.

english_meaning: To increase the stakes, demands, or risks in a situation. To raise the level of competition, expectation, or commitment in a negotiation or contest.
example_sentence: The rival company upped the ante by cutting prices further. He upped the ante in the negotiation by threatening to walk out. The new offer upped the ante and forced a quick decision. She upped the ante by demanding a promotion along with the raise.

english_meaning: To pursue pleasure or self-indulgence without regard to consequences. To follow an easy or pleasant path that leads to ruin. To live a life of ease and pleasure that ultimately leads to disaster. To choose immediate gratification over long-term well-being.
synonyms: ["Live recklessly","Pursue pleasure","Self-indulge","Take the easy way","Live for the moment"]
example_sentence: He walked the primrose path of luxury and excess. Walking the primrose path often leads to regret. They warned him not to walk the primrose path. The novel's protagonist walked the primrose path to destruction.

word: To wash one’s dirty linen in public
english_meaning: To discuss private or embarrassing matters where others can hear. To reveal family or personal quarrels openly. To expose shameful secrets instead of settling them privately. To air private disputes in front of outsiders.
synonyms: ["Air one's grievances","Reveal secrets","Make private matters public","Expose scandals"]
example_sentence: They argued at the wedding and washed their dirty linen in public. He warned his brothers not to wash their dirty linen in public. The interview was an unfortunate case of washing dirty linen in public. Families should settle disputes at home rather than wash their dirty linen in public.

english_meaning: To gain honor and prestige. To receive public recognition for achievement. To earn distinction through excellence. To achieve success and acclaim. To be rewarded with praise or awards. To gain a good reputation through outstanding performance.
synonyms: ["Gain recognition","Earn acclaim","Achieve distinction","Gain honor","Earn praise","Attain glory","Receive accolades","Win honors","Gain prestige","Make a name for oneself"]
antonyms: ["Lose reputation","Face criticism","Suffer disgrace","Bring shame","Be discredited","Fail","Lose honor","Receive condemnation","Fall into disrepute","Be ignored"]
example_sentence: She won laurels for her outstanding performance in the national science competition. The young athlete won laurels for his country by securing a gold medal. The company won laurels for its innovative environmental initiatives. Through years of dedication and hard work, he won laurels in the field of education.

english_meaning: To flatter or praise someone excessively in order to gain favor, advantage, or personal benefit. To behave like a servant toward someone influential. To seek favor through excessive praise. To act submissively for personal advantage. To engage in dishonest admiration.
synonyms: ["Flatter","Fawn on","Sycophant to","Butter up","Crawl to","Grovel to","Adulate","Praise excessively"]
example_sentence: Some employees toady to the manager just to get promotions. He refused to toady to wealthy politicians for personal gain. The young actor tried to toady to famous directors in the film industry. People who constantly toady to others often lose self respect.

english_meaning: To brown bread. To honor or celebrate. To ruin or destroy. Sliced bread browned by heat. Expression of good wishes. Person in trouble.
example_sentence: I had a slice of toast with butter for breakfast. I toasted the bread for two minutes. We raised a toast to their success. They toasted the couple at the wedding. After losing the map, we were toast. The fire toasted all the furniture.

english_meaning: A young child who is just learning to walk or has recently started walking, typically aged between one and three years. A very young child in the early stage after infancy.
example_sentence: The toddler took his first steps in the living room. She works at a nursery that cares for toddlers. Toddlers need constant supervision at home. The park has a special play area for toddlers. Every parent enjoys watching their toddler discover the world.

english_meaning: Any of the five digits at the end of the human foot. One of the small parts of the foot that help with balance and walking. The front part of a shoe, sock, or boot that covers the toes. To touch, push, or kick something lightly with the toes.
example_sentence: He stubbed his toe against the door frame. She stood on her toes to reach the top shelf. There was a hole in the toe of his sock. He toed the ball gently towards his teammate.

english_meaning: The hard protective covering at the tip of a toe. A thin plate of keratin growing over the upper surface of the toe. The nail on the foot that shields the sensitive skin underneath. A small hard plate on the toe that is trimmed to keep the feet healthy.
example_sentence: He cut his toenails after taking a bath. An ingrown toenail can be very painful. She painted her toenails a bright red. Runners should keep their toenails short.

english_meaning: With each other; in the company of one another. In combination, cooperation, or agreement. At the same time; simultaneously. Into a united or organized whole.
example_sentence: The family eats dinner together every evening. Let's work together to solve this problem. The two events happened together by coincidence. She gathered her notes together before the meeting.

english_meaning: The state of being close to one another in relationship or affection. A feeling of unity, warmth, and mutual support within a group. The quality of spending time and sharing experiences with others.
example_sentence: The festival celebrates the togetherness of the community. The family felt a strong sense of togetherness during the holidays. Shared difficulties created a spirit of togetherness among the team. The room was filled with warmth and togetherness.

english_meaning: A switch or lever that changes between two states or settings. To alternate between two options, modes, or conditions. A fastener or pin used to hold or secure something.
example_sentence: Press the toggle to switch the device on or off. The software allows you to toggle between day and night modes. Use the toggle button to enable notifications. The jacket has a wooden toggle instead of a button.

english_meaning: To work extremely hard for a long time. To move slowly and with difficulty. Exhausting labor or hard work. Long, tiring effort, especially physical.
example_sentence: Farmers toil in the fields from dawn until dusk. She toiled for years to complete her research. He toiled up the steep hill under the hot sun. Their success is the result of endless toil and patience. The workers were rewarded for their hard toil.

english_meaning: The ability or willingness to accept the existence of opinions or behavior that one dislikes or disagrees with. The capacity of an organism to endure unfavorable environmental conditions or substances. A fair and objective attitude toward those whose lifestyle differs from one's own.
example_sentence: Religious tolerance is a fundamental pillar of a peaceful society. Some people have a high tolerance for spicy food while others cannot handle it. The city is known for its cultural tolerance and diversity. Exposure to the sun helps build a tolerance to UV rays over time.

english_meaning: Willing to accept beliefs, opinions, or behaviour different from one's own. Patient and not easily offended or angered. Able to endure difficult conditions without being harmed. Broad-minded and fair towards others.
example_sentence: She is tolerant of other people's religious beliefs. A tolerant society allows peaceful disagreement. This plant is tolerant of dry soil and strong sun. He is remarkably tolerant with noisy children.

english_meaning: To allow the existence, occurrence, or practice of something that one dislikes or disagrees with. To endure or put up with someone or something unpleasant without interference. To be able to withstand the effects of a drug or environmental condition.
example_sentence: I cannot tolerate such rude behavior in my classroom. The government has decided to tolerate the small protests for now. Most plants cannot tolerate extreme heat without regular watering. She found it difficult to tolerate the constant noise from the construction site.

english_meaning: A red or yellowish fruit with a juicy pulp, used as a vegetable in cooking. It is a widely cultivated plant of the nightshade family. The fruit is commonly eaten raw in salads or cooked in sauces. It acts as a culinary staple in numerous global cuisines.
synonyms: ["Love Apple","Tom","Roma Tomato","Cherry Tomato","Nightshade Fruit","Beefsteak Tomato","Plum Tomato","Grape Tomato","Heirloom Tomato"]
example_sentence: I sliced a fresh tomato for the sandwich. She made a rich tomato sauce for the pasta. The garden yielded a large crop of tomatoes this year. He prefers to eat tomato soup when it is raining.

english_meaning: A large grave or a structure built to hold the dead. A place where someone is buried. It can be simple like a grave or elaborate like a mausoleum. Tombs are often designed to honor or memorialize the dead.
example_sentence: The ancient tomb attracted many tourists. Soldiers were buried in a tomb. The tomb was carved out of stone. We visited the tomb of the poet.

english_meaning: The words carved on a gravestone to commemorate a dead person. A memorial text giving the name, dates, and a short tribute to the deceased. An epitaph engraved on a monument marking a grave.
example_sentence: The tomb stone inscription was worn away by centuries of rain. He read the tomb stone inscription aloud to his children. The tomb stone inscription simply said, 'Beloved teacher and friend'. Historians study old tomb stone inscriptions for family records.

english_meaning: A large, heavy, and often scholarly book. One volume of a multi-volume work. A book, especially a very thick and serious one.
example_sentence: He pulled a heavy tome from the top shelf of the library. The professor has written several tomes on ancient history. She carried a huge legal tome under her arm. The old tome smelled of dust and paper. Reading such a thick tome takes weeks of patience.

english_meaning: The quality or character of a sound. The general mood or attitude expressed in speech or writing. A shade or variety of a color. The condition of firmness in muscles. To give a particular quality or character to something.
example_sentence: His tone of voice was calm and reassuring. The letter had a friendly tone. The walls were painted in soft tones of blue. Regular exercise helps tone your muscles.

english_meaning: To grasp or hold something firmly using tongs. A tool, usually made of metal, with two arms joined at one end (It is used to grip, lift, or turn objects, especially hot items like coal, food, or metal).
example_sentence: She used kitchen tongs to turn the meat on the grill. The blacksmith lifted the hot iron with long tongs. Please tong the ice cubes instead of using your hands. He carefully tonged the burning coal and placed it aside.

english_meaning: The soft movable muscular organ in the mouth used for tasting, swallowing, and speaking. A person's manner or style of speaking. A language spoken by a particular people or nation. A flap of material under the laces of a shoe. To touch or lick something with the tongue.
example_sentence: He burned his tongue on the hot tea. Sindhi is her mother tongue. She has a sharp tongue and often hurts people. The dog tongued the water from the bowl.

english_meaning: Saying something in a way that is not serious, usually joking or ironic, while pretending to be serious. It is used when someone says something that sounds serious but is actually meant as a joke, sarcasm, or irony. The speaker does not fully mean what they are saying and expects the listener to understand the hidden humor.
example_sentence: He said he is the best player in the world, tongue in cheek. She commented tongue in cheek that she loves waking up at 4 a.m. every day. The teacher said, tongue in cheek, that homework is a student’s favorite activity. He was tongue in cheek when he said he enjoys doing all the house chores alone.

english_meaning: A medicinal substance taken to give a feeling of vigor or well-being. Anything that invigorates, refreshes, or restores. Tonic water, a carbonated drink flavored with quinine. Giving a feeling of vigor. In music, the first note of a scale or key.
example_sentence: The doctor prescribed a tonic to help him regain strength. A walk in the fresh air is a wonderful tonic. She ordered gin and tonic at the restaurant. His kind words were a tonic to her tired heart. The song begins on the tonic of the scale.

english_meaning: A metric unit of mass equal to 1,000 kilograms. A large unit used to weigh heavy goods such as grain, coal, or steel. Also known as the metric ton. Informally, a very large quantity of something.
example_sentence: The truck was carrying twenty tonnes of wheat. One tonne is equal to 1,000 kilograms. The factory produces several tonnes of steel every day. They exported thousands of tonnes of rice last year.

english_meaning: Either of the two small masses of soft tissue at the back of the throat on each side. A part of the body's defence system that helps fight infection entering through the mouth and nose. A gland-like structure that often becomes swollen during throat infections.
example_sentence: The child's tonsils were red and swollen. The doctor advised removing his infected tonsils. She had her tonsils out when she was seven. Enlarged tonsils can make breathing difficult at night.

english_meaning: Something that seems so perfect, ideal, or advantageous that it is hard to believe it is real or genuine. It often implies skepticism or suspicion because reality rarely matches such perfection.
example_sentence: The deal seemed too good to be true. Her story was too good to be true. The offer is too good to be true. That job seemed too good to be true.

word: Too many cooks spoil the broth
english_meaning: When too many people try to manage one thing, it fails. When too many people work on the same task, they often create confusion, mistakes and poor results.
example_sentence: The project failed because everyone kept changing the design; too many cooks spoil the broth. When all siblings tried to plan the trip, nothing was finalized, proving too many cooks spoil the broth. The teacher let the whole class edit one essay, but it became confusing, showing too many cooks spoil the broth. The event was poorly organized because too many managers gave instructions; too many cooks spoil the broth.

english_meaning: One of the hard white structures in the mouth used for biting and chewing food. A hard bony growth set in the jaw of humans and animals. A projecting pointed part on a comb, saw, gear, or similar object. Strength or effectiveness given to a rule or law, as in giving teeth to a regulation.
example_sentence: The dentist pulled out his broken tooth. A baby's first tooth usually appears at six months. One tooth of the comb is missing. The new law has real teeth and heavy penalties.

english_meaning: To fight with full power, energy, and determination. It means struggling fiercely and with determination to achieve something or to defend oneself.
example_sentence: He fought tooth and nail to protect his family. They are working tooth and nail to finish the project on time. The two teams competed tooth and nail for the championship. She struggled tooth and nail to achieve her dreams.

english_meaning: Pleasing to the taste; delicious and tasty. Physically attractive or appealing (of a person). Pleasant or agreeable in general.
example_sentence: The chef prepared a toothsome meal for the guests. She ordered a toothsome dessert after dinner. This bakery is famous for its toothsome pastries. He gave her a toothsome smile from across the room. The reviewer described the dish as absolutely toothsome.

english_meaning: Of the highest quality or standard. Excellent and superior compared to others. First-class in ability, performance, or condition. Extremely good or outstanding. Considered among the very best.
example_sentence: She is a top-notch surgeon with years of experience. The hotel offers top-notch service to its guests. He gave a top-notch performance in the play. The company hires only top-notch engineers.

english_meaning: A transparent precious stone, usually yellow or golden brown in colour. A silicate mineral valued as a gem and found in several colours. A deep yellow or golden colour resembling the stone. The birthstone traditionally associated with the month of November.
example_sentence: The ring was set with a large golden topaz. Topaz is often confused with citrine. Her eyes were the colour of pale topaz. Blue topaz has become very popular in modern jewellery.

english_meaning: To fall down suddenly or to cause something to fall because it is not stable. To fall over because of imbalance. To push or cause something to fall. To overthrow a ruler, government, or authority. To collapse or break down after losing support. To defeat someone who is powerful or dominant. To lose stability and drop from an upright position.
example_sentence: The pile of books toppled over. He toppled backwards into the river. He brushed past, toppling her from her stool. The statue of the dictator was toppled (over) by the crowds. The church was prominently involved in the struggle that toppled the dictatorship.

english_meaning: Turned upside down or inverted. In a state of total confusion or disorder. Lacking organization or proper arrangement. Being in a chaotic or extremely messy condition.
example_sentence: The burglars left the entire house topsy-turvy after their search. His life turned topsy-turvy when he suddenly lost his job. The toddler's playroom is always in a topsy-turvy state. We had a topsy-turvy plan that changed completely by the end of the day.

english_meaning: A portable light usually powered by batteries. A stick with burning material at one end used for light or as a weapon. To deliberately set something on fire. A symbol of guidance, learning, or freedom. In some cultures, a source of enlightenment or hope.
example_sentence: He carried a torch through the dark cave. The Olympic torch was lit at the opening ceremony. Vandals torched the abandoned building last night. The teacher is like a torch that guides students.

english_meaning: Extreme suffer especially mental suffering. To make somebody suffer very much. To annoy somebody in a cruel way because of thing it amazing.
example_sentence: She suffered years of mental torment after her son's death. The flies were a terrible torment. He was tormented by feelings of insecurity.

english_meaning: Mentally or physically inactive; lacking energy or alertness. Sluggish and slow-moving. Dormant, as an animal in hibernation. Apathetic and dull in feeling or response. Lacking the vigour needed to act or grow.
example_sentence: The summer heat left everyone feeling torpid by midday. Trade remained torpid throughout the winter months. The bear lay torpid in its den until spring. He gave a torpid reply that showed no real interest.

english_meaning: A state of physical or mental inactivity and sluggishness. A condition of lethargy, dullness, and lack of energy. A state of dormancy in some animals. Apathy or lack of interest in anything.
example_sentence: After the heavy meal, a pleasant torpor settled over him. The bear remained in a state of torpor throughout the winter. The heat of the afternoon filled the town with torpor. She struggled to shake off the mental torpor of grief.

english_meaning: A unit of pressure equal to 1/760 of an atmosphere. A measurement specifically defined as exactly 133·322387415 pascals. A unit commonly used in vacuum physics to represent the pressure exerted by a millimeter of mercury. An absolute scale measurement based on a fixed relation to the standard atmosphere. A physical quantity used in engineering and medicine for measuring blood pressure or gases. A legacy unit of pressure named after the physicist Evangelista Torricelli. A scientific term for gauging the density of particles in a near-vacuum environment.
synonyms: ["Millimeter Of Mercury","Pressure Unit","mmHg","Absolute Pressure","Vacuum Measure","Pascal Equivalent","Barometric Unit","Physics Constant","Physical Measurement","Manometric Unit","Fluid Pressure Unit","Atmospheric Fraction","Scientific Standard","Quantitative Measure"]
example_sentence: The scientist recorded the pressure in the chamber as five Torr. Standard atmospheric pressure is approximately equivalent to seven hundred and sixty Torr. The vacuum pump reduced the internal environment to a very low Torr level. Blood pressure readings are historically related to the same scale used for a Torr measurement.

english_meaning: A strong and fast flow of something, especially water or a large amount of something happening quickly. Torrent refers to a powerful, rushing flow of water such as a stream after heavy rain. It is also used figuratively for a sudden and overwhelming amount of things like words, emotions, criticism, or events that come all at once with force.
example_sentence: Heavy rain turned the narrow stream into a dangerous torrent. She faced a torrent of questions after the announcement. A torrent of emotions swept over him during the farewell. The storm released a torrent of water down the hillside.

english_meaning: Very heavy and fast, usually used for rain. Describes something that falls or flows with great force and in large quantity, especially rain that is intense, continuous, and overwhelming.
example_sentence: Torrential rain flooded the streets within minutes. The match was cancelled due to torrential rainfall. Torrential storms caused serious damage to crops. We were caught in torrential rain on our way home.

english_meaning: Very hot and dry, especially describing weather or climate. Full of intense passion or emotion, especially romantic. Rapid, energetic, or difficult, as in a torrid pace or time. Scorching and parched.
example_sentence: They endured the torrid heat of the desert summer. The novel tells of a torrid love affair. The team had a torrid start to the season. Nothing grows in the torrid zone without irrigation.

english_meaning: A thin, round flatbread made from corn or wheat flour, commonly used in Mexican food. A soft, thin, round flatbread traditionally made from corn dough in Mexican cuisine. In many places, it is also made from wheat flour. It is used to prepare dishes such as tacos, burritos, quesadillas, and wraps. Corn tortillas are older and more traditional, while wheat tortillas are softer and more flexible.
example_sentence: She filled the tortilla with grilled chicken and fresh vegetables. Corn tortillas are commonly used to make tacos. He warmed the tortilla before serving dinner. The restaurant serves homemade flour tortillas.

english_meaning: Full of twists, turns, and bends; not straight. Winding or crooked in shape or path. Excessively lengthy, complex, and difficult to follow. Not direct or straightforward in expression or reasoning. Devious or deceitful in method or intention.
example_sentence: The bus climbed slowly along a tortuous mountain road. His tortuous explanation left everyone more confused than before. The company took a tortuous route to secure the contract. We followed a tortuous path through the narrow valley.

english_meaning: The action or practice of deliberately inflicting severe pain on someone as a punishment or to force them to do something. Great physical or mental suffering. To inflict severe pain on someone. To cause someone to suffer greatly in mind or body.
example_sentence: The prisoners suffered years of torture in the camp. Waiting for the results was pure torture for the students. It is against international law to torture prisoners. The dentist's chair was a real torture for the child. He would not torture an innocent animal.

english_meaning: Having been subjected to severe pain or cruelty. Showing signs of great mental or emotional suffering. Extremely complicated, distorted, or forced (of expressions, arguments, or reasoning).
example_sentence: The tortured prisoners were finally released after months. He wore a tortured expression throughout the interview. The novel describes the tortured mind of its main character. Her explanation felt like a tortured attempt to hide the truth. Many war survivors carry tortured memories for life.

english_meaning: A person who inflicts severe pain or cruelty on others, especially as a punishment or to obtain information. One who deliberately causes suffering.
example_sentence: The torturer was later brought to justice for his crimes. History remembers him as a cruel torturer of prisoners. She wrote a book about her escape from her torturers. The film exposes the identity of the secret torturer. No civilized society should ever protect a torturer.

english_meaning: The act of inflicting severe physical or mental pain on someone. Causing intense suffering. Extremely painful or distressing.
example_sentence: The soldiers were accused of torturing captured civilians. Torturing animals is a serious offence in most countries. The heat during the journey was absolutely torturing. Waiting for his call was a torturing experience for her. Constantly torturing yourself with guilt will not help.

english_meaning: Causing or involving severe physical pain or suffering. Extremely unpleasant, painful, or hard to endure. Relating to torture or cruel treatment. Mentally distressing or agonizing over a long period.
example_sentence: The prisoners endured torturous conditions for many months. Waiting for the results was a torturous experience for the family. He described the injury as a torturous, constant pain. The long march through the desert proved torturous for the soldiers.

english_meaning: To move restlessly from side to side while trying to sleep. To be unable to sleep peacefully because of worry, discomfort, or anxiety. To keep changing position in bed due to a disturbed or troubled mind. To spend a sleepless night due to stress or physical uneasiness. To roll about in bed without being able to rest properly.
example_sentence: He kept tossing and turning all night worrying about the exam. She tossed and turned in bed after hearing the sad news. I could not sleep and tossed and turned till morning. The uncomfortable heat made him toss and turn for hours.

english_meaning: A small child who is just beginning to walk or is still very young. It specifically refers to a toddler or young youngster. It can also mean a very small amount of a liquid, typically a small glass of strong alcohol like rum or whiskey. Additionally, as a verb, it means to add up or total a set of numbers, often followed by 'up'. This term is frequently used in British English to describe both the measurement of spirits and a young person.
example_sentence: The little tot took his first wobbling steps toward his mother. He poured himself a small tot of rum before sitting by the fireplace. The accountant began to tot up the daily expenses on a ledger. Each tot in the nursery was given a colorful toy to play with. We need to tot up the scores to see who won the game.

english_meaning: To walk or move unsteadily as if about to fall. To sway on one’s feet due to weakness, drunkenness, or age. To move with weak and shaky steps. To be on the verge of collapse. An unstable walking motion.
example_sentence: The old man tottered across the road with a stick. The child tottered a few steps and then fell. The tower tottered dangerously in the earthquake. She tottered to bed after the long journey.

english_meaning: To communicate with someone, usually for a short time, in order to check progress, exchange updates, confirm plans, or maintain connection. It is commonly used in professional and informal contexts when people want to reconnect after some time.
example_sentence: I will touch base with you tomorrow about the meeting. Let us touch base next week to review the project progress. She touched base with her manager before submitting the report. We should touch base after the workshop to discuss feedback.

english_meaning: A superstition to wish for luck. Prevent bad luck after saying something positive. Express hope that a good situation will continue. Show humility after talking about success, to avoid appearing overconfident. Protect oneself from the “evil eye” or bad fate.
synonyms: ["Hope for the best","Pray for good luck","Knock on wood"]
example_sentence: Touch wood, everything goes well. I’ve never failed an exam, touch wood. Our team has been winning every match so far, touch wood. She’s never been late to work, touch wood. The weather’s been perfect for our trip, touch wood.

english_meaning: A standard, criterion, or test used to judge the quality or truth of something. Also a stone used for testing precious metals.
example_sentence: They tend to regard grammer as the touchstone of all language performance. Until relatively recently, the Japanese car industry was the touchstone of international success. Perfect service is the touchstone of a fine restaurant.

english_meaning: To arrive or reach a place safely. To land on the ground (aircraft or spacecraft). In American football, it means scoring by carrying or catching the ball in the opponent’s end zone.
example_sentence: Our flight touched down before night. The plane touched down safely after a long flight. The spacecraft touched down on the moon’s surface. He scored a touchdown in the final seconds of the game. We touched down in Karachi at 6 PM.

english_meaning: A person who is physically and emotionally strong. Someone who is very determined and difficult to defeat. A resilient individual who can endure hardship without giving up. A stern or uncompromising person in dealings.
synonyms: ["Resilient Person","Strong Individual","Survivor","Fighter","Determined Person","Hard Nut To Crack","Badass","Unyielding Person","Stalwart","Rugged Individual"]
example_sentence: She survived the harsh winter alone in the cabin because she is a tough cookie. You cannot easily intimidate him since he is known to be a tough cookie in negotiations. Despite all the setbacks, the team captain proved to be a tough cookie. The new manager is a tough cookie who demands strict discipline from everyone.

english_meaning: A problem, situation, or person that is very difficult to deal with, understand, or solve. Something requiring extra effort, skill, or patience to handle.
example_sentence: The case is a tough nut to crack. This math problem is a tough nut to crack. He is a tough nut to crack; he never shares his feelings easily.

english_meaning: The business of providing services for people who travel for pleasure. The activity of travelling to places for holidays and sightseeing. The industry connected with hotels, travel, and holiday attractions. Travel undertaken for recreation as an economic activity.
example_sentence: Tourism brings a large share of income to the region. The government is investing heavily in tourism. Winter tourism has grown rapidly in the northern valleys. The pandemic badly affected international tourism.

english_meaning: A person who travels to a place for pleasure or interest. Someone visiting a country or city on holiday. Relating to travellers or holiday visitors. A visitor who sees the sights of a place.
example_sentence: Thousands of tourists visit the old fort every year. The tourist asked for directions to the museum. This street is full of tourist shops and cafés. Foreign tourists praised the hospitality of the locals.

english_meaning: To make something, especially a person's hair, untidy or messy. It often involves ruffling, tangling, or disheveling the appearance through physical contact. This action is usually associated with a playful or affectionate gesture, such as rubbing a child's head. It can also describe the state of being rumpled or disordered in general. The word implies a soft, haphazard mess rather than destructive damage.
example_sentence: She reached out to playfully tousle her younger brother's hair. The strong wind began to tousle the grass across the open meadow. He woke up with his hair in a tousle after a long night of sleep. The puppy would tousle the rug every time it ran through the room. It is fun to tousle the feathers of the soft toy.

english_meaning: In the direction of a person, place, or thing. Getting nearer to a particular time or point. In relation to or concerning someone or something. For the purpose of helping to achieve or pay for something. Showing a particular attitude or feeling about someone.
example_sentence: She walked slowly towards the gate. The meeting was held towards the end of March. His attitude towards his colleagues has improved. They donated a large sum towards the new hospital.

english_meaning: The wide tube that carries air from the larynx down to the bronchi. The airway commonly called the windpipe. A cartilage-ringed tube that keeps the breathing passage open. The main channel through which air reaches the lungs.
example_sentence: Air travels down the trachea to reach the lungs. The trachea is supported by rings of cartilage. A blocked trachea is a medical emergency. The doctor inserted a tube into the patient's trachea.

english_meaning: A surgical procedure that creates an opening in the windpipe through the neck. An operation performed to help a patient breathe when the airway is blocked. The artificial opening itself, usually kept open with a tube. A treatment often used for patients needing long-term ventilation.
example_sentence: The doctors performed a tracheostomy to secure the patient's airway. He was able to breathe comfortably after the tracheostomy. Nurses clean the tracheostomy tube several times a day. The tracheostomy was closed once he recovered.

english_meaning: A rough path or road, usually beaten by use. A mark or series of marks left by a person, animal, or vehicle. A pair of rails on which trains run. A prepared course for racing or running. A single song or piece on a recording. To follow the trail or movements of someone or something. To monitor the progress or development of something.
example_sentence: We followed a narrow track through the forest. The hunters tracked the deer for hours. The train stopped because of a problem on the track. The third track on the album is my favourite.

english_meaning: A person who follows the trail of people or animals. A device or software that monitors the location, movement, or progress of something. A tool used to record habits, spending, or fitness activity. Someone who hunts by following tracks.
example_sentence: The skilled tracker followed the leopard's footprints for miles. Police placed a GPS tracker on the stolen car. She uses a fitness tracker to count her daily steps. A simple budget tracker helped him control his spending.

english_meaning: The grip of a wheel, tyre, or foot on a surface that prevents slipping. The act of pulling something over a surface. Support, popularity, or progress that an idea, product, or movement begins to gain. A medical treatment in which a steady pull is applied to a limb or muscle.
example_sentence: The tyres lost traction on the icy road. His new idea is finally gaining traction with investors. Good boots give better traction while climbing. The patient's broken leg was placed in traction.

english_meaning: A trade deficit happens when a country imports more goods and services than it exports to other countries. An economic condition in which the total value of a country's imports is greater than the total value of its exports during a specific period. It shows that the country is buying more from foreign countries than it is selling to them. A continuous trade deficit may affect the economy, currency value, industries, and employment.
synonyms: ["Negative trade balance","Import surplus","Trade gap","Unfavorable balance of trade","Economic trade shortfall"]
antonyms: ["Trade surplus","Positive trade balance","Export surplus","Favorable balance of trade"]
example_sentence: Pakistan faced a trade deficit because imports increased rapidly. A large trade deficit can weaken a country's economy over time. The government introduced new policies to reduce the trade deficit. Rising oil imports contributed significantly to the national trade deficit.

english_meaning: To buy or sell something in order to move to a cheaper or smaller item than the one owned before. To exchange a possession for one of lower value, especially a house or car. Of consumers, to switch to less expensive brands or products.
example_sentence: After retirement they decided to trade down to a smaller house. Many shoppers trade down to cheaper brands during a recession. He traded down from a luxury car to a compact model. Families are trading down as household budgets shrink.

english_meaning: A situation in which gaining one benefit requires giving up another. A balance between two desirable but competing things.
example_sentence: There is a trade-off between speed and accuracy. The cheaper model involves a trade-off in durability. Remote work offers flexibility, but the trade-off may be less face-to-face contact. Every design decision includes some trade-off.
